News.title: Trump launches ‘Operation Economic Outcast’ on Iran as he tries to isolate regime with damaging new sanctions
News.content:
DONALD Trump has launched his crushing “Operation Economic Outcast” on Iran by threatening crippling sanctions on any country propping up the regime.

The US president last week vowed to unleash the “MOST CRUSHING ECONOMIC OPERATION EVER TAKEN” to strong-arm Tehran into accepting his peace terms.



Washington has now upped the ante with a new plan to slap severe sanctions on any country maintaining economic ties with the regime.

Iran has meanwhile vowed it will retaliate against any country participating in the US-led isolation campaign.



With the war dragging on to the six-month mark, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced “Operation Economic Outcast” as a “warning shot” to Iran‘s allies.

Bessent said that the US was giving them a chance to “remedy bad behaviour” but stopped short of naming specific countries or laying out a timeline.

“Today, in that same spirit, we are launching an economic onslaught against Iran’s financial connections around the globe,” he said.

“Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone.”

Bessent declined to answer whether the move would target China, which bought 80 per cent of Iran’s ship oil last year.

But he said: “We want to make clear here today that no one is above the reach of US sanctions.



“That if they facilitate transactions and are part of the ecosystem that turns Iranian oil into money, into repression, they will be targeted.”

Bessent said that the US had identified countries who continued to deal with Iran and would set individual deadlines to cut off ties or face sanctions.

He added: “Any entity that facilitates money laundering on behalf of Iran will be removed from the US dollar system. The clock just started ticking.”



Trump, he said, was making direct calls to world leaders to request that they “cease their interactions with the regime”.

Bessent did not elaborate on whether Trump had spoken with Xi Jinping after a successful summit in Beijing last month.

China’s embassy in Washington told reporters: “Regarding the ​Iran issue, sanctions and pressure do not help resolve the problem.

“China calls on the relevant parties to take responsible actions and resolve the issue through political and diplomatic means.”

Xi is set to meet Trump in Washington in late September, but fresh sanctions could sour prospects for extending a deal struck last November to keep Chinese rare earths flowing and cap US tariffs.



Iran brushed the sanctions off with the country’s finance minister saying it was “fully prepared” for them.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Ali Madanizadeh also accused the US of wanting to “wage economic terrorism”.

“We know how to play this game. This time, they should not think our response will be purely defensive and that we will only defend ourselves.”

News.title: Ukraine gives Britain ‘goldmine’ of secret battlefield data to help build AI weapons & protect bases from Russian spies
News.content:
UKRAINE has given Britain access to a treasure trove of top secret battlefield data to develop new AI weapons and protect bases from Russian attacks.

It comes as the UK granted Kyiv the blueprints to Storm Shadow long-range missiles, sparking a furious reproach from Vladimir Putin and his Kremlin warmongers.



Andy Burnham has now struck a deal with Volodymyr Zelensky to use Ukraine‘s coveted Avengers AI Labs, which holds millions of pieces of real-life combat data gathered from the war.

The UK will become the first foreign country to access thousands of cameras and infrared sensors that have tracked Russian tanks, troops, artillery, air defences and drones, creating a “goldmine” for training AI.



The Ukrainian military said its systems are now capable of detecting 70 per cent of all Russian targets after combing through years of data collected throughout the war.

British scientists and tech firms will now be able to use the data to develop cutting-edge defence technology.

And the first system is already about to be deployed at a UK military site to spot protesters and hostile spies trying to gain intelligence.

It turns buried fibre-optic cables into giant AI-powered sensors and could eventually be used to protect airports, prisons, railways and power stations.

Britain will in return give Ukraine access to its universities, researchers and tech firms to help Kyiv develop new battlefield technology.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said: “By combining the UK’s world-leading scientists, engineers and tech companies with Ukraine’s unique battlefield experience and data, we will strengthen both of our nations’ defence and security.”



The deal could also “revolutionise all parts of public life, from air traffic control to train systems,” the Ministry of Defence said.

Until now, British defence companies have relied on Ukrainian drone operations posted online, which offer just a snapshot of drone strikes and surveillance missions.

It comes at a crucial time for the UK, with Moscow orchestrating a series of surveillance operations on European military bases and nuclear sites.



Britain has also been targeted by drones trying to access sensitive facilities with drones launched from its shadow fleet vessels.

The UK and Ukraine are also collaborating on a second project to build low-power AI chips that could create more durable and intelligent drones and robotics.

Burnham hailed the “ground-breaking partnership” as he visited Kyiv on his first foreign trip as Prime Minister.

He said: “Ukraine has become one of the world’s leading innovators in defence technology, forged through courage, ingenuity and the hard lessons of war.”

The PM said the deal will give Britain “the opportunity to develop the technologies of the future, changing lives here in Britain and saving lives on the battlefield in Ukraine.”



It comes as Russia has accused the UK of “participating” in the war and warned that there would be “consequences” over supplying weapons to Ukraine.

Kremlin mouthpiece Dmitry Peskov blasted Britain for “adding fuel to the fire” for giving Zelensky information on the components on Storm Shadow missiles so that Kyiv can manufacture the weapon itself.

But Burnham hit back and said: “Who started the fire? That’s the question, isn’t it?”



Foreign minister Sergei Lavrov said that Russia would target and “destroy” facilities producing the missiles.

It comes amid mounting pressure on Putin’s war machine.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Ukrainian forces have repeatedly pummelled the nation’s equivalent of Amazon and are systemically blasting apart their fuel hubs.

For a third night in a row, Ukrainian drones have blitzed Ozon, Russia’s second-biggest online retailer, in an attempt to bleed Putin‘s war chest dry.

News.title: Council house tenants face the boot if they live in squalor and neglect their gardens, Reform warns
News.content:
COUNCIL house tenants could be given the boot if they live in squalor and fail to maintain their gardens, Reform UK has warned.

Nigel Farage’s party has promised a major shake-up of social housing including building more than 50,000 council homes a year.



But Reform chairman Lee Anderson said hard-up Brits expect council house tenants living in accommodation subsidised by the taxpayer to be left in a “reasonable” state.

He said: “People who live in subsidised housing – paid for, subsidised by the hard-working British taxpayer – what is wrong with expecting them to keep their house to a reasonable standard?”



Mr Anderson warned that councils failing to screen tenants properly was “creating mayhem and disturbances on these brand new housing estates.

He added: “The hard-working British taxpayer, the alarm clock people who get up at five or six o’clock in the morning, go to work and they see the house next door with four foot of weeds, dustbin not been emptied for three weeks, and a waft of weed coming out the window – it’s not acceptable.”



His comments come as Reform unveiled its plans to overhaul social housing in Britain.

Young married couples who work and have children would be moved to the front of the queue as well as veterans.

Mr Farage’s party wanted to revive the Right to Buy policy.

This is channelling an old policy put forward by Margaret Thatcher in the 1980s.



Foreign nationals living in social housing will be evicted within a short-time frame as a Reform government takes power.

News.title: Adult film star and influencer Christian Styles dies aged 29 as heartbroken family pay tribute
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

ADULT STAR GONE Adult film star and influencer Christian Styles dies aged 29 as heartbroken family pay tribute

AN ADULT film star and content creator has died aged 29 following a “sudden and heartbreaking” loss as family and friends pay tribute.

Zachary Jaghab, who boasted over a million followers on his Instagram, died on August 20.



Zachary, whose stage name was Christian Styles, has been remembered as “the sweetest man” following his tragic death.

He was a successful influencer and is survived by his parents and two siblings.



Born and raised in Michigan, Zachary first broke into the adult industry in 2021.

Across his social media he has amassed a large following, particularly on X where he promoted his OnlyFans work.



In an online GoFundMe, a representative for the family said: “This unimaginable loss has left a beautiful Canton family grieving the passing of someone deeply loved.

“As they face the pain of losing Zack, Johnny and Ellen are also carrying their own serious health struggles, including cancer, making this season even more overwhelming.”

People have been quick to flock online posting their tributes to the young man.

One person said: “Rest in peace sweet angel. You were and are so loved.”



Another said: “We will miss you terribly.”

A third said: “Rest in peace Christian. May you find lots of joy and happiness in the everafter.”

A final said: “Christian leaves behind much more than images, videos, or memories.

“He leaves a lasting mark on our community and on everyone who connected with him, followed him, and shared part of his story.”

Zachary’s cause of death is not currently known.

News.title: Horror moment mafia boss is shot dead at point-blank range by assassin after his gang was ‘involved in blood feuds’
News.content:
THIS is the horrifying moment an Israeli mafia don embroiled in “blood feuds” is shot dead at point- blank range.

Arch-criminal Yanis Yushvaev was assassinated as he left a petrol station near Caesarea, a town around 30 miles north of Tel Aviv.



Distressing CCTV footage, which The Sun has chosen not to show in full, sees a gunman wearing a hat, hoodie and glasses casually walk up a short flight of stairs.

Yushvaev, 40, is seen exiting the building flanked by two associates as the assassin pressed up against the glass door.



Moments later, the shooter pulls out a pistol and fires into the back of Yushvaev’s head as the three men have their backs turned.

The crime boss is seen tumbling down the stairs as the gunman flees on foot.



Yushvaev was critically injured and pronounced dead shortly afterwards.

Cops said the killing was criminally motivated and have launched a major manhunt for suspects who they believe fled in a vehicle.



Yushvaev was one of Israel’s most feared gangsters and was repeatedly arrested in connection with shootings, arsons and violent criminal underworld clashes.

Police described him as the leader of an organised crime group associated with Israel’s Caucasus community that was involved in a number of feuds.

A decade ago, Yushvaev was shot and wounded in Hadera, a city just north of Caesarea, but recovered from his injuries and bolstered his influence.



Police accused him of targeting the home of a Hadera businessman and wounding a civilian in shootings last June, but he was released without charge.

Yushvaev’s death comes just six months after he was arrested at Tel Aviv’s Ben Gurion airport on his way back from Moscow.

In that case, intelligence suggested that he had returned with the intention of harming rival gang members, Ynet reported.

He was eventually released due to insufficient evidence.

Yushvaev was indicted in 2021 after threatening to murder a businessman if he didn’t pay a $1.1million (£800,000) debt.



The mafia boss was known to demand “complete loyalty” from his henchmen.

He would “almost never” talk on the phone to evade wiretaps, leading to a police source saying it was frustratingly “hard to convict him”.

Yushvaev’s killing comes as Israel grapples with a growing organised crime problem.

Feuds have increasingly spilled into public arenas, with thirteen attacks reported in just a number of days, according to The Telegraph.

Branches of the popular sushi chain Japanika have recently been targeted with grenades, gunfire and arson attacks in what cops have linked to clashes between the Mosli (Jewish) and Jarushi (Arab) crime families.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Murders are reportedly sharply on the rise, with 309 recorded in Israel last year, a 109 per cent increase on the 148 victims in 2022.

National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir has been criticised for his inaction and denied accusations that he is treating it as an internal Arab problem.

News.title: Lindsay Clancy’s lawyer breaks silence on bombshell mistrial motion – & says medicated, ‘beat up’ mom has ‘no mindset’
News.content:
LINDSAY Clancy has been left struggling as her blockbuster murder trial nears its end, her lawyer has revealed after his dramatic bid to have the case thrown into a mistrial.

Clancy, 36, is accused of murdering her three young children at her Duxbury, Massachusetts home in January 2023, but has pleaded not guilty on the grounds she was suffering from postpartum psychosis.



Her attorney Kevin Reddington spoke exclusively to The U.S. Sun outside Plymouth Superior Court on Monday afternoon, shortly after jurors were sent home early following a dramatic showdown over testimony about Clancy’s Catholic faith.

“Lindsay is, you know, she’s pretty beat up and is used to not having support, and I think it means a lot to her,” Reddington told The U.S. Sun.



Hundreds of people have rallied behind Clancy during the trial, with supporters wearing pink gathering outside the courthouse.

Reddington said he has made sure Clancy knows about the backing she has received.

“I’ve tried to tell her that there’s a lot of people that are behind her and at least recognize the fact that she’s a nice person and was dealt bad by the medical profession,” he said.

Asked how Clancy was coping as the trial moves toward its conclusion, Reddington said, “She doesn’t have a mindset, you know, she just listens and sits there.”



He later said Clancy was “under medication” and “doing okay” while being treated at Tewksbury Hospital.

His comments came just after Reddington asked Judge William Sullivan to declare a mistrial over testimony from the prosecution’s forensic psychologist, Dr Kirk Heilbrun.

The dispute erupted after Heilbrun brought Clancy’s Roman Catholic background and the concept of sin into his testimony while discussing her state of mind surrounding suicide.

Reddington stressed afterward that Heilbrun had not actually used the words “mortal sin” on Monday.

“They didn’t say mortal sin today,” he said outside of court.



“They made reference to the Roman Catholic religion and sin, but they didn’t use the mortal sin analogy today.”

That distinction came after religion had already sparked controversy earlier in the trial, when Clancy’s former mother-in-law was questioned about whether murder was considered a “mortal sin.”

“I believe it was intentional misconduct,” Reddington told Sullivan during arguments outside the jury’s presence.



Sullivan denied the motion but sharply questioned why Clancy’s religion had been raised at all.

“How is any of that proper at this point?” the judge said before deciding to give jurors a forceful instruction to disregard the evidence.

He then told the panel that “the religion that the defendant was raised with” was irrelevant before sending jurors home early on Monday afternoon.

Reddington said afterward that the ruling did not shake his confidence in the jury.

“I knew that Judge Sullivan would exercise his discretion, and he would give a strong instruction if he denied the motion,” he said.



“So that’s what he did.”

Asked whether he feared jurors would struggle to put the religious testimony out of their minds, Reddington said, “No. I have no doubt that the jury will listen to the judge’s instructions and be able to overlook it.”

And when asked outside of court whether the drama had changed his mindset heading toward closing arguments, he replied simply, “Not at all. Nope.”

Still, the veteran defense lawyer refused to predict an outcome.

“It’s a trial. You never know. Up and down. You’re happy. You’re not. Who knows?” he said.



“But yeah, it’s been a good trial. I think the evidence has come out and I feel pretty good about it.”

Asked whether Monday’s religious testimony could eventually provide grounds for an appeal, Reddington said he was focused on avoiding that scenario altogether.

“Well, you have to be found guilty before you do an appeal,” he said. “And I’d rather not have her found guilty.”

The mistrial drama capped an already fiery day in court.

Earlier Monday, Reddington tore into prosecution psychiatrist Dr Avram Mack over his experience and conclusions about Clancy’s mental state.



At one point Mack appeared to smile, prompting the lawyer to snap: “What are you smiling for? This is not funny, sir.”

Judge Sullivan also reprimanded Mack during the tense questioning, telling him, “You don’t really ask a lot of questions. You answer the questions.”

Several jurors were seen shaking their heads and rolling their eyes during parts of Mack’s testimony, while Clancy later appeared to smirk after he was dismissed from the stand.

Heilbrun then took the stand and challenged the defense claim that Clancy was suffering from postpartum psychosis and obeying a command hallucination when she killed Cora, five, Dawson, three, and eight-month-old Callan.

The psychologist testified that her account of hearing a voice for only about 18 minutes was highly unusual and said his assessment suggested “exaggerated or fabricated hallucinations.”



He instead offered a theory of “suicide combined with altruistic filicide,” saying Clancy may have believed her children would suffer if she died and left them behind.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Clancy admits strangling the children on January 24, 2023, but has pleaded not guilty and argues she was not criminally responsible because of her mental illness.

Prosecutors say she understood that what she was doing was wrong.

News.title: Great-gran, 101, arrested for dealing drugs after ‘being found with bags of skunk she was selling to locals’
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

GRANJA DEALER Great-gran, 101, arrested for dealing drugs after ‘being found with bags of skunk she was selling to locals’

A 101-YEAR-OLD great-gran has been arrested for allegedly dealing drugs after she was found “selling bags of skunk”.

Esther Ogunmabo was taken in on Saturday after being caught selling cannabis in Nigeria, the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency said.



The old lady was found carrying “retail sachets of skunk, a strain of cannabis weighing 90 grams, which she claims she sells to locals” according to Femi Babafemi – the agency’s director.

According to officials, Esther began selling the contraband after her local shop was burnt down in a fire.



They also claimed one of her daughters, who lives in Lagos, was the key supplier of the drugs.

It is believed the centenarian would receive a batch of drugs every four days and sell it in smaller quantities to paying customers.



Shortly after being arrested, Esther was bailed and provided with counselling due to her age.

Her daughter has also since been arrested.

The case has quickly caught widespread attention due to the OAP’s age, with some labelling her “Granny Escobar”.

One person said: “Serious Retirement plans.”



Another joked: “Grandma only thought she was selling vegetables.”

A third said: “101 yrs and still hustling them streets.”

A final simply put: “Free Great Grandma.”

The agency claims this is part of a wider crackdown on drugs across the country’s coast.

It claims to have intercepted a wooden boat last Friday, believed to be transporting drugs to Cameroon.



It reports having arrested three individuals onboard and seizing more than 42kg of contraband.

News.title: It is irresponsible for social media giants to allow teens to glory in driving at shocking speeds on wrong side of road
News.content:
Video nasties

SOCIAL media sites have no business making money from allowing teens to glory in driving at shocking speeds on the wrong side of the road.

It is wholly irresponsible for the likes of TikTok to encourage reckless law-breaking with such fatal consequences.

Two brave armed officers — one an Iraq war hero — were killed by a runaway car in Middlesbrough.



Two of the “joyriders” were thugs who previously posted videos of high-speed chases for mindless “likes”. Other social media accounts linked to the car’s passengers show men in balaclavas on motorbikes and speeding cars.



That investigators say there is no evidence of filming in this particular case doesn’t lessen the shattering senselessness of the deaths of PCs Tom Clough and Matthew Blades.

How social media giants respond to public outrage over algorithms that push such violent content will tell us whether they prize profit over responsibility.

Breaking Vlad

ANDY Burnham’s steadfast support of Ukraine might be the most welcome move of his premiership so far.

Providing the blueprints so Kyiv can make its own long-range Storm Shadow missiles will worry Putin, even if they will take time to build.

But Burnham must also realise how much Britain is at risk, too.

So far he has been less than clear over spending plans for our Armed Forces.

It’s no use handing cash to Ukraine while leaving our own defence well short.



Gas blast

BRITAIN’S dash for Net Zero has made our country worse than the economic basket case of Venezuela.

So says Jim Johnson, boss of one of the country’s oldest energy firms Hunting, who says “crazy” Government policies mean he’ll never invest in the UK again.

He said: “The reality is that Britain has become uninvestable. Everything your politicians have done has shown me that we cannot trust them.”

Johnson’s words make for grim reading for Chancellor John Healey, desperate for growth to balance the books.

It’s also another reminder of the folly of smashing our North Sea gas and oil industry with massive taxes.



Free enterprise

ANDY Burnham must understand he will never fix soaring youth unemployment without freeing up businesses to grow.

Labour seems to think only State schemes and subsidies are the answer.

But cutting the sky-high taxes that stop firms hiring youngsters would be faster, cheaper, and far more likely to work.

News.title: More than 70,000 social and affordable homes to be built across England
News.content:
The 22-year-old spent the final months of her pregnancy and the first weeks of her son's life living in a hotel.

She says she has no idea how long she will be expected to stay there but was told it would only be temporary.

"I'm just scared when he gets older, when he starts crawling around, I can't even allow him to crawl in such a place like that because it's so dirty," she says.

While pregnant, Natasha says her room became infested with ants, which she repeatedly reported before eventually being moved into another room.

But her problems didn't end there.

While Natasha has her own bathroom, she shares a kitchen with around 60 other residents. She says the hotel is home to a mix of people, not just mothers and babies, and that she does not always feel safe using the shared space with Zayd.

Natasha describes living there as feeling "like a prison". She says visitors are not allowed, meaning friends and family can not come to help her with her five-week-old boy.

"I just want somewhere peaceful for him and calm. Somewhere nice where I can bring him up," she says.

She is one of the 1.34 million households on social housing waiting lists as of March 2025, the latest government figures.

London will see the largest share of funding, although no figure has been given for how many homes will be built in the capital.

Ministers said Monday's allocation was the first stage of the 10-year programme and more than Â£16bn remains to be allocated outside London.

Housing Secretary Angela Rayner suggested some of the new homes will be built by councils, saying she and the prime minister were "doing everything we can to get councils building once again".

Burnham had previously promised "the biggest council house building programme since the post-war period", and the government said millions extra would be given to councils to support their housebuilding plans and help with expertise.

But the announcement stops short of clarifying how the funding will be split between council homes and those provided by housing associations.

News.title: Lockerbie bombing trial postponed days before it was due to start
News.content:
The trial of a Libyan man over the Lockerbie bombing has been postponed for a third time, after new evidence on the 37-year-old case came to light three days ago.

Jury selection was due to get under way in Washington DC on Wednesday but the BBC understands a new start date has been set for January next year.

Lawyers acting for Abu Agila Mohammad Kheir Al-Marimi said "newly discovered evidence" previously unknown to the defence and prosecutors from the US government emerged on Friday 21 August.

Al-Marimi has denied building the bomb that destroyed Pan Am Flight 103 on December 21, 1988, killing 270 people.

His lawyers told the court: "Constitutional and ethical obligations require the defence to investigate this development."

They said they met Al-Marimi on Sunday and he agreed that they should ask for the postponement.

News.title: Beyond China's humanoid robots, a quieter machine revolution is unfolding
News.content:
"I take a nap and the world changes," says Chen Tianyu.

His world certainly does. The 28-year-old keeps up with the latest technology by spending his spare time in factories that are switching to automation. That way he knows what to prioritise when teaching his class about artificial intelligence (AI) and robotics.

In front of him, around 30 college students are studying code. One of them is typing furiously as his eyes dart from the screen to the robot: "The idea is it will grab that cylindrical piece and move it over there."

A line of industrial robots are waiting to be programmed, and in another part of the classroom, students are trying to develop robotic medical instruments. As he guides them, Chen declares: "If you are not needed by the world of AI and robotics, then you'll definitely be among those eliminated".

For the people in this room, this is a step - or rather a leap - towards a future that China is meticulously building: Xi Jinping's $20bn (Â£14.7bn) plan to put his country at the forefront of innovation and in direct competition with the US.

The evidence is all around them. They are in the Hangzhou Technician Institute, one of several huge, purpose-built vocational schools that want to churn out the next generation of tech-savvy engineers. The campus sits on the outskirts of Hangzhou, a former imperial capital whose futuristic skyline is just the first hint of its role as a global tech hub.

Across the country, there are more than two million robots working in China's factories - which is more than anywhere else - and they are continuing to scale up at extraordinary speed.

News.title: UK drone factories may face attacks from 'unknown sources', says Kremlin adviser
News.content:
Andrei Fedorov, an adviser to the Kremlin, says there might be a "semi-military" response against UK drone factories by "unknown sources" over the sharing military blueprints with Russia.

His comments on BBC Newsnight come as UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham says he plans to travel to the US next month with European leaders to lobby US President Trump on Ukraine's defence needs.

In an interview with Bloomberg, Burnham said, "I'm looking forward to going to New York in September," when the UN General Assembly will meet.

He said that while the details were not "fully confirmed", it is "likely" he will go. The trip would be his first to the US since becoming prime minister in July.

"Leaving today, I'm quite clear what I need to do in the next few weeks," he said following his official visit to Ukraine on Monday, during which he promised to continue pressuring Russia.

The UK has also agreed to hand over blueprints for British-made components for the Scalp missile, a French version of the UK's Storm Shadow cruise missile. The blueprints will allow Ukraine to produce the long-range weapon domestically.

Fedorov, who is Russia's former deputy foreign minister, said Putin was facing "serious" pressure "to undertake certain measures against UK". Asked on BBC Newsnight where the pressure was coming from, Fedorov responded, "public opinion polls, it's coming from journalists, from mass media".

Asked what a "semi-military" response might look like, Fedorov said "it could take the form of something might happen with enterprises, with factories which are producing drones for Ukraine."

"They could be attacked not by Russia, but by from unknown sources," he said.

The comments are in line with those made by Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov on Monday, when he criticised the UK's decision to share the missile blueprints. Peskov said it prevented "even the slightest progress" towards achieving peace.

He told reporters on Monday that the Russian military was already gathering data to locate any missile production sites to destroy them.

"Britain is involved in this war on the side of the Kyiv regime. Britain methodically and regularly adds fuel to the fire," he added.

In response, Burnham said: "Who started the fire? That's the question, isn't it?"

Burnham's visit to Ukraine was his first official international visit. He met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Kyiv and chaired his first meeting of the "coalition of the willing", set up by the UK and France under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.

Burnham has been reaffirming the UK's support for Ukraine in the wake of escalating Russian strikes in recent weeks - including one last week on a shopping centre that killed at least 16 people.

Ukraine has been relying on American supplies of the Patriot interceptor missiles, which are used to combat Russia's ballistic missiles, but stockpiles are running low due to the war in Iran, leaving Ukraine vulnerable to Russian attacks.

Zelensky has said he is hoping to secure 300 patriot missiles ahead of winter, when Russia is likely to increase its attacks on energy infrastructure, as it has done in past years.

In the interview with Bloomberg, Burnham said that he felt "really confident" that the issue was "fixable". But he pointed out that it wasn't only the US who could supply Ukraine with Patriots.

"There are other players who could help in the mix who we have influence with," he said. "It's probably going to be a solution that involves a lot of layers and a lot of negotiation."

In July this year, three weeks after offering Ukraine the right to produce Patriots itself, Trump backtracked, saying, "We have not agreed to that. We're talking about it. But it's a hard thing to give away, that kind of technology."

"These weapons are incredible. We have to be very careful about letting somebody build them," Trump told a cabinet meeting.

In a joint statement after the meeting in Ukraine, Burnham and co-chairs French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the group would aim to strength Kyiv's air defences "as a matter or urgent priority".

They also condemned Moscow's "systemic and escalating strikes against Ukraine's cities, critical infrastructure and civilians" and pledged to "constrain Russia's war chest through sanctions and actions against the "shadow fleet".

In a statement ahead of the visit, Burnham said: "On Ukraine's 35th anniversary of independence, the Ukrainian people should be in no doubt: the UK is behind you today and for as long as it takes.

"I am proud of the contribution our country has made to Ukraine and I want the Ukrainian people to hear it directly from me that our support will not waver. After all, Ukraine's security is our security."

He said the friendship Ukraine shared with the UK would "long outlast Russia's illegal war", adding: "Russia should be in no doubt of our resolve. We will not back down until there is a just and lasting peace."

News.title: The grieving family who says the coroner's courts aren't working
News.content:
Sarah thought she knew what she was getting into when she attended a coroner's court in May 2024 to discuss the death of her second cousin.

Her day job as a murder detective meant she was used to courts, to judges, to legal argument. What she wasn't prepared for was a coroner's court. "I felt like I was on trial," she recalls of her first hearing, in Woking, Surrey. "I remember just feeling completely railroadedâ¦ It [was] far more hostile than I had ever expected."

Her cousin, Daniel Lindsay, died in 2023, aged 41. He had lived at a home in Surrey that specialises in caring for people with learning disabilities. Daniel also had Down Syndrome and type 1 diabetes.

As his death was unexpected, his case was referred to the coroner for an inquest.

What followed was one of the most stressful experiences of Sarah's life. She discovered new details about how her cousin lived, and his cause of death. The family initially thought Daniel died from a heart attack - but over the inquest, they learnt that was wrong. She had expected the process to be emotional; what she didn't predict was just how complex and frustrating it would be, at times leaving her tearful and furious.

Coroners examine deaths that are not straightforward, like unexpected or violent deaths, or those that take place in state custody. Every year, thousands of British families rely on these courts for crucial answers. For many, an inquest provides the key interaction with the arms of the state at a time of trauma.

News.title: Kit Harington joins HBO's Harry Potter series as Gilderoy Lockhart
News.content:
Kit Harington has been tapped to join the highly anticipated Harry Potter TV series as the wizarding world's celebrity-turned-Hogwarts instructor Gilderoy Lockhart, HBO confirmed to the BBC.

Harington is replacing actor Nicholas Hoult who could not film season two of the series due to a scheduling conflict.

Best known for playing Jon Snow for eight seasons in the award-winning series Game of Thrones, Harington also appears in the BBC and HBO financial drama Industry. The casting marks the English actor's third collaboration with the American network and streamer.

Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone is due to premiere on Christmas this year on HBO Max.

Season two will adapt the second book in the series by JK Rowling, The Chamber of Secrets, which chronicle's Potter's second year at the magical school.

"Before we begin year two at Hogwarts, there has been a slight change due to schedule: Kit Harington will be stepping into the role of Gilderoy Lockhart," a story post reads on the official Harry Potter Instagram account.

The new series adaptation of the best-selling books stars newcomer Dominic McLaughlin as the boy wizard, Alastair Stout as his best friend Ron Weasley and Arabella Stanton as the young witch Hermione Granger.

Oscar-nominated actor Jon Lithgow has been cast as Hogwarts headmaster Albus Dumbledore and Nick Frost as gamekeeper Rubeus Hagrid.

News.title: Organised crime arrests as police investigate A66 crash that killed two officers
News.content:
Twelve people have been arrested as part of the investigation into the A66 crash that killed seven people, including two police officers.

Nine men and three women, aged between 19 and 61, have been arrested across Teesside on suspicion of a range of offences including possession of a firearm and being part of an organised crime group.

In the early hours of Saturday, a Volkswagen Passat that had been pursued by police travelled the wrong way down the A66 near Middlesbrough and crashed into an oncoming police car - two PCs and all five Passat occupants died.

Cleveland Police said it was investigating "serious criminal activity that resulted in this fatal incident".

PC Tom Clough, 38, and PC Matthew Blades, 37, died in the crash, as did Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jacob Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, Theo Rae, 17, and 17-year-old Cole Robert Worthy.

Earlier, Cleveland Police released more details of its investigation into the lead-up to the crash and information about the 12 people it had arrested.

The force said:

It received several reports of two vehicles "being driven dangerously" on Saturday morning

The first vehicle, believed to be a Volvo XC60, was seen "ramming properties" in the Middlesbrough area

The second vehicle, a Passat, is believed to have been associated with this activity

Both vehicles were operating with cloned number plates but were picked up by automated number plate recognition technology

The Volvo has been recovered in Middlesbrough

Four of the five people in the Passat had previous convictions

Assistant Chief Constable Wayne Fox said the investigation had been "fast moving and complex".

He said: "The events of that tragic night will have a lasting and profound impact on the Cleveland area and the communities we seek to protect.

"We have a duty to respond to, and thoroughly investigate, the serious criminal activity that resulted in this fatal incident and to bring all those responsible to justice."

News.title: HPV home-testing kits available for women in England who have missed cervical screening
News.content:
Dr Sue Mann, national clinical director for women's health, said: "Offering millions of women an alternative test they can do from the comfort of their own homes will be a game-changer â making it easier than ever for them to get tested.

"There are lots of reasons that may stop women from getting their cervical screening â embarrassment, lack of time or worries about discomfort â and these kits provide a discreet and convenient option we hope will encourage more women to take up the life-saving test."

The kits contain a swab, similar to a long cotton, bud which is used to collect a sample from the vagina.

It is then sent back to the NHS and if high-risk HPV is found, individuals will be invited to book a follow-up cervical screening appointment.

High-risk HPV increases the risk of cervical cancer, but it does not mean a woman will automatically develop it.

Trials of the self-testing in London suggest it could lead to one in 10 women to come forward for screening â boosting uptake by around 400,000 a year.

Other parts of the UK are also looking at introducing self-testing.

Women aged 24 to 64 are invited for cervical screening every five years â or more frequently if HPV is detected.

Through a combination of HPV vaccination, which is offered to teenagers, and improved screening, the NHS is hoping to eliminate cervical cancer by 2040.

The NHS says cervical screening appointments with a clinician is still the best way to prevent cancer â and even if you have missed an appointment you can still come forward for one.

News.title: Briton fighting for Russia killed in Ukraine
News.content:
A British national has been killed in Ukraine while fighting for Russia.

Bradley Townsend is said to have died following an attack by a remote-controlled FPV drone in Ukraine's eastern Donetsk region. His death, on 10 June, is believed to be the first of a British citizen fighting for Russia in the conflict.

The 33-year-old left his home in Barnsley, South Yorkshire, earlier this year after telling his family he was going to Romania, according to the Yorkshire Post, external.

The Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) confirmed it was aware of reports a British national had died in Ukraine, adding it was in contact with his family.

The news emerged as Andy Burnham arrived in Kyiv for his first foreign trip as UK prime minister.

The visit coincides with the 35th anniversary of the country's independence from the Soviet Union.

The government has agreed to hand over blueprints for British-made components for the Scalp missile, a French version of the UK's Storm Shadow cruise missile - allowing Ukraine to produce the weapon domestically.

News.title: Teenager arrested after four viable devices found in security alert
News.content:
A 16-year-old boy has been arrested under the Terrorism Act after a security alert in Omagh, County Tyrone.

Police carried out a planned search on Monday at an address in the Gardenville Avenue.

Police said four viable explosive devices were found and removed from the property for forensic examination.

Nearby residents who had been asked to leave their homes during the alert have since returned.

Det Insp Winters urged the public not to speculate about the incident.

"It's important to stress that, while the suspect has been arrested under the Terrorism Act, our investigation to establish a motive remains very much ongoing."

News.title: Man charged with murder after house fire
News.content:
A man has been charged with murder, attempted murder and arson following a fire in west London that left a woman dead and eight others in need of hospital treatment.

Pawel Kulpa, 34, faces one count of murder, eight counts of attempted murder and one count of arson with intent to endanger life.

The charges come after a fire at a residential address on Berkeley Avenue, Hounslow, at about 01:15 BST on Wednesday, 19 August.

A 48-year-old woman died in hospital while another woman, 40, remains in hospital in a life-threatening condition. Kulpa is due to appear at Willesden Magistrates' Court on Tuesday.

News.title: Prince Harry steps down from African wildlife charity board
News.content:
The Duke of Sussex has stepped down from the board of an African wildlife charity whose rangers had been found to have committed human rights abuses against indigenous people.

A spokesman for Prince Harry confirmed he was stepping down after being president for the charity, African Parks, for six years before becoming a member of its board of directors in 2023, but said he remains a "supporter of its mission".

Last year the organisation admitted human rights abuses were committed by its rangers in Congo-Brazzaville.

Prince Harry's resignation comes shortly after it was announced he was relocating with the Duchess of Sussex, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet from California to the UK.

Prince Harry's spokesman said "the Duke is proud of his 10 years with African Parks and fully supports the ongoing strengthening of its board.

"His commitment to conservation in Africa continues, and he remains a supporter of African Parks' mission."

African Parks manages around 20 national parks and protected areas across 12 countries.

It was subject to an independent human rights investigation into allegations guards managed and paid by the charity had beaten, raped and tortured indigenous people in the Odzala-Kokoua National Park.

The charity said in 2025 it had improved its safeguarding processes both in the Odzala-Kokoua National Park and institutionally.

Announcing a "governance refresh of its board of directors", the charity thanked Prince Harry for his association, saying he had "brought global attention to the urgent need for biodiversity protection for the benefit of people and wildlife, and has contributed greatly to promoting philanthropy for the cause of conservation in Africa".

It added: "The duke remains deeply committed to this cause, and remains a strong supporter of African Parks' work."

The charity's website says Prince Harry served as part of the expert team that helped implement the first phase of the 500 Elephants project, which was "one of the largest and most significant elephant translocations in conservation history".

It saw wildlife experts move elephants from a park in Malawi to help increase population in areas where they have been heavily poached.

Prince Harry has said helping move elephants to safer homes was an "amazing" experience.

The Sussexes are back in the spotlight after the revelation last week they were returning to the UK this month after enrolling their children to start at a British school in September.

No change is expected to the official status of Prince Harry and Meghan and they will remain as private individuals.

Their pending return to the UK has raised questions on their security arrangements.

Last year, Prince Harry lost a legal challenge over the levels of security he and his family are entitled to while in the UK.

It is unclear what provisions will be made for their security once they return to the UK.

The couple's plans while they are in the UK are also unclear.

The BBC learned the Duchess of Sussex was in talks to return to acting with a role in Netflix series The Gentlemen, which would be her first significant acting role since her marriage to Prince Harry.

In early 2020, the Sussexes left the UK and stepped back from their royal duties before settling in California in March that year.

News.title: Snooker champion Graeme Dott guilty of child sex abuse
News.content:
Former world snooker champion Graeme Dott has been found guilty of child sexual abuse.

The 49-year-old denied two charges of lewd and libidinous behaviour towards a girl and a boy between 1993 and 2010.

During a trial, the High Court in Glasgow heard that Dott had exposed himself and inappropriately touched a primary school girl in the 1990s and attacked a young boy between 2006 and 2010.

Lord Harrower told Dott, who won the World Snooker Championship in 2006, he would be sentenced at a separate hearing in Edinburgh on 29 September.

Dott, from Glasgow, covered his face with his hands and shook his head while the verdict was delivered by jurors following a five-day trial.

He previously called the allegations made against him "disgusting".

News.title: Drugs dug up at Creamfields site ahead of festival
News.content:
Huge stashes of illegal drugs have been found buried underground at a festival site days before the event was due to begin.

More than 80,000 music fans will head to Creamfields Festival in Daresbury, Cheshire, from Thursday.

About 204 canisters of nitrous oxide - known as laughing gas - and large bags containing ecstasy, MDMA and ketamine tablets were dug up by police during a pre-event search of the grounds, Cheshire Police said.

Supt Andy Blizard said: "Every year, we counter a number of brazen individuals who think they can outsmart us by concealing drugs from view or burying them at the site months in advance."

"There is a zero-tolerance policy regarding drugs," he said.

News.title: Man charged with manslaughter in burglary case
News.content:
A man has been charged with manslaughter after a 75-year-old woman died following a suspected burglary in north London.

Police were called to Tollington Park in Finsbury Park on the night of 11 August after reports of a burglary.

Rose Smith was taken to hospital, where she died the following day. An 81-year-old man was also taken to hospital and was discharged the next day.

Jeffrey Dean Rose, 46, of Apsley Close, North Harrow, has been charged with manslaughter and aggravated burglary. He is due to appear at Barkingside Magistrates' Court on Tuesday.

He was arrested on Friday, 21 August.

In a statement released earlier on Monday, Smith's family described her as an "outgoing woman" who loved "bingo, going to cafÃ©s with her friends and, above all, spending time with her family".

They described their loss as devastating, adding: "She was the life and soul of every party. She had a wonderful personality, a big heart and a way of bringing laughter and happiness wherever she went.

"We want people to remember Rose for the person she truly was - loving, fun, kind, sociable and full of life."

News.title: Graduate job vacancies drop by almost 50% in a year, survey suggests
News.content:
The number of graduate jobs has fallen almost in half in the past year, according to new figures, as employers cut entry-level roles in favour of AI and battle rising costs.

Jobs website Adzuna said it had just 8,383 graduate vacancies listed in July, down from 15,397 at the same point last year.

Adzuna also found competition among job seekers across all levels is rising, with an average of 2.14 job seekers per vacancy in July, up from 1.93 a year earlier.

However, some have said the data might not be reflective of the whole graduate job market and may instead suggest a shift in the way the roles are advertised.

Businesses have said employer national insurance and minimum wage hikes have made hiring more expensive, particularly for junior staff.

The number of graduate vacancies listed hit its lowest level since Adzuna started recording such data in 2016. The firm pointed to a peak for graduate roles in 2017, when it had more than 55,800 listed on its website. That is more than six times the number of roles listed on the site in July.

Andrew Hunter, the co-founder of Adzuna, said the figures show "employers still haven't found a reason to open up hiring" for recent graduates.

But graduate jobs expert Charlie Ball said the numbers might not be as bad for graduates as they first appear.

He said they could instead suggest that firms are advertising fewer roles specifically for graduates, even if the roles themselves still exist and end up being filled by graduates.

From his experience in the sector, Ball said the graduate market has "not collapsed" but added: "We know the graduate jobs market is weak. We know it's not in great shape."

Official figures show the UK's youth unemployment rate - which covers 16-to-24-year-olds - was 16.2% in the three months to March 2026. The number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) is now over one million.

Young people have told BBC News previously they have applied for hundreds of jobs before even receiving a response.

They also expressed frustration at the growing number of employers using AI to screen applications.

Former government minister Alan Milburn is leading a major review of the youth unemployment crisis. He has previously said the number of entry-level jobs is shrinking, as is the number of part-time jobs traditionally filled by teenagers and students.

The Adzuna data also showed vacancies for jobs in travel, teaching and construction rose in recent weeks.

But sectors including healthcare, nursing, hospitality and logistics posted fewer vacancies.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham recently changed the rules for public contracts so that companies bidding for them have to show how they will create jobs and training opportunities.

A government spokesperson said on Monday: "The latest figures show there are 253,000 more people in work than this time last year with unemployment continuing to fall.

"We are determined to go further to restore opportunity for young people through our Â£2.5bn youth employment package which will deliver almost one million opportunities to earn or learn."

Jimmy Kimmel says he’s weighing whether to retire from his ABC late-night show but is afraid he will come to regret it, while his wife wants him to carry on because his work is “incredibly important right now”.

Asked if he feared looking back after ending Jimmy Kimmel Live! and wondering why he stopped, he told Dax Shepard on the Armchair Expert podcast: “I do. I’ve that. I know people who’ve been in that situation. It’s funny. People make a big show of like, ‘I am done and I am tired doing this’, and then they make a lesser comeback trying to do the same thing. And that’s always a bummer. And I always look at that and go, ‘Oh, is that going to be me?’”

Kimmel, 58, has hosted Jimmy Kimmel Live! since 2003, making him the longest-tenured host of the current crop of American late-night TV shows.

His contract runs through May 2027.

Kimmel agreed a one-year extension with Disney, which owns ABC, in December 2025, about three months after the network suspended his show over his comments about the murder of conservative activist Charlie Kirk. The suspension was reversed six days later, with Disney saying that it had held “thoughtful conversations” with Kimmel.

open image in gallery Molly McNearney, Kimmel’s wife of 13 years and his show’s co-head writer and executive producer, says she’s conflicted about what Kimmel should do ( AFP/Getty )

Kimmel imagined how his younger self would react to the idea of giving up a job he was once thrilled to be in.

“Do you ever think to yourself, ‘How would I explain this to me at 25 years old, just giving up, just letting it go?’ I know that 25-year-old me will be like, ‘Are you crazy?’ I would have just been so excited to work at a place that had a snack table that was free.”

Molly McNearney, Kimmel’s wife of 13 years and his show’s co-head writer and executive producer, said she was conflicted about what Kimmel should do.

“It definitely appeals to me for the nervous system of the household. I also feel like Jimmy has like a fly rod in one hand and like a torch in the other right now. It is like he deserves to go out there and just be on the river and relax, but I also want him to keep fighting,” she told Shepard.

McNearney said that she felt a “sense of desire to not quit” because she believed Kimmel’s work was “incredibly important right now”.

“And yes, I know we’re doing it in a vacuum but I think it’s giving people a feeling of their voices being heard, and I think it’s important,” she said.

“But as his wife, I really would like him to be able to not do this show anymore so he could relax.”

She would be happy, McNearney said, for the show to end “in a great way”.

open image in gallery The uncertainty around late-night television has been heightened by the cancellation of Stephen Colbert’s The Late Show , which ended its run on 21 May after 11 years ( Getty )

However, Kimmel was certain that ending his show would not mean stopping work altogether. “It depends on what you mean by retirement,” he said.

“I’m never going to stop doing things. So, it’s just a different scenario.”

In June, Kimmel told Vulture that things were “tumultuous” after his contract extension.

“It’s important to me to be responsible,” he said on leaving, adding that he “could go out in a blaze of glory and get a lot of applause for it, but it would be a very selfish thing to do”.

The uncertainty around late-night television has been heightened by the cancellation of Stephen Colbert’s The Late Show, which ended its run on 21 May after 11 years.

Kimmel told Vulture that he felt “a little bit defeated” by the decision. “In a lot of ways, I feel like I’m looking at my own future,” he said.

Russ Abbot, who was once one of the BBC’s biggest stars, has opened up about leaving showbiz behind – saying his brand of comedy fell out of fashion when “alternative” comics and “political correctness came in”.

The retired comedian, 78, first rose to fame as a singer and drummer in British comedy show band, the Black Abbots, before he moved into TV presenting, hosting Russ Abbot’s Madhouse and The Russ Abbot Show for the BBC in the Eighties.

His last TV role was in BBC comedy Boomers with Alison Steadman, Philip Jackson, and June Whitfield. When the show was cancelled after two seasons in 2016, he officially retired and moved to Portugal.

open image in gallery Russ Abbot with his wife Patricia ( Getty )

Speaking about leaving show business, Abbot – who was born Russell Allan Roberts – told The Guardian that while he was disappointed when Boomers was cancelled, it isn’t true that he was embittered by the comedy landscape changing and that he wasn’t being offered any “straight roles”. He actually chose to leave the industry as his manager was retiring and he “thought it was a good time to call it quits and spend more time with [wife] Trish”, according to the publication.

“I’ve seen something on YouTube saying ‘The tragedy of Russ Abbot’ and ‘He’s run away to Portugal’,” he said. “I’ve had a wonderful career. Wonderful!”

Although he did note that his brand of sketch comedy fell by the wayside in the Nineties when “new wave” comedy came in.

“Alternative comedy. I thought, alternative comedy? What’s it alternative to? If the thing’s funny, it’s funny,” he said. “Political correctness came in, and you can’t laugh at each other and you can’t laugh at yourself.

“At the same time, a lot of comedy started going blue and I think: I’m not going down that road.”

Abbot now splits his time between Barbados and the Algarve with his wife Patricia, whom he married in 1967. The couple share four children.

open image in gallery Russ Abbot with Philip Jackson, James Smith and Nigel Planer in ‘Boomers’ ( BBC )

Abbot joined the cast of BBC One’s Last of the Summer Wine in 2008, taking on the role of Luther “Hobbo” Hobdyke in the last few series before its cancellation in 2010. He also appeared in Hotel Babylon, Casualty, The Sarah Jane Adventures, and The Last Detective.

In the Eighties, Abbot briefly launched a pop career, releasing the single “Atmosphere” in 1987. The track made it to number seven in the British music charts and in 2020, a campaign was launched by two university students to make it Christmas number one, with the song getting airtime on BBC Radio Nottingham.

A British man has died fighting for Russia after being killed in a drone attack in Ukraine, according to a report.

Bradley Townsend, 33, from Barnsley in South Yorkshire, is reported to be the first UK national killed fighting for President Vladimir Putin.

According to LBC, the former fisherman travelled to Moscow in April where he met other British pro-Russian fighters Aiden Minnis and Ben Stimson who are thought to have recruited him online.

He was killed in a “storm operation” on 10 June, according to a Russia-linked social media account seen by LBC.

Townsend was described as a “warrior in a holy war” who had “sacrificed his life for the cause” by the account.

The Independent understands that the FCDO is aware of reports of a British national that has died in Ukraine and are in contact with his family. The foreign office advises against all travel to Russia and its ability to provide consular support in these circumstances is severely limited.

Bradley Townsend ( YouTube )

Tributes posted by pro-Russian accounts on social media refer to Townsend by his callsign “Badger”. “Ultimately, he sacrificed his life for our cause,” wrote one person based in Russia, according to his account. “His service was brief but he blazed the brightest star.”

In a video with Minnis about the mission, he said: “I’m just a normal working class lad from Yorkshire. I came with the idea that I probably wouldn’t be able to go home. I’d definitely get persecuted if I went back.

“But this was my own decision, I wasn’t pushed into anything. I’m not here for a suicide mission, but I understand that’s what can happen.”

People who knew Townsend told The Sun earlier this year that he had informed his family he would be travelling to Romania. They were said to be distraught when they learned that he had opted to fight for Moscow.

Others who said they knew him on social media said that he had struggled with addiction in previous years. Previous reports had suggested that he may have been groomed into the action online.

In response to reports that Townsend had travelled abroad in support of Russia, the UK prime minister’s official spokesperson told media at the time: “We stand steadfast in support of Ukraine. That support has not wavered in the face of ongoing attacks in the Middle East - that’s where our focus is and where everyone’s focus should be.”

Russia has been criticised for the treatment of its soldiers, with those who have escaped describing harrowing “meat-storms”, a tactic that is part of Russia’s “meat grinder” strategy, sending waves of men to wear down Ukrainian forces.

A report last month suggested that soldiers were lasting an average of 20 minutes when they reach the frontline due to drone attacks.

Putin’s military has suffered 1.4 million casualties on the battlefield including an estimated 450,000 deaths since February 2022, according to the Centre for Strategic and International Studies.

Kemi Badenoch “had no respect” for former Conservative prime minister Rishi Sunak and secretly tried to bring him down before the last general election, a new book has claimed.

Ms Badenoch, who succeeded Mr Sunak as Tory leader after the 2024 election, thought he was “rude to her” and wanted to “take him out without being seen to wield the knife”. And, says the book, her disloyal antics contributed to the scale of the Tory election defeat.

They are among the dramatic claims made in a new book about Mr Sunak by Britain’s leading political biographer Sir Anthony Seldon, which is being serialised in The Independent.

Seldon says relations between Mr Sunak and Ms Badenoch had never been warm.

He claims she was covertly involved in a failed bid to replace Sunak in No 10 in 2023 – the year before the election – around the time his government was rocked by cabinet resignations over immigration.

According to Seldon, after meeting Ms Badenoch to reject her call for tougher immigration laws as demanded by rebel Tories, furious Mr Sunak claimed they wanted to provoke him into telling them to “f*** off”, as an excuse to make Tory divisions even worse.

open image in gallery Insiders say Badenoch thought Sunak was ‘rude to her’ ( House of Commons )

Seldon’s book, Sunak at 10: The Last Conservative PM? says Ms Badenoch, who was at the time business secretary, backed dissident Tory MPs defying Mr Sunak because, according to one source, “Kemi did not respect Rishi – she thought he was rude to her.”

She told others conspiring against Mr Sunak over immigration that if they got enough Tory MPs to support them she would give him an “ultimatum” – if he refused to back down she would resign from the cabinet in protest, writes Seldon.

“Some plotters were more bullish, insisting she had promised she would ‘take him out’,” he adds.

Ms Badenoch and her team had been “mulling over” triggering a cabinet mutiny against Mr Sunak to force him out since Robert Jenrick, who has since defected to Reform, resigned from the cabinet in December 2023, states Seldon.

She phoned several cabinet ministers asking them “if anyone was interested in changing the captain”.

Her main worry was not Mr Sunak’s fate, but her desire “to avoid the image of wielding the knife”.

Seldon says he was informed by one of Mr Sunak’s cabinet ministers: “Kemi was not well behaved. Her team were agitating.”

An unnamed Tory MP, who is current member of Ms Badenoch’s front bench, told Seldon she was “a menace who orchestrated trouble in the cabinet” when Mr Sunak was struggling to make his mark in No 10.

open image in gallery Insiders say Badenoch had been ‘mulling over’ triggering a cabinet mutiny against Sunak ( AFP/Getty )

Former Tory MP Danny Kruger, who defected to Reform last year, told Seldon that Ms Badenoch “definitely wanted it [to oust Sunak from No 10 and replace him] but was concerned about being a fag-end prime minister”.

The reason Ms Badenoch eventually decided against challenging Mr Sunak before the July 2024 election had nothing to do with loyalty, argues Seldon.

It was because it was too close to polling day – and she thought she would be blamed for the near certain defeat.

Seldon argues that hostility towards Mr Sunak, fomented by Ms Badenoch and other Tories, did indeed play a part in Labour’s landslide victory.

Seldon says he was told by an insider that Ms Badenoch “was actively looking at bringing Sunak down, constructing imaginary cabinets and offering jobs”.

Mr Sunak talked her out of it and Ms Badenoch “kept her powder dry”.

The book suggests another reason Ms Badenoch backed away from challenging Mr Sunak was not out of loyalty to him – she feared if she did force him out, the Tory crown would be “snatched” from her by cabinet rival Penny Mourdant.

The machinations provoked the usually mild-mannered Mr Sunak to rage against what he called “attention-seeking” rebel Conservatives.

Seldon says Mr Sunak told his aides: “They probably want me to tell them to f*** off so they can pontificate, but I have a country to run. I’m not going to rise to the bait!”

Seldon adds: “The price of all their unrest… as Sunak foresaw, was to depress the party’s voting support as the electorate was sick of Tory infighting.”

Ms Badenoch has always strong denied being disloyal to Sunak.

Extracted from ‘Sunak at 10: The Last Conservative Prime Minister?’ by Anthony Seldon and Tom Egerton, Atlantic Books. On sale 27 August, hardback, £25

News.title: My quest to the most northerly point of the British Isles: A journey around the ‘island above all others’
News.content:

I spend perhaps an unhealthy amount of time staring at the Maps app on my phone, zooming into remote roads, tiny islands, or the middle of vast plains peppered with isolated buildings. One place I always come back to – via satellite image, that is – is the Shetland Islands, or more specifically, Out Stack, a small skerry in the North Atlantic Ocean marking the northerly point of the British Isles. There’s just something so satisfying about an endpoint, an extreme boundary, that keeps piquing my curiosity during my late-night virtual explorations.

So when I found myself this summer standing on the cliffs of Shetland’s Hermaness National Nature Reserve, looking directly out at the uninhabited rocky islet that poses as the final full stop of Britain, I finally understood why Romantic poets found our country’s nature so powerfully awe-inspiring. Other walkers we chatted to along the cliffs also shared these feelings; we were all harbouring a triumphant secret that day about what it's like to be the most northerly people in the country.

Getting to this viewpoint on the cliff’s edge takes just over an hour on a moderate hike across Hermaness, found at the tip of Britain’s northernmost inhabited island, Unst. The trail up the cliff was an exciting quest, but so too was the pilgrimage that involved two London Tubes, one train, two flights, two small ferries, a car ride and then the hike to what arguably is one of the UK’s most magnificent viewpoints. We sat for a good hour watching the Atlantic waves crash onto Out Stack with nothing but a vast stretch of sea reaching out to the horizon. As the last landmass any traveller would encounter before reaching the North Pole if they sailed directly north, it is not an exaggeration to say that I felt I was perched on the edge of the world.

open image in gallery Muckle Flugga lighthouse (L) and Out Stack, the northernmost point in the British Isles (R) ( Amelia Neath/The Independent )

Spectacular as it was, I soon came to realise that my hyperfocus on Out Stack had almost made me miss out on what the rest of the island had to offer. The previous day, I arrived on Unst using one of Shetland’s inter-island ferries and met with two women who have helped transform the island’s visitor experience. Jane Macaulay and Sharyn Emslie are part of Wild Skies, a team of locals who have created trails around Unst that bring people to some of the island's most outstanding locations to witness the beautiful northern latitude skies, as well as interesting historical points.

“The trails are a celebration of natural heritage,” Jane explained. “Unst has a huge amount to offer and people can come and do whatever they like.” She said visitors also come to the island as it is one of the richest Viking heritage areas in Europe, with over 60 longhouses uncovered in the fields from when Shetland was under Norse rule.



You can’t drive a minute without stumbling on another piece of history. The remains of traditional crofthouses are just as frequent as Unst’s inhabited homes, many of which belonged to the ancestors of current residents who just one day stepped out the door and never came back when electricity was introduced to the island. It was mind-blowing to see a place in the UK which shows the passage of time in such a tangible way.

open image in gallery Traditional croft houses on Unst ( Amelia Neath/The Independent )

“It's also a geologist's dream,” Jane continued. “There's an ophiolite, which was the sea crust 420 million years ago, pushed up by the tectonic plates when the continents were moving towards each other.” Not forgetting bird enthusiasts – Unst is a haven for camera-ready colonies of gannets and puffins bobbing about on the sea cliffs.

After snacking on caramel wafers and sipping from coffee flasks during a picnic inside Skidbladner, a full-size replica of the ninth-century Viking Gokstad ship, we set off to tick off some Wild Skies stops, each with wooden posts that give snippets of information, or play poetry, local dialect and music audios. On our way up to one stop, we tracked across the Keen of Hamar nature reserve, a barren desert of serpentine rock that came from the ophiolite crust. Our eyes were glued to the ground until we found dainty Edmondston’s Chickweed, an endemic wildflower found nowhere else in the world.

open image in gallery Sharyn, Amelia and Jane on the Keen of Hamar ( Amelia Neath/The Independent )

At the top, there was an almost uninterrupted view of the sky and the horizon, which we took in while listening to traditional fiddle tunes from the Wild Skies post. Due to Unst’s location and lack of light pollution, these stops give visitors the best possible views of the Northern Lights in the winter months. In the summer, they offer the chance to experience the Simmer Dim, where the sun remains in the sky for around 18 hours on the longest days, and even when it does dip below the horizon, the twilight sky remains a bright milky colour.



We couldn’t leave Unst without ticking off some of the “most northerly in Britain” things to do. We posted cards in the most northerly post box, before driving to Skaw, Britain’s northernmost beach, where there is a clear view of the Saxa Vord spaceport that is soon due to test rocket launches — a project that has divided local opinion over environmental concerns versus economic benefits for the community. Then a quick Tennet’s pint at Balta Light, the most northerly pub, before dinner at the recently opened furthest north restaurant, Da Otter’s Neuk for fish and chips.

open image in gallery Saxa Vord, as seen from Skaw, Britain's northernmost beach ( Amelia Neath/The Independent )

That night we sauntered over to the Bathasound Town Hall for a community event hosted by university students from St Andrews, which was followed by ceilidh dancing. Reluctant to join in at first due to our shoddy dancing skills, we were soon linking arms and skipping around with locals and other visitors as traditional tunes floated from the fiddles and accordions of the Unst Music and Dance Band. Unst is one of the most remote places to live in the UK, but strong community connections are all the better for it.

open image in gallery Balta Light, the northernmost pub in the British Isles ( Amelia Neath/The Independent )

“There's such a close, tight-knit community,” Sharyn had said earlier that day. “Everyone's so helpful, and they get things done here. They don't just talk about doing stuff. They really do it.”

“It's something to do with our geography because we're at the end of the line,” added Jane. “It's to do with pride of place and identity and belonging, and people are very strong about their connection with the land and the sea.”



Seeking my own connection with this extreme land, the next morning we set off to Hermaness for our hike. It was misty as we walked along a boardwalk over the peaty bogs, then we were guided by wooden posts as the ground got firmer. The mist was not moving, and as we ascended the hill I started to feel a slight dread that we had come all this way just to stare at a veil of fog.

open image in gallery After the fog cleared, it was a beautiful day at Hermaness National Nature Reserve ( Amelia Neath/The Independent )

Luckily for us, what happened next was akin to some sort of cinematic suspense motif. As we continued the walk along the cliff edge, we first saw what we thought was water, and then, suddenly, a faint outline of rocks emerged. Next, the UK’s most northerly lighthouse, Muckle Flugga, began to appear before us on an islet of rocks, then I suddenly caught sight of Out Stack. There it was. I couldn't believe it. We jumped for joy, and admittedly, I shed a few tears. Here I realised how Unst lived up to its nickname in more ways than its geographical location - “the island above all others”.



How to do it

Flights to and from Sumburgh airport on Shetland are available with Loganair from most major Scottish airports. NorthLink also runs overnight ferries between Lerwick and Aberdeen, which is cheaper than flying and allows you to bring a vehicle.

We hired a car with Bolts Car Hire that we picked up from the airport and dropped off in the ferry port. While there are some buses on Shetland, I’d advise having a car to get to places quickly. Watch out for sheep on the roads as they like to perch on the tarmac.

We pre-booked inter-island ferries sailings, which only last around five to 10 minutes, as they can get busy. To get to Unst, we took the ferry from Toft (on the mainland) to Ulsta (on the island of Yell), we then drove across Yell to the Gutcher ferry terminal, and caught another ferry to Belmont on Unst. Be aware that ferries are often delayed or cancelled.

Where to stay

We stayed at Winwick House in Balthasound, the home of Unst local Willie, who transformed his spare rooms into guest accommodation with en-suites. He offers a cooked breakfast in his dining room and told us stories of island life as we tucked in.

Amelia was a guest of Promote Shetland and VisitScotland.

News.title: We can’t let ‘body shaming’ stop us calling out the terrifying skinnification of celebrity culture
News.content:
