World.title: Greece seeks to cash in on Odyssey ‘hype’
World.content:
Perhaps most crucially for the Greek economy, officials are now seeking to translate that renewed interest in the Cyclops and man-eating Laestrygonians into tourist revenue.

The Greek National Tourism Organization organized a press trip to Odysseus’ home island of Ithaca — to which he struggled to return after the Trojan War — that resulted in a 162-page publication by Le Figaro magazine, titled “In the Footsteps of Odysseus.”

The Peloponnese region is creating a thematic travel program, called “The Odyssey Route — Homer’s Peloponnese,” which will likely be ready by November. The regional authorities are currently designing the signs and website that will guide tourists.

“The aim is to link Homer’s epics and the film production, connect the production locations with other locations in the Peloponnese, associated with the myth itself,” said the deputy regional governor for tourism in the Peloponnese region, Thanasis Michelongonas.

Such locations include the islet of Cranae, where, according to legend, Paris of Troy took Helen for their first night after abducting her from Sparta. Or the tiny islet of Pefnos, where Zeus took refuge in the form of a swan and seduced (or assaulted) Leda, who subsequently gave birth to the famous egg from which Helen of Troy hatched.

“We want to capitalize on the hype created,” Michelongonas said. “Expectations are probably greater than reality. Of course, that doesn’t change the fact that we’ve received a great deal of publicity, worth millions and it’s up to us to make the most of it.”

World.title: Trump’s Arctic saber-rattling boosts Iceland’s pro-EU campaign
World.content:
With Russia and China both pushing to secure Arctic resources, questions about global alliances are becoming increasingly vital to the 270,000 Icelandic voters heading to the ballot boxes across the weather-beaten volcanic island.

Reykjavík’s former mayor, Dagur Eggertsson, a prominent figure in the pro-EU “Yes” campaign, said that Trump’s threats to Greenland were weighing on voters’ minds and sparking debate about Iceland’s strategic position.

“This issue is not settled,” the Social Democrat member of parliament said of U.S. ambitions to control Greenland, whose coast is less than 300 kilometers from Iceland. “Trump has been quite outspoken, not only last year, but again and again. This is something that people on the streets think about.”

While Trump has rowed back on some of his more bellicose posturing to seize Greenland at the beginning of the year, he still insisted at a NATO summit in Ankara in July that the territory “should be controlled by the United States, not by Denmark.”

Facing that kind of regional tension, Eggertsson, who also chairs Iceland’s delegation to the NATO Parliamentary Assembly, echoed Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney in mapping out the stakes: “Small and middle powers need to stick together.”

In the case of Iceland, he insisted this meant closer ties to Europe. “The matter is more urgent now than before,” he said.

World.title: Saudi Arabia to invest €6B in massive French theme park site
World.content:
This article is also available in: French

The massive project is being built on the former site of Mirapolis, a massive theme park that has been shuttered since 1991. | Patrick Hertzog/AFP via Getty Images

PARIS — Saudi Arabia will spend €6 billion to build a massive entertainment complex boasting three theme parks near Paris, French President Emmanuel Macron said.

Macron and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman signed an agreement formalizing the deal to build what the French leader called “a new global destination” at the Elysée Palace on Monday. It is expected to create 22,000 jobs, Macron said.

The massive project, which Macron said will also include hotels, catering facilities and housing for young workers and students, is being built on the former site of Mirapolis, a massive theme park that has been shuttered since 1991. Among the parks being built is one centered around manga, as POLITICO reported earlier this month.

World.title: How a 17th-century Irish law is shielding Big Tech from class actions in Europe
World.content:
At the same time, the EU's landmark 2020 Representative Actions Directive that enabled class action across Europe stipulates that these cases can only be filed by non-profits, who tend to rely on outside funding to cover the huge costs of taking on Big Tech.

Ireland is the only EU country with such a restriction — a rule rooted in legal concepts dating back to the Middle Ages that were written into Irish law in 1634. And it is holding back rights activists from raising funds to mount new, big cases against tech giants.

Five non-profits are registered in Ireland to take class actions under the new directive, three of which (the Irish Council for Civil Liberties, Noyb and Digital Rights Ireland) have a track record of taking on Big Tech.

So far, only one class-action case has been lodged: the Irish Council for Civil Liberties filed the first such case in Ireland last year against Microsoft over its online advertising system. They were able to fund it through their general budget, which comes from donations and philanthropic grants.

“To take complex litigation like this in Ireland costs at least €1 million in the first instance. We cannot take multiple cases unless the State allows us to raise the necessary funds,” said Johnny Ryan, director of the Irish Council for Civil Liberties' enforcement unit, pointing out the organization doesn't have the resources to launch more challenges.

He characterized the EU's requirement that non-profits lead class action cases and the Irish law's ban on raising outside funding as the “fatal contradiction” for Europeans seeking compensation from Big Tech.

World.title: Mirapolis : l’Elysée et l’Arabie saoudite officialisent un investissement à six milliards
World.content:
Le démarrage du chantier, situé à Courdimanche (Val-d’Oise), n'a pas encore de date officielle. | Patrick Hertzog/AFP via Getty Images

Trois parcs d’attractions vont sortir de terre sur le site de l’ancien parc à thème de Mirapolis.

PARIS — Mirapolis, c’est désormais signé. Près d’un mois après les révélations de POLITICO sur le projet de résurrection de l’ancien parc d’attractions du Val-d'Oise grâce à des capitaux saoudiens, l’Elysée et Riyad ont signé lundi un accord actant ce méga-investissement, lors de la visite à Paris du prince héritier Mohammed ben Salmane.

L’investissement prévisionnel s’élève à 6 milliards d’euros et prévoit la création de 22 000 emplois, selon les éléments communiqués par l’Elysée à l’issue de la cérémonie de signature. Il comprend le développement de trois parcs à thème et de loisirs, accompagnés de services d’hébergement et de restauration, ainsi que la construction de logements, notamment destinés aux jeunes actifs et aux étudiants.

“Une annonce hors normes (...) du jamais vu depuis Disneyland Paris”, s’est réjoui Emmanuel Macron sur X.

World.title: Burnham ups the ante in fight against Russia — and leaves Merz in the shade
World.content:
The trip gave Burnham his first chance to show his commitment to the Coalition of the Willing — a grouping of Ukraine’s allies championed by his predecessor, Keir Starmer — as he co-chaired its latest meeting with French President Emmanuel Macron.

Burnham was allowed to enjoy the limelight as the only E3 leader to attend the session in person, with Macron hosting Saudi Arabia’s Mohammed bin Salman and Merz attending to a domestic crisis.

Sitting alongside Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Burnham said Russian threats against the U.K. will not deter him and show British assistance is having an impact.

The British PM said: “It’s clear Russia is running out of options so Putin is now hoping he can win through a campaign of terror using ballistic missiles against Ukrainian civilians.”

The new agreement on missiles is unlikely to have any short-term impact on Russia’s war against Ukraine, but represents a gradual shift in the U.K.’s posture towards deeper cooperation with Kyiv and sharper confrontation with Moscow.

Burnham has also signed a deal allowing the U.K. to access Ukraine’s Avengers AI lab, allowing both sides to collaborate on the development of new battlefield technology, using sensors and cameras to capture and collate information on objects such as tanks, artillery, air defense systems and drone targets.

World.title: Moving to the countryside for a home: young people flee city housing costs
World.content:
Spain has a housing problem that has been getting worse for years and has already changed the way its young people think about their future. Buying a flat in Madrid, Barcelona or Málaga is, for most people under 40, a mission impossible. Renting on your own is no more viable: those who move out alone devote on average 98.7% of their salary to housing.

 

The result is a generation that feels trapped: only 14.5% of young people aged 16 to 29 have managed to move out, and the average age for leaving the parental home has risen to 30, compared with 26 in the European Union. According to data from the National Statistics Institute (INE), 44.3% of young people aged 26 to 34 were still living in the family home in 2025.

The previous generation was able to buy flats, cars and even second homes on an average wage. Today that is a pipe dream. With a shortage of housing and strong demand, purchase prices rose by 14.7% year on year in the past 12 months and rents by 10.9%, according to Bankinter, while wages for under-35s have barely grown in real terms.

On top of this comes the overcrowding of cities, which have become urban spaces hosting more people than they can cope with, with high levels of pollution and where it is impossible to find the rest and disconnection that still exist in the countryside. For all these reasons, more and more young people are swapping cities for depopulated villages where buying a home has not yet become an unattainable luxury.

The village as a solution

In Spain it has always been a summer tradition to go back to the village. Every child had a village to go to, and those who did not went with friends to their grandparents' village. The youngest enjoyed those communities, far from the hustle and bustle of the city, during their holidays: afternoons swimming in the river, a sandwich with sliced luncheon meat for tea, laughter and games with cousins.

Those children are now adults who see buying a home in a big city as hugely complicated, so they are starting an exodus in reverse to that of their grandparents and parents, heading back to small municipalities where buying a house does not mean an Herculean effort.

In this context, some of the generation who should now be buying their first flat in the city have started to look elsewhere. According to a Fotocasa Research study carried out in the first half of 2026, 13% of people looking for a home in Spain plan to move in the coming months to a municipality with fewer than 10,000 inhabitants. They are not retirees seeking peace and quiet. They are young people, in the middle of their working lives, with a life project still to build.

The study draws a clear profile: they are on average 35 years old, with incomes of between 1,000 and 3,000 euros a month, and in many cases they still live with their parents.

Most of them come from Catalonia (22%), Andalusia (19%) and Madrid (18%), and the most revealing point is that the majority are not from major capitals but from medium-sized cities: 44% currently live in municipalities with more than 50,000 inhabitants that are not provincial capitals. They are people who have already taken a step back from the big city and are now ready to take another.

Place of origin of those who are going to move to a rural area. Fotocasa

A generational shift, not a fad

"The traditional image of rural repopulation is changing. Today the people who want to settle in a village are mainly young, of working age and with a life project still to build," says María Matos, head of research and spokesperson for Fotocasa.

Matos says this trend shows that rural areas are starting to establish themselves as a real residential alternative, although she warns that "for this opportunity to translate into a genuine demographic recovery, it will be essential to go on boosting employment, services, connectivity and infrastructure that can attract and retain people on a stable basis."

The age factor says it all: the youngest, aged 18 to 24, make up 23% of those planning to move to a rural area, while those aged 25 to 34 account for 38%. These are age groups that in the past would have been the first to look for a flat in the city. Today they are the first to give up on that option.

Chart showing the intention to move to a rural area by age. Fotocasa

The most common living arrangements among those planning this move are to live with a partner and children (31%) or with their parents (30%), which reinforces the idea that many of these moves are not a purely vocational choice but also a response to the impossibility of accessing decent housing in urban environments.

"Empty Spain" as a safety valve

What for decades was a problem – rural depopulation, the exodus of young people to the cities – is now, paradoxically, turning into an opportunity. Villages have homes available and at affordable prices.

What they often do not offer is stable employment, quality healthcare, schools, high-speed internet or public transport, because as depopulated areas they have seen few improvements in these basic services. That is the knot that has to be untied if the neo-rural phenomenon is to move from being a statistical trend to becoming a real solution to Spain's housing crisis.

For now, the figures suggest there is a generation willing to give it a try. A generation battered by constant crises that is not asking for luxuries: it is asking to be able to live in a decent and independent way, to have a roof of its own and build a future. And it has reached the conclusion that, in Spain in 2026, that may be easier in a village in Teruel or Cuenca than in any neighbourhood in the big cities.

World.title: Trump administration plans to revoke 200,000 visas of asylum seekers
World.content:
The Trump administration said on Monday it is planning to revoke business and tourism visas of 200,000 foreigners who have applied for or are currently seeking asylum in the United States.

 

Unless challenges or revised, the move would mark the largest single mass revocation of visas in US history.

“We are coordinating with DHS to identify and revoke the nonimmigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the United States claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently,” State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said.

He did not comment on the exact number of visas that would be revoked, claiming that "the number of revocations remains dynamic and will be done on a rolling basis".

In the coming weeks, the State Department is expected to announce the revocation of B1 and B2 visas issued between 2016 and 2026 for those that have sought or are currently seeking asylum, according to documents obtained by press agency The Associated Press and two US officials that spoke on condition of anonymity.

B1 visas are typically issued for business trips and B2 visas for tourism, family visits and medical care. Current applicants for both categories are asked to confirm that they are not seeking asylum in the US and provide proof that they intend to return to their home countries.

The revocation of the visa would not immediately result in the deportation of the individual, the officials clarified, but those with pending asylum cases would lose their status as business or tourism travellers.

The move is the latest in the Trump administration’s broader immigration crackdown, which has intensified since President Donald Trump returned to office for his second term.

The administration has already tightened restrictions on visa applicants, including requiring applicants to provide their social media histories, imposing expensive bonds before visas can be processed, and complete visa bans on citizens of certain countries.

On Friday, a judge struck down a Trump administration policy implemented earlier this year that suspended the visa issuance of immigrant visas from 75 countries.

US District Judge Jeannette Vargas, who was appointed by former President Joe Biden, said the policy was "contrary to law and in excess of statutory authority," arguing that it undermines Congress's requirement that consular officers are at the forefront of making visa decisions.

World.title: US Treasury Secretary launches 'Operation Economic Outcast' aimed at isolating Iran
World.content:
The United States is launching what it has branded "Operation Economic Outcast" against Iran as Washington seeks to sever Tehran's financial lifelines amid the ongoing war.

 

In a press conference on Monday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent outlined a new, "unprecedented campaign" against Iran and its "enablers," describing it as an "economic onslaught" aimed at isolating the Iranian regime.

"Treasury has mapped every node, every facilitator, and every network that Iran has used to smuggle oil and evade sanctions," he said. "Beginning today, the actions of Treasury and other agencies will tighten the noose and block every potential source of revenue that funds the IRGC and the evil Iranian regime".

"Any entity that facilitates money laundering on behalf of Iran will be removed from the US dollar system," he continued, adding that US President Donald Trump was contacting unspecified world leaders requesting that they stop working with Iran.

As part of the campaign, the Treasury Department announced on Monday that it had also "issued determinations against five critical sectors - digital assets, technology, gold, aviation, and shipping - that the Iranian regime uses to try to prop up its failing economy."

Moving forward, Bessent said Iran was now left with "a very clear choice."

"Complete global isolation and a subsistence economy, or a path back to normalcy, with an opportunity to rejoin the global economy".

A small boat sails past cargo ships and other commercial vessels anchored in the Strait of Hormuz off Bandar Abbas, Iran, Wednesday, Aug. 5, 2026. Amirhosein Khorgooi/ISNA via AP

Bessent's warning comes around six months after US and Israeli strikes on Iran marked the beginning of the war in the region, which the Trump administration says aims to ensure Iran can never obtain a nuclear weapon.

The conflict has largely ground to a stalemate in recent months, with negotiations faltering and a growing dispute over the Strait of Hormuz.

The strategic waterway, a crucial oil and gas transit chokepoint that connects the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea, has been a sticking point in talks between Washington and Tehran, with both sides claiming control over the passage.

World.title: UK to share SCALP missile blueprints with Ukraine as Coalition of the Willing meets in Kyiv
World.content:
Ukraine has moved a step closer to producing SCALP cruise missiles at home after Britain agreed to provide information on UK-made components of the Franco-British weapon.

 

The decision clears the way for the missiles to be assembled in Ukraine following months of negotiations between Kyiv and Paris over licensing and local production.

Luke Pollard, the UK's Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, said the move should strengthen Ukraine’s defensive capabilities.

The air-launched cruise missile, known as SCALP in France and Storm Shadow in Britain, has a range of more than 250km and is designed for precision strikes against pre-planned, fixed targets.

Ukraine has already used the missiles against Russian military targets and infrastructure, including command posts and defence-industry facilities in occupied Ukrainian territory and inside Russia.

The UK became the first country to provide Ukraine with long-range cruise missiles in 2023.

Three years later, the technology transfer marks a further shift in western support - as governments move from supplying finished weapons to helping Ukraine manufacture its own sophisticated systems.

The announcement came as the Coalition of the Willing met in Kyiv, where protecting Ukraine from intensifying Russian missile attacks was high on the agenda.

In a joint declaration, the allies condemned Russia’s “systematic and escalating strikes against Ukraine’s cities, critical infrastructure and civilians” and pledged to strengthen Ukraine’s air defences “as a matter of urgent priority”.

The gathered leaders also committed to sharing relevant technologies, including through the Anti-Ballistic Missile Coalition, as Ukraine prepares for another winter of Russian attacks on its cities and energy infrastructure.

Coalition of the Willing meeting, in Kyiv, Ukraine, Monday, Aug. 24, 2026. AP Photo

Ukraine’s most urgent military need remains defences against ballistic missiles, for which it is critically dependent on US-made Patriot systems and PAC-3 interceptors.

Kyiv has been pressing Washington not only for additional interceptor missiles but also for permission to manufacture them domestically, which would give Ukraine a more reliable long-term supply.

US President Donald Trump had previously appeared to green light the idea.

At the NATO summit in early July, Trump said Washington would grant Ukraine a licence to produce the interceptors.

But three weeks later, he said no final decision had been taken, describing the transfer of the technology as a significant step.

US ambassador to NATO Matthew Whitaker subsequently said no long-term production agreement was likely before the winter and stressed that PAC-3 technology remained tightly controlled under US export rules.

The mixed signals come as Ukraine runs low on Patriot interceptors amid an intensifying Russian ballistic missile campaign and ahead of expected attacks on the country's energy network over the winter.

World.title: Houthis claim strike on Saudi tanker in latest Red Sea escalation
World.content:
Yemen's Houthis said on Monday that their forces hit a Saudi oil tanker in the Red Sea with a ballistic missile, as the Iran-backed group continues to pursue a maritime blockade of the Bab el-Mandeb strait, another crucial artery for global shipping.

 

"The strike was accurate and direct, resulting in a fire breaking out aboard the vessel and causing a number of other ships that were present in the target area to flee," the Houthis said in a statement.

"This targeting comes as part of the implementation of the Armed Forces' decision to ban maritime navigation by the Saudi enemy."

The Houthi claim came hours after a British maritime agency said a tanker struck by an "unknown projectile" caught fire off Saudi Arabia's Red Sea coast.

"The Company Security Officer reported a tanker has been struck by (an) unknown projectile causing a fire to the vessel on the main deck," said the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations.

"All crew are safe and accounted for and no environmental impact has been reported," it added.

The incident took place 63 nautical miles west of the Saudi city of Yanbu, the agency reported. Yanbu lies hundreds of kilometres north of Yemen.

British maritime security firm Vanguard Tech also said a Saudi-flagged vessel had been hit by a missile and caught fire.

The Bab al-Mandeb strait, which connects the southern Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean, carries roughly 12% of global maritime trade.

The Houthis disrupted it severely with their campaign against Israel-linked shipping during the Israel-Hamas war in Gaza, claiming it was in a show of support for Palestinians.

The Bab el-Mandeb campaign comes at a time when the Strait of Hormuz, the Gulf's other critical chokepoint, remains under blockade after the US-Iran war continued following the collapse of the interim deal between the two sides.

The Houthis have reportedly held talks with Tehran on instituting a toll for cargo ships passing through the strait akin to the one Iran is eyeing for Hormuz.

Turning up the heat

The group — formally known as Ansar Allah — has been attacking Saudi Arabia's ships after declaring a maritime blockade of the country last month.

Hostilities erupted in July after the group welcomed an Iranian plane in Yemen's capital Sana'a, setting off a spate of tit-for-tat attacks.

The Houthis have hit Saudi tankers in the Red Sea and attacked Yemeni government forces since the latest round of fighting broke out.

They have also repeatedly targeted Saudi Arabia's oil infrastructure and airports.

Riyadh has since launched air strikes on Houthi military positions and infrastructure in Hodeidah, Yemen's main Red Sea port.

The blockade has threatened Saudi Arabia's ability to export millions of barrels of crude oil per day.

On 31 July, Riyadh announced a new multinational maritime defence coalition, with 14 countries, including Pakistan, Turkey and Egypt, signing a founding statement to protect Red Sea shipping.

Embroiled in more than a decade of its own war, Yemen became the latest country to be dragged into the Iran war last month, when the Houthis upended a 2022 truce with the country's internationally recognised government.

The Houthis, who came to power in late 2014 after storming Sana'a and seizing the presidential palace and key military sites, forcing Yemen's government into exile, are part of Tehran's so-called Axis of Resistance.

The Axis is a loose network of militant groups in several countries in the region, including Hezbollah in Lebanon, Hamas in Gaza and militias in Iraq, which are all backed, trained and equipped by the IRGC to varying degrees.

While the Houthis do not control the part of Yemen’s coastline along Bab el-Mandeb, they hold territory less than 100 kilometres away.

World.title: UK firm running Portugal's largest solar plant files for insolvency
World.content:
The British company Welink Energy Portugal 2 UK, which owns Solara4, the largest solar power plant in the country, has entered insolvency proceedings, according to a report published this month by consultancy BDO, cited by the weekly newspaper "Expresso" (source in Portuguese). The case concerns a large-scale project in the Algarve region with 219 MW of installed solar capacity, according to the Welink Group website (source in Portuguese).

 

Located in Alcoutim, Solara4 has been in operation for five years, having been inaugurated in 2021, but has been facing a series of setbacks. According to the same report, since quoted by several national media outlets (source in Portuguese), this solar plant "has been through a combination of operational and market challenges that have adversely affected its performance and cash flow generation".

The document further states: "Electricity production has consistently fallen short of initial forecasts. At the same time, the Iberian energy market has seen significant growth in solar generation capacity. This increase in supply has driven down wholesale prices, which at times drop to zero or into negative territory." Due to the confluence of these factors, "revenues have been lower than expected".

However, as reported by "Expresso", disputes between the British company and the contractor, China Triumph International Engineering (source in Portuguese), a subsidiary of a Chinese state-owned industrial conglomerate, as well as fires and other technical problems, have also hampered Solara4's operations.

Despite this turbulent trajectory, the "Jornal Económico" (source in Portuguese) reported in 2024 that Welink had decided to "hybridise" the solar plant, through a €400 million investment to boost solar capacity while also adopting wind power and battery storage solutions.

The initial idea was to enable uninterrupted electricity production by installing a further 50 MW of solar capacity, 264 MW of wind power through 40 turbines and a 100 MW battery energy storage system (BESS), for a "total of more than 600 MW of installed capacity upon completion", according to the Welink Group's own website.

However, the ambitious project received an unfavourable opinion from the assessment committee led by the Portuguese Environment Agency (source in Portuguese) (APA), which considered that it would not be "compatible with safeguarding the environmental values present in the affected area". The plan was later revised, cutting the number of planned wind turbines to just over half, and was put out to public consultation. However, the APA has not taken any definitive decision on the matter.

All this came after Solara4 had already been close to being sold. And indeed, within the insolvency process now under way, the priority, once again, is to find new investors willing to buy the asset, the weekly "Expresso" further reports.

World.title: Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan strengthen ties as Israel tensions rise
World.content:
Tensions between Turkey and Israel have intensified after an Israeli airstrike targeted a Syrian military airbase near the Turkish border. The strike came days after Turkey’s new military pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan.

Advertising

Ankara swiftly condemned Tuesday's Israeli airstrike on Syria’s Abu Duhur military airbase, 70 kilometres from its border, calling it illegal and a breach of Syrian sovereignty.

Ankara is a key ally of Syria's new authorities. Israel justified its actions, accusing Turkey of seeking to expand its military footprint in Syria, which it sees as a serious threat.

“Israel is uneasy about the Turkish presence in Syria, and Turkish ambitions to play a major role in Syria’s future are unsettling from an Israeli perspective,” explains Turkey expert Gallia Lindenstrauss of Israel's Institute for National Security Studies.

“There's concern that Turkey will establish its own bases in Syria,” she added.

Israeli-Turkish tensions have risen over Israel’s war in Gaza and Lebanon, and Ankara’s support of Hamas, evolving into a broader regional rivalry.

“In general, there's uneasiness [in Israel] about Turkey's assertiveness, both in Syria and in the Mediterranean and other parts of the Middle East and the greater regional arena," said Lindenstrauss.

Landmark agreement

Earlier this month, Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan made headlines by signing a landmark military accord in the Saudi city of Mecca. Known as the Mecca Accord, this alliance pledges mutual defence if any member is attacked, akin to NATO’s Article 5.

Turkish international relations expert Soli Ozel claims the impetus for the agreement is uncertainty around Washington’s willingness or ability to protect its regional allies amid ongoing tensions involving Iran.

“Undoubtedly, the United States is proving to be an increasingly unreliable partner. Countries worldwide, especially in the larger Middle East region, are looking for other ways to provide security for themselves,” said Ozel.

Iran says ‘Muslim Nato’ pact reflects retreat from US security umbrella

The Mecca Accord members view each other as bringing complementary strengths to deal with shared concerns.

"Pakistan brings military capabilities and is a nuclear power. The Saudis have the money. Turkey has a budding defence industry and a large army. It claims not to be against any country, but I think those three parties agree that Iran is a destabilising actor, as is Israel,” explained Ozel.

The Mecca Accord is set to boost defence and intelligence ties, with Saudi Arabia expected to bolster Turkey’s expanding defence sector.

But many analysts see Iran and Israel as the accord’s principal focus.

“The deal is meant to signal both to Iran and Israel that they will be isolated in the region if they continue with assertive, belligerent policies,” said Asli Aydintasbas of the United States-based Brookings Institution.

Turkey steps up as Europe's indispensable and uncomfortable defence partner

'Two axes in the Middle East'

Despite Iran’s recent attacks on Saudi Arabia, Aydintasbas argues that while the Mecca Accord has a mutual defence clause – meaning an attack on one member is an attack on all – Turkey and Pakistan will not be drawn into a conflict with Iran.

“We know that they have no desire to get involved. But it does mean there will be greater military cooperation,” said Aydintasbas.

Countering Houthi rebel attacks in the Red Sea on Saudi tankers could be the first real test of the alliance.

But Aydintasbas cautions that the Mecca Accord will not replace the US as the “ultimate security provider” for the region. Instead, it's more about burden sharing, a move that fits well with Washington’s wider agenda.

Washington has given its blessing to the accord, and expansion talks are already under way.

European Union slams 'inflammatory' Houthi Red Sea tanker attack

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan hinted that Egypt could be the next member, with Turkish media reporting that Egypt’s foreign minister will join his Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani counterparts for a meeting in Istanbul later this month.

“Developments in Egypt are of major concern to Israel,” said Lindenstrauss. But she believes the Mecca Accord is an opportunity for Israel, given there are mutual concerns among its allies over the Accord.

“Israel already has very close relations with Greece, Cyprus, the United Arab Emirates and India,” she noted. "And I do envision a deepening of this relationship. And so we have the formation of two loose axes in the Greater Middle East."

World.title: US: Trump administration plans to revoke up to 200,000 visas from asylum seekers
World.content:
The State Department is reportedly looking to revoke the visas of up to 200,000 foreigners who sought asylum after entering on tourist or business visas, in what could be the largest mass visa revocation in US history.

United States President Donald Trump's administration is preparing to revoke the business and tourism visas of foreigners who applied for or are currently seeking asylum in the country, the State Department said in a statement on Monday.

It didn't say how many visas would be affected, but the Associated Press put the number at up to 200,000, citing State Department documents ‌and ​two US officials. If carried out, it would be the largest single mass revocation of visas in US history.

What did the State Department say about revoking visas?

The State Department is expected to announce the revocations in the coming weeks, targeting so-called B1 and B2 visas issued between 2016 and 2026 to holders who have sought or are now seeking asylum. These visas are generally issued for business travel, tourism, family visits or medical care.

"We are coordinating with DHS to identify and revoke the nonimmigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the United States claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently," State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said, referring to the Department of Homeland Security.

He declined to give a specific number, saying the count "remains dynamic and will be done on a rolling basis."

Officials said the revocations would not necessarily lead to immediate deportation. Most people with pending asylum cases would instead be recategorized, losing their status as business or tourism travelers, according to officials who spoke to AP on condition of anonymity.

Trump's America: End to the American dream for immigrants? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Trump official slams visa use

Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau criticized the use of tourist and business visas as a path to asylum claims.

"People in the US and all over the world are fed up with bogus asylum claims," he wrote on social media platform X, adding, "Asylum isn't supposed to be a loophole to circumvent immigration law."

He separately alleged that the US immigration system "has long been swamped by frivolous asylum claims" and cited the case of a Colombian national who entered the US on a tourist visa in 2015 before applying for asylum.

Applicants for B1 and B2 visas are currently required to affirm they will not seek asylum and to demonstrate intent to return to their home countries. It remains unclear how many current visa holders have actually filed for asylum.

Who has been impacted by Trump's immigration crackdown?

The move is the latest in a series of visa restrictions under Trump's second term, which has included expanded social media vetting, new bond requirements, and outright bans on visa issuance for citizens of certain countries.

The State Department said it has revoked roughly 175,000 visas over the past 18 months, citing reasons ranging from criminal convictions to public criticism of US policy, particularly regarding the Middle East. The administration has also targeted "birth tourism," and has repeatedly sought to end birthright citizenship. Courts, including the Supreme Court, have rejected those efforts.

H1-B and the AI revolution: Threats to your tech career? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Rights groups have criticized the broader immigration crackdown, arguing it has infringed on free speech and due process rights while creating an unsafe environment, particularly for ethnic minorities who could face racial profiling. The administration maintains the crackdown is intended to strengthen domestic security.

Despite campaigning largely on illegal immigration, the administration has also tightened legal immigration pathways, including through new, costly fees for certain work visa applicants. Several aspects of the crackdown are facing ongoing legal challenges.

World.title: Tornado in France damages homes, injures dozens
World.content:
A tornado tore through southwestern France, uprooting trees, damaging dozens of homes and causing transport chaos across the region.

A tornado damaged dozens of homes and injured around 40 people after tearing through a village in southwestern France on Monday, officials said.

The town of Pomas in the foothills of the Pyrenees mountains, home to around 1,000 people, was hit the hardest.

The tornado damaged approximately 300 homes in the village, uprooting trees and ripping the roofs off some buildings.

The tornado left a trail of damage in its wake Image: Idriss Bigou-Gilles/AFP

Fifteen of the injured, including a pregnant woman whose house collapsed while she was inside, were brought to hospital, AFP reported.

More than 120 firefighters and emergency personnel were sent to the scene to help with clean-up efforts, local officials said.

Emergency shelters have been set up for people whose homes were damaged.

What else do we know about the tornado in southern France?

Meteo-France, the national weather service, said the storm packed winds as high as 117 kilometers (73 miles) per hour in the nearby village of Arquettes-en-Val.

French authorities had issued orange storm alerts for much of the country's south and southwest. Several areas were affected by power cuts and severe transport disruption.

Around 2,800 households were still without power on Monday evening, officials said.

France sees several dozen tornados on average each year Image: Christian Dussaud/Bestimage/IMAGO

Roads were closed due to fallen trees, and trains were delayed, while airports in Bordeaux, Marseille, Nice and Toulouse, as well as Paris, reported flight delays and cancellations, Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot said.

The third stage of the Vuelta a Espana, due to take place in the Aude department, was canceled after a hailstorm interrupted the cycling race.

World.title: Haiti: Gang members kill dozens near Port-au-Prince
World.content:
At least 40 people were killed, some of them execution-style, during the attack in Kenscoff. The local mayor described "a night of terror" in the town that has been plagued by gang violence for months.

At least 40 people were killed after gang members attacked displaced persons sheltering inside a church outside Haiti's capital city, Port-au-Prince, the local mayor and the United Nations said Monday.

"We have counted around 40 bodies. Searches are continuing. Some people are still missing," Kenscoff mayor Massillon Jean told the AFP news agency.

Several of those killed on Sunday night had already fled violence earlier this year, Jean said.

"The bandits raided a displaced persons camp located in a church. They executed several people. There are fatalities and dozens of wounded. Some people were abducted by the criminals," Jean said.

Many of the victims had already been displaced by gang violence Image: Patrice Noel/REUTERS

What do we know about the attack near Haiti's capital city?

The UN said the attack had left at least 47 people dead and more than 22 injured and warned that casualty estimates could still change.

Rights group RNDDH said between 30 and 40 people were killed and 15 to 20 were injured during the attack, which started at around 10:30 p.m. on Sunday.

In a statement, the office of Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé condemned the "heinous attack," adding that security forces were on the highest alert and reinforcements were being deployed.

Residents have called for the local police chief to resign amid allegations that police failed to protect people sheltering in the church, which is just minutes away from the police station.

Kenscoff lies in the hills outside the Haitian capital and has been plagued by gang violence for months.

Early last year, gang attacks resulted in more than 260 people being killed and 200 homes destroyed or set ablaze, displacing 3,000 people, according to the UN. At least 10 more attacks have taken place since.

Residents confronted police on Monday after the gang raid the previous night Image: Fildor Pq Egeder/REUTERS

Kenscoff is in a strategic location overlooking several routes into Port-au-Prince.

"Kenscoff will not be abandoned. Haiti will not be handed over to bandits. The Republic will prevail," the statement said .

What is the security situation in Haiti?

Haiti's capital and the surrounding regions have increasingly come under the control of an alliance of criminal groups in recent years.

Attempts by the international community to support Haiti's ill-equipped police force have failed to rein in the violent gangs.

Haiti is the poorest nation in the Americas. The Caribbean country suffers from deep-seated political instability, corruption, natural disasters and gang violence.

The UN estimates that nearly 1.5 million Haitians are currently displaced out of a total population of 11 million people. More than five million face severe food insecurity.

The violence worsened in 2024, after criminal groups sparked a wave of violence that culminated in the unelected prime minister resigning.

The last time Haiti held an election was in 2016. Its previous president, Jovenel Moise, was assassinated in 2021 and has not been replaced.

Haiti is scheduled to hold elections in December this year.

World.title: Sudan: US proposes expanding UN arms embargo
World.content:
The US has called for a UN arms embargo for Darfur to be broadened to the whole of Sudan. The change would require Security Council approval, with Russia warning it would hurt the Sudanese army.

The United States on Monday proposed expanding an existing UN arms embargo for Darfur to cover all of Sudan.

The proposal was put forth by US Envoy Massad Boulos during a UN Security Council meeting in New York.

"The brutality of the war waged by the Rapid Support Forces [RSF] and the Sudanese Armed Forces has discredited their claims to be legitimate governors of the Sudanese people," said Boulos, who warned that "external financial and military support is fueling the conflict and risks drawing neighboring states deeper into war."

Boulos said the US wants to expand the embargo geographically as well as materially in order to cover unmanned aerial vehicles and related technologies. Moreover, the US plan would see the number of experts monitoring the embargo increased.

The Darfur embargo has been in place for two decades and will expire on September 12, 2026, if not amended or renewed.

An expansion would require a Security Council vote.

Sudan wants 'technical extension' but warns against hampering army

Sudan's UN envoy urged members to endorse a "technical extension" of the existing embargo while warning against changes that would hamper the army.

"Sudan suffers the most from weapons and their illegal flow. However, expanding such a sanctions regime will weaken the protection of civilians," said Al-Harith Idriss al-Harith Mohamed.

Russia, which holds veto powers in the Security Council, has voiced skepticism over changes to the existing deal, saying that expanding the embargo could impact the Sudanese army's effectiveness.

Escaping death in Sudan's civil war To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

UN Sudan experts say sophisticated weaponry suggests 'external support'

Before Boulos articulated the US position, UN Under Secretary General for Political and Peacebuilding Affairs Rosemary Di Carlo warned that a "worrying aspect of the conflict in Sudan is its increasing complexity."

"Sophisticated weaponry," she said, "continues to point to ongoing external support to both parties."

The UN's humanitarian chief, Tom Fletcher, also made note of the fact that, "in recent weeks, fighting in Sudan has been characterized by the heavy use of drones and localized ground combat in areas less affected by rainy season conditions."

The war in Sudan, now in its fourth year, has killed tens of thousands and displaced millions of civilians.

While Sudan's army holds sway in the country's central and eastern regions, western and parts of southern Darfur are under control of rival Rapid Support Forces.

Darfur, a vast western region the size of France, has seen some of the worst violence of the conflict, with repeated attacks on displacement camps and ethnic massacres that kill thousands at a time.

World.title: US announces bid to further isolate Iran economically
World.content:
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has outlined what he called "unprecedented" moves to isolate Iran economically. He said it will focus on third countries, warning those who don't comply will "share" in the isolation.

The US on Monday announced what it said would be an "unprecedented" bid to constrict Iran's economy, by targeting its trading partners, as the war in the Middle East continues with no real resolution or progress in sight.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's much-hyped press conference did not include any solid measures or announcements, but he said to expect them to follow fairly rapidly in the course of the week.

He laid out plans for what he called the "economic asphyxiation" of the regime in Tehran, implying this would be achieved in large part via secondary sanctions on Iran's trading partners.

"Around the globe, our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone," Bessent told a press conference. "We are going to hold everyone accountable."

What did Bessent say about the plans?

Bessent called the program "Operation Economic Outcast" and again sought to liken it to the "Economic D-Day" mentioned last week by US President Donald Trump, an analogy that prompted ridicule because of how poorly it seemed to fit the circumstances.

"In the Second World War, D-Day marked the historic beginning of a campaign with our Allies to target and drive the enemy from its positions, including those in third counties," Bessent said, in an apparent effort to salvage the historical allusion.

It would target Iran "and its enablers," he said.

"Iran now faces a very clear choice, with only two paths before them: Complete global isolation and a subsistence economy, or a path back to normalcy with an opportunity to rejoin the global economy," Bessent said.

He said the Treasury had mapped "every node, every network, every facilitator that Iran has used to smuggle oil and evade sanctions," and said it would now start to "tighten the noose" to constrict "every potential source of revenue that funds the IRGC and the evil Iranian regime."

Can Iran survive Trump's new sanctions? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Carrot and stick both brandished at third countries

There would be a "zero leakage approach," he said, adding that for third parties it was "no longer acceptable to operate in the grey spaces of this conflict."

"The president is making phone calls to world leaders with specific requests to cease their interactions with the regime. We are already seeing results," Bessent said, without elaborating.

"Those who stand with the United States will reap the rewards of our partnership," Bessent said. "Those who tether themselves to the Iranian regime should expect to share in the isolation of a withering regime."

He said the US would issue various countries a defined timeline to cooperate and steps to take, or to face consequences.

Bessent said he would not 'name names' when it came to countries issuing a willingness to cooperate, but said that Trump could be 'persuasive' when trying to secure cooperation from third parties Image: Evelyn Hockstein/REUTERS

How has Iran responded to the new sanctions?

Responding to the latest US sanctions on Monday, Iran's Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh predicted "another defeat" for Washington, saying Tehran had a "two year plan" to counter the sanctions.

"They have done everything they could to test the determination of the Iranian people and the country's officials, but they have failed every time. It seems they wished to suffer yet another defeat," Madanizadeh told state television.

"We've been waiting for these plans for a long time, and the government is and was ready and has a two-year plan to manage these events."

Over the weekend, the head of Iran's top security body warned that Tehran would see any country's support of the US measures as an "act of war."

Supreme National Security Council leader Mohsen Rezaei said Iran would "retaliate in a seismic manner" to the sanctions by targeting other oil-shipping routes from the Persian Gulf.

"If the economic war ​continues, not a single drop of oil will be exported, neither through the Strait of Hormuz nor from anywhere in the Persian Gulf," Rezaei said.

Why is the US having to focus on third countries?

Iran has already been living under international sanctions for decades. The US does almost no bilateral trade with Iran and has very little direct economic leverage over it.

Prior to the war, Iran's two biggest trading partners by far were China — arguably the country and entity that has most effectively stood up to past attempts at economic intimidation from the Trump administration — and the United Arab Emirates. The UAE last week announced it was suspending all trade, commercial exchanges and financial transactions with Iran until further notice.

NATO member Turkey and neighboring Iraq both do a substantial amount of business with Iran.

Russia is also a valued trading partner, albeit one with no need of Iranian fuel exports.

Germany is Iran's largest European trading partner, but volumes barely exceeded a billion euros in 2025 (not much more than the US figures) with provisional government figures suggesting the levels will roughly halve to record lows this year amid the war.

Bessent said he would not "name names" when it came to whose cooperation the US would seek or demand.

Ahead of Monday's press conference, China's Foreign Ministry said Beijing was monitoring developments closely and would do what is necessary to protect its rights. The ministry also added that sanctions and pressure tactics do not help resolve problems.

'Economic D-Day'

In a post on X prior to Monday's announcement, Bessent described the sanctions as "the single greatest financial offensive ever marshaled against an adversary."

He said US President Donald Trump had "dismantled Iran's military capabilities," destroyed nearly 100% of its military factories and "buried its nuclear program."

"We are now entering the endgame," he added.

Hours ahead of the announcement on Monday, Trump said Iran was "completely collapsing" in a post on social media.

Last week, the US president announced what he called an "economic D-Day" for Tehran, threatening harsher sanctions targeting not only Iran but also countries that continue to do business with it.

"Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains the tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone," Bessent said on Monday.

The current situation in the Iran war

The Middle East war began on February 28 when Israel and the US carried out strikes on Iran, killing Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. Tehran responded with strikes on energy infrastructure and US bases in the Gulf region.

While the two sides have stopped the bombing, talks to end the conflict have stalled, with control over the Strait of Hormuz remaining a key sticking point. Iran has effectively closed the waterway, crucial for global oil and gas shipments, while the US maintains a blockade of Iranian ports.

Under a memorandum of understanding signed in June, the two sides had 60 days to negotiate an end to the war and reach an agreement on Iran's nuclear program. But that period expired last week with no signs of a deal.

Meanwhile, Pakistan's army chief was due in Iran on Monday as part of efforts to revive diplomatic talks in the conflict.

And on Tuesday, Oman's foreign minister is set to meet his Iranian counterpart to continue talks on the Strait of Hormuz.

World.title: DR Congo peace roadmap: Will the fighting finally end?
World.content:
A new roadmap sets out the conditions toward peace in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). But disagreements over M23 rebels, Rwanda's role and security concerns remain, and could still derail the process.

Representatives of the Congolese government and the Rwanda-backed M23 rebel group agreed on a roadmap for peace after negotiations in Geneva.

It builds on the US-brokered framework signed in Doha last year, and sets out steps and timelines for negotiations and implementation: a ceasefire monitoring mechanism is also due to receive support from the UN peacekeeping mission, MONUSCO.

The United States, Qatar, the African Union (AU) and Switzerland have all expressed their support for the process as brokers of the push for peace.

However, it is not a full peace plan with bindíng resolutions and terms; rather, many aspects of the push will still need to be fine-tuned.

The new diplomatic initiative could nevertheless be offering fresh hope following years of bloody conflict in eastern DRC; fighting in the region has killed hundreds of civilians and displaced millions since 2022. The M23 rebel group continues to control large parts of North Kivu and South Kivu — two provinces in eastern DRC that are highly coveted for their minerals.

As disagreements remain over key issues, doubts continue to cast a shadow over the prospect of a lasting peace.

How a drone strike on M23 triggered new DRC clashes To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

From signature to implementation

"There are likely to be many more bumps on the road — disagreements remain over issues including sanctions against M23, the release of detainees and the timing of political reforms. So this remains a very fragile commitment," Alex Vines, Africa program director at the European Council on Foreign Relations, told DW.

Conflict analyst Clifton Chifuwe, executive director of the Centre for Peace Research and Advocacy (CPRA), a local NGO that focuses on conflict management, agrees with that assessment, pointing to the presence of multiple armed groups in the area, the deep level of mistrust between DRC and Rwanda, and competition over eastern Congo's mineral wealth.

He believes that the biggest of the challenges across the board is to turn this roadmap into action.

"Signing it is easier than implementing it on the ground," Chifuweexplains.

Chifuwe told DW that independent monitoring mechanisms and the involvement of all key stakeholders will be essential for any peace to hold.

One year under M23 rule in Goma To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Rwanda's role in the conflict

Rwanda has repeatedly rejected accusations that it backs M23 rebels — though international groups maintain the view that the small neighboring nation is deeply entrechned in the conflict.

Kigali's relationship with the rebel group therefore remains central to the peace process, says Vines:

"Rwanda's good faith and its relationship with M23 is a really key consideration. Kigali's buy-in to any agreement and influence over M23 is key."

Rwandan President Paul Kagame's comments at a press conference on August 24 further underline the complexity of the issue; Kagame rejects the narrative that Rwanda is responsible for the current conflict, blaming factions within the DRC instead.

He links any Rwandan involvement in the conflict to what he describes as a longstanding security threat from the other side of the border, naming the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR) armed group — which fights against M23 rebels alongside the Congolese military — as his main target.

Kagame said that "if this problem of the FDLR is not resolved," Rwanda would act to protect itself "at any cost."

Residents of eastern DRC are desperate for peace and stability Image: Jospin Mwisha/AFP

Mixed messages of hope and skepticism

There also are signs and reasons for cautious optimism: Chifuwe highlights that the roadmap focuses on a sequenced implementation plan, with monitoring initiatives to be put in place to help identify warning signs before any violence resumes.

These international mediators will also have to maintain pressure on the parties while ensuring regional concerns are heard.

In this context, Vines believes that US and Qatari involvement remains important, while stressing that African input through the AU must not be ignored.

All parties involved have signed off on a pledge to "pursue negotiations towards comprehensive peace and conflict resolution" — for now.

DR Congo and Rwanda hope for peace and minerals deal To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What does peace mean for the displaced?

Ultimately, the roadmap will not be measured by the signatories' attitudes but by results for thousands upon thousands of people in the eastern DRC, who remain displaced.

"The real test is ... whether ordinary Congolese people become safer and better off," Chifuwe says emphatically, highlighting also the restoration of state authority and the management of mineral resources as key objectives that need to be achieved.

For Congolese civilians, the diplomatic language carries a personal meaning: One refugee named Linda Kasongo finds herself stuck in Zambia five years into the conflict.

She told DW that she wants to return home, but can't even entertain the thought, since violence on all sides continues to wreck lives and livelihoods in her war-torn home region.

"I hope it works out because I want to go home," Kasongo says. "I want to be with my people. I miss my people. I miss my home."

For many displaced people in the regional capital Goma and beyond, there is little to return to Image: Jospin Mwisha/AFP

Edited by: Sertan Sanderson

World.title: The new Bundesliga season is here, but has the glow gone?
World.content:
Another Bundesliga season arrives, but are the golden years of Germany's top football league already over, and what can it do to change its course?

The 64th season of the Bundesliga is here. The tiny team from Elversberg will become the 59th club to play in the league, Ismael Saibari is Harry Kane's new back-up at Bayern Munich, Schalke return after three years away, and Kathleen Krüger is Head of Sport at Hamburg.

Coming off an XXL World Cup and a new broadcasting deal in the US, the Bundesliga is looking to step forward into a new era. But beyond the loyal support of club fans both domestic and abroad, has the international appeal of the league, particulary in the key US market, worn off?

"It would be hard to argue that the Bundesliga has not suffered some back-sliding in their standing. When Bayern and Dortmund met in the Champions League final [in 2013], I believed it was just the league announcing its superiority with intent to stay at the pinnacle of club football in Europe. I couldn't have imagined that might have been the brief apex," Randall, a US-based Cologne fan who has been watching the league for 16 years, told DW.

"Frankly, the Bundesliga has likely already seen its popularity at its peak. It is only downward from here."

Dominik Schreyer, a professor of sports economics at Germany's Otto Beisheim School of Management, doesn't believe that is the case though.

"I would be cautious about declaring the Bundesliga’s golden era over," Schreyer told DW.

"The league still has full stadiums, strong clubs, excellent players and coaches, and a distinctive football culture."

Schreyer does admit though, despite the league's great reputation of player and coach development, failing to retain players like Erling Haaland or Florian Wirtz makes it more difficult to increase the reach of the league.

"Bayern’s prolonged dominance has reduced uncertainty at the top, while the Premier League has developed a major financial and distribution advantage. The problem is therefore not simply a lack of talent or stories, but the Bundesliga’s limited success in turning those strengths into regular international viewing habits."

Club support strong, but league lacking luster

Robin Austermann, Bundesliga Americas executive vice president, said in the statement about the new Bundesliga broadcasting deal in the US that Bundesliga fans in America had grown by "43% over the past five years."

This is obviously a positive, although it would be intriguing to know how much growth had been made per year. For some fans though, beyond supporting their team, the league is lacking.

"Honestly, for pure viewing I prefer the Premier League since in their league at least three or four teams can win the title," Dave, a US-based Schalke fan since 1974, told DW.

"There is no doubt that both the Bundesliga and the second division are the envy of other countries from the attendance and management perspectives but I feel that the overall competitive sporting quality has declined. I absolutely believe that the Bundesliga has lost some of it's luster and reputation."

Cologne fan Randall agrees.

"You get a little drama around the border between the last Champions League slot and Europa League, but that doesn't really get the blood pumping how, does it? I still love watching the league, but I still have days on which I wonder if a Super League would really have been such a bad thing if it returned some competitive balance to the Bundesliga."

Borussia Dortmund fans are one of the most famous groups of fans in both the Bundesliga and Europe Image: Piroschka Van De Wouw/REUTERS

How can the Bundesliga change its course?

Much of the desire for change has to do with the lack of competition at the top. Bayern have won 13 of the last 14 titles. Some believe a more equitable distribution of TV revenue is a possible way forward.

"The market has become more fragmented, abundant, and competitive," Schreyer said.

"Availability no longer guarantees attention. Viewers increasingly encounter football through individual players, creators, highlights, short-form content, and major tournaments before deciding whether to watch full matches. The Bundesliga therefore needs a clear path from initial discovery to repeated viewing and, eventually, fandom."

Whatever the choice, the change needs to be made without losing what sets the league apart, namely the competitive ticket prices and passionate fan base. German football fans offered a vision for football in the country back in 2020 after the COVID-19 pandemic, but the gap between the rich and the poor in European football continues to widen.

"I think throwing out what makes German club football great in pursuit of competing in the market with the Premier League would be folly," Randall said.

Schreyer believes the major clubs and established stars are the strongest way to capture audiences' attention.

"Once viewers are engaged, the league’s wider strengths, including supporter culture, historic clubs, player development, Schalke’s return, and Elversberg’s rise, can deepen that interest," he said.

This Bundesliga season a pivotal moment for the league

Clearly, the US view is only one slice of the Bundesliga's market. Fan numbers doubled in Brazil between 2018 and 2024 to 24 million, and community initiatives through Bundesliga Common Ground have helped build interest in countries all over the world such as Thailand and Vietnam.

But the new deal in the US is perhaps revealing when it comes to the challenge the Bundesliga currently faces to position itself globally.

"A lot of fans were disappointed by the league’s move to go with Fandango this next season," said Jody, who has been watching German football since 2006.

"If the Bundesliga wants to grow in the US, they need to look at what NBC did when it won Premier League broadcast rights. It needs a more mainstream distribution in the US and more publicity of the league to draw new viewers in."

Schreyer argues that this is not the entire story.

"The new deal should ultimately be judged by whether it helps rebuild demand, not by potential reach alone," he said.

Criticism is something the Bundesliga has become familiar with in recent years. But off the back of a World Cup in the US, a key target country where a new broadcast deal was recently agreed, this feels like a pivotal moment for the league's development.

Edited by: Chuck Penfold

World.title: Trump says Canada to face 50% auto, steel tariffs from 2027
World.content:
The latest threat comes after the neighbors failed to reach a deal to avert a 50% US levy on a range of other Canadian goods. Ottawa says it plans to impose retaliatory tariffs.

US President Donald Trump said Monday he would impose a 50% tariff on Canadian automobiles, car parts and steel from January 1, 2027.

The announcement comes amid an escalating dispute between the two neighbors following the collapse of trade talks last week.

"Build in the US ⁠and ​there are ​ZERO TARIFFS. ​Canada will be ‌treated like a ​[US] State ⁠no longer!" Trump wrote on social media, using his trademark all-caps style.

"On Trade, ‌and in other ways, also, ‌they ​are among the worst Nations in the World to deal with. They feel entitled, and ​yet, WE DON'T NEED CANADA, THEY NEED US!" the US president added.

The current US tariff affecting Canadian autos stands at 25%.

Breakdown in negotiations

The two countries have blamed each other after failing to reach a trade deal late on Friday to avert US levies of 50% on a range of other Canadian products — from hockey sticks and fishing rods to wine and dairy products. Those tariffs went into force on Saturday.

The tariffs affect $20 billion (€17 billion) worth of goods, covering about 5% of what Canada ships to the US each year.

Trump hits Canada with 50% tariffs in major trade escalation To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said his country would impose retaliatory tariffs from September 8 that would cover steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper and electronics.

The US currently accounts for roughly 70% of Canadian exports, making Ottawa potentially more vulnerable in the standoff.

No further negotiations are currently scheduled.

Trading blame

Carney accused Washington over the weekend of using "economic integration as a weapon" and said his country had been "attacked" by the new American tariffs.

"They asked too much and offered too little," Carney said.

US chief trade negotiator Jamieson Greer, meanwhile, said the US was compelled to act after a year of retaliation by its neighbor.

"We've said enough, and so we've taken countermeasures. Our interest is in protecting American workers and protecting American supply chains," he said.

Canada is yet to comment on the additional tariffs announced by Trump on Monday.

World.title: ‘Pequeña guerra perfecta’, retorno al nacionalismo sangriento de los noventa en los Balcanes
World.content:
Las guerras de la antigua Yugoslavia, que tiñeron Europa de sangre en la última década del siglo XX, comenzaron y acabaron en Kosovo. En 1989, cuando Yugoslavia estaba a punto de romperse por todas sus costuras, el líder serbio Slobodan Milosevic aprovechó el 600º aniversario de la batalla del campo de los Mirlos —en la que, según la tradición, los ejércitos cristianos perdieron frente a las huestes turcas, aunque básicamente toda la historia es una leyenda— para exaltar los peores instintos del nacionalismo. Kosovo concentra todos los mitos de la historia de Serbia, en forma de agravios milenarios, y Milosevic supo agitarlos para llevar a cabo su campaña de guerra, limpieza étnica y genocidio en Croacia, Bosnia y, finalmente, en esta provincia —ahora un Estado independiente todavía no reconocido por el conjunto de la comunidad internacional— que cuenta con un 90% de habitantes albaneses y un 10% de serbios.

En 1999, cuando ya habían cometido el genocidio de Srebrenica en Bosnia, los paramilitares serbios se lanzaron sobre Kosovo, en una campaña de terror y limpieza étnica que provocó una intervención de la OTAN. Pequeña guerra perfecta, la novela de Elvira Dones, escritora de origen albanés en lengua italiana, cuenta esta historia a través de tres mujeres encerradas en un apartamento, aterrorizadas cada vez que salen a la calle porque los milicianos ultranacionalistas utilizaban las violaciones como arma de guerra y podían matar impunemente a cualquiera por la calle.

El libro refleja el ambiente de terror en el que se sumergieron no solo los habitantes de Kosovo, sino de todos los Balcanes, en aquellos años de violencia étnica, en los que te podían matar solo por tener un determinado apellido. Una salida a por comida en Prístina, la capital de Kosovo, refleja el terror que miles de personas sufrieron durante años, víctimas de un odio irracional, aunque perfectamente planificado y manipulado. “Una mujer aprieta el paso delante de ella, vuelve la cabeza un par de veces para preguntarle algo, pero se arrepiente y acelera de nuevo. Dos camiones abarrotados de soldados serbios pasan de largo a toda velocidad, Nita se detiene en la puerta de una tienda abandonada tratando de dominar el pánico”, escribe Dones en un libro que describe la violencia desatada por los ultranacionalistas serbios, sin ahorrar detalles. Así relata, por ejemplo, un asesinato casi aleatorio: “Lo mata porque busca entre los kosovares que huyen los coches que más le gustan. Ya les ha requisado cinco vehículos a esos cerdos albaneses. Cuando regrese a Serbia, abrirá un garaje y ganará dinero a espuertas”.

Dones cuenta cómo la guerra afecta a personas concretas, pero resulta imposible no leer esta historia sin pensar en los discursos ultras que se han multiplicado en Occidente

El libro no pretende ser una advertencia sobre la Europa actual y el peligro que representa agitar fantasmas de odio y exclusión, pero lo es. Dones cuenta cómo la guerra afecta a personas concretas, pero resulta imposible no leer la historia de estas tres mujeres atropelladas por fuerzas oscuras que políticos oportunistas y crueles pusieron en marcha sin pensar en el presente, en los discursos ultras que se han multiplicado en Occidente en las últimas décadas, sin pensar en el odio al otro convertido en un arma política. “La Historia. Esa pobre desgraciada, utilizada por los que eran valientes para jugársela en una desquiciada orgía de palabras y plomo. Nita, en cambio, deseaba erradicar la Historia de la faz de la tierra”, escribe Dones. En los Balcanes, esta Historia, manipulada, transformada, mezclada con la leyenda, fue una fuente de dolor y destrucción durante una década. Y no está nada claro si hemos aprendido aquellas lecciones.

World.title: Adiós a los ladrones de guante blanco: Europol alerta de robos cada vez más violentos en los museos
World.content:
Puede que Hollywood siga romantizando los robos de guante blanco en museos a base de ingenio, humor y glamur, como hizo en El secreto de Thomas Crown, en la saga de Ocean’s Eleven o, más recientemente, en la versión modernizada de Arsenio Lupin para la serie de Netflix basada en el mítico personaje del “caballero ladrón” del novelista francés Maurice Leblanc. Pero la realidad, como demuestran algunos de los incidentes más recientes, entre ellos el nada romántico y pacífico pero muy real atraco de joyas de la Corona francesa en el Louvre hace un año, dista mucho de la ficción y tiene un tono mucho más siniestro: según Europol, estos delitos son cada vez más violentos.

“Los robos en museos son cada vez más agresivos, con un giro hacia métodos violentos y coercitivos”, advierte la agencia de cooperación policial europea en el informe Cambio de tácticas, cambio de objetivos: la naturaleza cambiante de los robos en los museos, publicado este lunes. Según Europol, que repasa algunos de los principales atracos a museos de los últimos años en Europa, especialmente en Francia y Países Bajos, se observa una tendencia creciente al uso de “mazos, hachas y hasta explosivos” para forzar el acceso a las obras de arte resguardadas, o incluso el empleo de armas de fuego para “intimidar al personal de seguridad o los visitantes”.

Uno de los ejemplos usados para explicar el cambio en los métodos, nada sofisticados y sorprendentes por su sencillez y eficacia, es el espectacular atraco en el Museo del Louvre del 19 de octubre de 2025. Fue increíble no sólo porque ocurrió en el museo más visitado del mundo, sino por la manera en la que actuaron los atracadores: a plena luz del día, poco después de que abriera la pinacoteca. Accedieron a través de una escalera de obra al balcón que da a la Galería de Apolo y, armados con radiales, rompieron las vitrinas donde se exponían las joyas de la Corona francesa y se llevaron nueve piezas. Una de ellas, la corona de la emperatriz Eugenia de Montijo, cayó al suelo durante la huida. Es lo único que se ha podido recuperar de un botín valorado en 88 millones de euros.

El atraco fue perpetrado en siete minutos y con violencia, a ojos de los presentes en la sala y del personal de seguridad, que no pudieron hacer nada porque, como se vio en vídeos de las cámaras de seguridad, los asaltantes les amenazaron con las radiales para que no interviniesen. Días después se detuvo a los cuatro miembros del comando, todos con antecedentes por robo por encargo o violencia, pero sin responder a un perfil de traficantes de bienes culturales. La muestra de esa falta de “profesionalidad” —otro de los rasgos distintivos nuevos, alejados de las tradicionales redes más especializadas y no violentas— fue que olvidaron objetos que permitieron su posterior identificación.

Un modus operandi similar siguieron los ladrones del violento golpe que sufrió el museo Cognacq-Jay de París un año antes, el 20 de noviembre de 2024, cuando cuatro personas asaltaron la pinacoteca poco después de las 10 de la mañana y se llevaron varias tabaqueras de oro y piedras preciosas. En el robo, también destacado por Europol como ejemplo de los nuevos atracos con violencia, los ladrones accedieron al museo armados con bates de béisbol y hachas y rompieron las vitrinas a hachazos mientras otros dos esperaban en motos a la salida. El atraco duró cuatro minutos, mientras los turistas paseaban tranquilamente por otras salas del museo.

Sopletes y preciosas

Un mes antes del robo del Louvre, otros dos museos franceses fueron objeto de asaltos: el Museo de Historia Natural de París, donde un individuo se llevó varias piezas tras romper las vitrinas con un soplete, y el Museo Nacional de la Porcelana en Limoges, en la región de Nueva Aquitania, donde los asaltantes se llevaron varias cerámicas chinas valoradas en 9,5 millones de euros.

Y es que no está cambiando solo el método, subraya Europol, también está variando el objetivo de dichos robos: en los dos últimos años, el objetivo más buscado son metales y piedras preciosas, como sucedió también en el robo en el Museo Drents de Assen, Países Bajos, donde fueron sustraídas varias piezas arqueológicas de oro procedentes de Rumanía. Pero cada vez más también se roban “objetos culturales chinos”.

“Los ladrones han sustraído objetos de oro como pepitas, monedas de oro y piezas decorativas de oro, así como joyas con piedras preciosas”, resume la agencia policial europea, que considera que estos objetos son muy apreciados por los ladrones debido a su “creciente valor” y a que los metales preciosos “pueden ser fácilmente fundidos, sin dejar rastro alguno para las fuerzas del orden, lo que facilita las ventas ilícitas durante el proceso de receptación”. Algo parecido sucede con las joyas, cuyas piedras preciosas pueden ser “fácilmente extraídas y revendidas”.

En la mira de los ladrones en los últimos años están también objetos culturales chinos, sobre todo “platos de porcelana china de los siglos XII y XIII, jarras procedentes de la dinastía Ming y jarrones chinos de bronce con esmaltes de colores que datan de las dinastías Ming y Qing”, señala el informe, que recuerda que estos objetos tienen una “alta demanda” y “probablemente” son fácilmente vendidos en el mercado de arte.

World.title: El Barcelona empieza a olvidarse de Julián Alvarez
World.content:
Al Barcelona no le bastaba con el ruido mediático alrededor de Julián Alvarez. También quería escuchar rugir al Metropolitano. Esperaba, en definitiva, algo similar a lo que ocurrió el domingo pasado: el argentino sufrió el escarnio de la afición del Atlético de Madrid. Una pitada sonora que terminó con el club madrileño escondiendo al delantero tras el empate contra el Villarreal. “Se decidió que no se acerque con los compañeros a saludar a la gente, separarlo para que fuera a los vestuarios”, comentó Diego Pablo Simeone. El mismo problema de todo el verano. La misma solución. Ninguna.

La pasada semana, en las oficinas del Barcelona hablaban de que el lunes se tomaría una decisión definitiva sobre Julián Alvarez. Según explicaban, querían ver cómo evolucionaba el fin de semana. Tenían dos frentes, uno en el Martínez Valero; otro en el Metropolitano. El Barça sonrió en los dos. En la casa del Atlético, la hinchada pitó a Julián y, frente al Elche, Hansi Flick le demostró a la dirección deportiva que su premisa era acertada. Al menos, que por ahora así lo parece. “Si no traen a Julián me arreglo con lo que tengo”, había asegurado, durante todo el verano, el preparador alemán.

Flick pidió a Gordon y a Adeyemi. Flick le entregó a Raphinha la llave del vestuario y del área.
