World.title: In a first, Census 2027 will not record data on begging
World.content:
NEW DELHI: In a departure from previous exercises, Census 2027 will not record data on begging separately, with the questionnaire having omitted the category 'beggars and vagrants etc' from the list of 'non-economic activity'.

This, as per sources, is due to the very less return in this category in the last census; just around 3.8 lakh non-workers and marginal workers declared themselves as 'beggars and vagrants' in Census 2011.

Another key change in is the inclusion of 'natural calamities' as a 'reason for migration', in addition to work, business, education, marriage, moved after birth, moved with household and 'any other'.

While the 2011 census and earlier had listed 'beggars and vagrants etc' as marginal and non-workers engaged in 'non-economic activity' - in addition to students, household duties, dependents, pensioners, rentiers and others - they will now be counted among 'others'; as a result, the number of beggars in the country or their classification by age, religion, state/UT, educational status etc will no longer figure in census tables.

Sources said the count of 'beggars and vagrants' returned by previous census exercises was not considered reliable, as many respondents in this category were reluctant to return themselves as such due to associated social stigma. "Census rules require the enumerator to record the occupation/non-economic activity as declared by the respondent," an officer said. The count of non-worker beggars/vagrants was thus recorded at around 3.8 lakh in Census 2011, 6.3 lakh in Census 2001 and around 5.4 lakh in Census 1991.





As for the new census fields 'father's particulars' and 'mother's particulars' - which will capture date and place of their birth as well as religion - sources said they need to be filled only where the mother and father are not listed in the same household or are no longer alive. The enumeration form already records the religion and date and place of birth of each member of the census household, including parents.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

Sources told TOI that some of the trends that may emerge from recording religion of both parents include generation-wise prevalence of inter-faith marriages and history of religious conversion.

Also, date and place of birth of parents will give the aggregate data on how many Indians fulfil citizenship criteria as per Citizenship Act.

While the latest questionnaire seeks details like mobile number, Aadhaar, voter ID and Indian passport number, where "available", technically requiring every individual having these documents to share their number, sources said the enumerators have been trained to only persuade the respondents to do so, by assuring them that all individual data will remain confidential. If the respondent is still reluctant, the enumerator shall leave these fields empty.

"Even blank fields will enable the census team to cull out data on which of the documents - Aadhaar, voter ID and passport number - respondents are most reluctant to share due to privacy concerns," an official told TOI.

World.title: UPI completes 10 years of digital payments, sees 13,000-fold surge in transaction volume, 4,000-fold rise in value
World.content:
The Unified Payments Interface (UPI), launched on 25 August, 2016, by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) has completed 10 years of transforming digital payments in India.

UPI has emerged as the backbone of India’s digital payments ecosystem and a critical driver of financial inclusion, the Union Finance Ministry said.

Over the decade, UPI’s annual transaction volume expanded from 1.78 crore transactions in FY17 to over 24,162 crore transactions in FY26, representing a 13,000‑fold surge in transaction volume.

Transaction value rose sharply from ₹0.07 lakh crore in FY17 to approximately ₹314 lakh crore in FY26, translating into a more than 4,000‑fold increase in transaction value, the ministry said.

UPI is currently operational in 11 countries.

“UPI has emerged as one of the most successful pillars of India’s Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI), providing an interoperable, real-time payments platform that enables seamless peer-to-peer and peer-to-merchant transactions through a single application,” it said.

“Today, it is the preferred mode of payment for millions of users, transforming the way India transacts. By bridging the digital divide, advancing financial inclusion, and expanding access to digital financial services, UPI has empowered individuals and communities across the country while driving broad-based economic participation,” it added.

“The unprecedented scale, reliability, and interoperability achieved by UPI have received global recognition, with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) acknowledging it as the world’s largest real‑time payment system by transaction volume, underscoring India’s leadership in building scalable, inclusive, and innovative digital public infrastructure,” it further said.

World.title: Land subsidence causes cracks in hospital in Jharkhand's Giridih
World.content:
Multiple cracks developed in a colliery hospital building in Jharkhand's Giridih district on Tuesday (August 25, 2026) morning following land subsidence in the area, an official said.

The incident took place in Baniyadih village in the Mufassil police station area, which is within the command area of Central Coalfields Limited (CCL).

No one was injured in the incident, officials said.

CCL Area General Manager K.S. Gaiwal said officials reached the spot after receiving information about the subsidence and took steps to prevent people and animals from entering the affected area.

"The area will be monitored for the next few days to assess whether the subsidence is increasing or subsiding, following which further action will be taken," he said.

Another official said a few staff members were present inside the hospital building when the incident occurred. "There were no patients in the hospital as the area had witnessed land subsidence earlier as well," he said.

World.title: Onam 2026: How Onam is redefining heritage with bold flavours and modern weaves
World.content:
As Onam 2026 approaches, here is our curated guide from Thiruvananthapuram, Kochi, Chennai, Coimbatore, and Bengaluru covering everything from elaborate restaurant thalis to convenient takeaway sadya boxes.

We consult chefs on how they are reimagining the traditional sadya; we ask celebrities how they are honouring the old traditions.

We also speak to fashion designers and women-led artisan collectives on their Onam collections. Keralam’s harvest festival is getting deconstructed from its predictable avatar with designers spotlighting fresh perspectives and imagery related to Onam in their new collections.

Scroll on for our full curation of Onam 2026 stories — food, fashion, and festivities across India.

World.title: Keralites’ to-do list during Onam now features leisure travel too
World.content:
Preetha Cheerambathel, 56, wore the look of quiet contentment that comes from fulfilling a long-cherished wish as she stepped out after partaking in the famed Vallasadya — the grand ritual feast associated with Onam — at the Aranmula Sree Parthasarathy Temple in Pathanamthitta district, Kerala.

The feast was part of a budget pilgrimage package run by KSRTC, covering five temples linked to the mythical Pandavas across Pathanamthitta and Kottayam districts. Preetha and her husband Sidharthan from Punnayurkulam in Thrissur, had long wanted to experience the Vallasadya. Last year, however, they missed out as the nearest KSRTC depot at Ponnani did not operate a trip under the package.

“So when it was announced this time, we grabbed the opportunity. We gathered a group of friends and relatives to join us, and the experience was thoroughly enjoyable,” says Preetha, a regular patron of KSRTC’s budget tourism packages tailored to fulfil the travel dreams of commoners.

And the cash-strapped KSRTC is not complaining, as it taps into the Onam season, which is fast emerging as a favourite travel season for Keralites.

“We have scheduled 350 trips under the Temple package during this Onam season, which is a 50% increase from the previous season. Already, 200 trips have been operated from depots across the State, and services will continue until the Vallasadya concludes next month. Alongside Munnar and Gavi, this has become one of our most popular packages,” says R. Udayakumar, chief traffic manager, KSRTC Budget Tourism.

Yet, not all travellers are looking for domestic experiences. Overseas packages are also witnessing soaring demand during the festive season. “Onam is the second busiest travel season in Kerala after the summer holidays, thanks to school vacations and bonuses for the salaried class. Vietnam has now emerged as one of the most sought-after destinations overtaking the once-popular Singapore–Malaysia–Thailand circuit, offering rich experiences at affordable rates. Europe too remains a strong draw, as we are handling multiple groups in both circuits,” says Benny Panikulangara, a veteran of three decades in the tourism industry.

Clint K. John, who runs a hospitality business and travels frequently during Onam, observes that the festival has transformed what was once a lean period for inbound tourism in Keralam’s tourism calendar into a lively season. Keralam’s reputation as a literate, safe destination - especially for women - amplified by social media posts from domestic and international visitors, has only added to the appeal, he notes.

Tapping boat races

K. Rajkumar, CEO of Kerala Travel Mart, could not agree more. “There is immense potential to develop Onam into a distinct cultural tourism season, separate from the domestic and international seasons that begin in October and November respectively. The tourism department can harness the popularity of boat races, our unique tourism product, by locking the Champions Boat League schedule at least a year in advance. Races are held across 12 venues starting with the Nehru Trophy in Alappuzha and ending with the President’s Trophy in Kollam. This would allow tour operators to include the races in brochures for targeted marketing of both national and international tourists,” he says.

But not everyone is travelling this Onam. For K. Amina, who has been organising women-only tours for nine years, this is the first Onam she has had to cancel plans. The war in West Asia driving airfares sky-high derailed her Onam itinerary. A Thailand trip had to be scrapped after ticket prices soared to ₹45,000, compared to just over ₹26,000 for Bali last Onam.

“Many airlines cancelled group bookings, forcing us to rebook at inflated rates, which wrecked our entire budget,” Amina rues.

World.title: A new President, a possible visit: What next for Delhi-Dhaka?
World.content:
(This article is part of the View From India newsletter curated by The Hindu’s foreign affairs experts. To get the newsletter in your inbox every Monday, subscribe here.)

Veteran Bangladeshi politician Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir was sworn in as the country’s 23rd President on Friday (August 21, 2026), following a parliamentary vote — the first in 35 years. The top office fell vacant after Mohammed Shahabuddin, who was in 2023 elected unopposed as the nominee of ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina’s Awami League (AL), resigned last month. It was halfway into his five-year term and about two years after Ms. Hasina was ousted.

The political churn that Bangladesh began witnessing two years ago continues . While more than one country in South Asia witnessed dramatic youth-led protests and subsequent regime changes, collapsing these varied political and economic contexts may not be helpful. The leaders and parties that replaced the old political order in Sri Lanka, Nepal, and Bangladesh, bring specific characteristics, as well as baggage, to governance, shaped by the complex political histories of each of these countries. Each story is different, and distinct.

President Alamgir is no new entrant to politics. He was a university student at a time of tumult and nationalist consciousness and later joined the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), and rose to become its General Secretary. Do read Kallol Bhattacherjee’s engaging profile of ‘The man who steadied the ship’ to understand Mr. Alamgir’s political journey. He also shares little nuggets about the leader, known to be “a master of marathon meetings, sustained simply by cups of tea”.

In an interview with The Hindu in February this year, Mr. Alamgir, who was then in charge of the Ministry of Local Governance, Rural Development and Cooperatives, described the period under Ms. Hasina as “very difficult”. Sharing his views on PM Hasina’s return, he said: “There is a popular demand to punish her, and we believe that India should hand her over to us. But not handing over Sheikh Hasina to Bangladesh will not be a deterrent to build trade and commercial ties. We want to build even better ties.”

In this context, the speculation over the possible visit of Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to India merits attention. The likelihood of PM Rahman’s visit to India next month for the BRICS Summit “remains slim” unless an appropriate environment based on “mutual trust” is created, along with a “dignified invitation” from New Delhi, his Foreign Affairs Adviser Humaiun Kobir has said. Dhaka is in “no hurry” to arrange a top-level visit without clearly defined national interests, he said.

New Delhi could not make up its mind with the messaging, it appeared. An email to the media by the Rashtrapati Bhavan on Friday (August 21, 2026) briefly created the impression that the long-under-discussion visit of Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman would take place soon. However, soon another release came from the Rashtrapati Bhavan negating the previous note, saying, “A press release issued on the subject ‘No change of guard ceremony this Saturday’, which was issued on August 21, 2026, stands withdrawn,” Kallol Bhattacherjee reported.

Bangladesh, on the other hand, has been unambiguous in articulating its expectations, demanding that India create “propitious” circumstances for the visit by extraditing deposed Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina and the suspected killers of radical student leader Osman Hadi.

Can India really extradite Sheikh Hasina under the 2013 treaty with Bangladesh? Kallol Bhattacherjee takes us through the legal implications in this explainer.

As we wait to see how New Delhi navigates this sensitive concern with Bangladesh, tell us what you think.

World.title: Gurmeet Ram Rahim gets 21-day furlough
World.content:
Dera Sacha Sauda chief Gurmeet Ram Rahim Singh, serving a 20-year jail term for raping two of his disciples, has been granted a 21-day furlough. Sources said on Tuesday (August 25, 2026).

He will stay at his Sirsa-headquartered Dera during the period, they said.

It will be the 17th time Ram Rahim will move out of the prison since his conviction in August 2017.

The Dera chief is currently lodged in the Sunaria jail in Haryana's Rohtak.

In May, he was granted a 30-day parole. He was granted a 40-day parole in January.

World.title: Why has Maharashtra drafted a law to rein in coaching centres?
World.content:
Maharashtra has released a draft law — the Maharashtra Private Coaching Centres (Registration and Regulation) Bill, 2026 — intending to rein in coaching centres in the State, which drew attention during the NEET-UG 2026 paper leak.

The draft bill released on August 22 focuses on the prevention of the integration of school coaching centres, the prohibition of coaching centres operating from basements, mandatory registration, regulations concerning fees and safety standards, the implementation of a grievance redressal mechanism, and penalties for violations.

The bill drew criticism from private coaching institute union, calling it “oppressive” and “unrealistic”.

According to the draft bill document, the objective is to “provide a framework for the registration and regulation of private coaching classes, especially concerning the education imparted, the mental well-being of the students, and the facilities provided to them. It also aims to establish provisions for the effective redressal of grievances and related issues.”

No school-coaching integration and other clauses

The proposed draft bill targets school-tuition partnerships, specifically addressing the school-coaching nexus. It proposes a minimum strength of 25 students to register as a private coaching class. The bill excludes government schools and non-academic activities like sports, dance, art, yoga, and counselling.

The private coaching institutes need to fulfil government-prescribed formalities, covering registration and renewal of the registration certificate. No coaching centre should engage a tutor with qualifications less than graduation, make misleading promises for enrolments, or enrol students below 13 years of age.

The draft bill prevents centre owners from mid-course fee hikes and requires refunds within 10 days if a student withdraws. It focuses on safety measures, including parking facilities, 1 square meter per student, fire and building safety certificates, first aid, clean drinking water, CCTV with 1-month footage retention, separate and accessible toilets, and a complaint box.

It also asks centres to provide a weekly off, no tests the day after a holiday, a maximum of five teaching hours/day, career counselling beyond just engineering/medicine, no batch segregation based on merit, access to a counsellor.

What is the need for regulations?

In the wake of the NEET paper leak matter in May, where nine of 13 people were arrested in Maharashtra, with the primary accused being the founder of reputed NEET coaching centres, the state has proposed a draft bill to regulate the operations of coaching centres.

On May 27, the consortium, comprising nine coaching class owners’ associations from across the State, held a symbolic day-long protest at Azad Maidan in Mumbai, demanding mandatory registration of all private coaching classes and penalties for the integration of school-coaching centres. At least 50,000 coaching class owners are associated with nine associations, having at least 5 to 6 lakhs students enrolled with them.

The coaching centres in the State had no regulations, including licensing, safety audits, or fee caps. For operational centres, it is mandatory to register the centre within six months of the bill using an online portal. All registrations will be valid for three years.

State School Education and Sports Department released the draft Bill, inviting suggestions and objections from the public till September 4.

After review of the objections and suggestions, if any, the bill will be finalised, requiring all private coaching centres to register, regulate their fees and adhere to all the terms under the law.

Flak from coaching centre union

The private coaching institute union, with which at least 50,000 classes are associated, criticised the bill, saying it is “oppressive” and “unrealistic”. The union cited an instance: “It is unrealistic that a fine of one to five lakh rupees will be imposed for violating minor conditions.”

The minor conditions are not clearly defined in the draft. Several clauses in the draft will also create opportunities for corruption at the level of the investigating officers, indicating that there are no reforms in the government’s educational system.

“Several homemakers conduct tuition classes in batches from their homes; how will they fit under this bill? If the government does not relax the strict conditions in the draft while enacting the law, we will agitate, said the consortium vice president and spokesperson, Bandopant Bhuyar.

Maharashtra fifth to join the party

Maharashtra is a late entrant in regulating coaching classes. In January 2024, the Centre issued guidelines to regulate centres and a prohibition on coaching centres’ claims of “100%” selection guarantees. Based on this, the States, including Haryana, Rajasthan, Assam, and Jharkhand government enacted laws in their respective States. All the State laws cover mandatory registration, a ban on misleading s, safety standards, penalties, and access to counsellors.

However, Maharashtra has a lower size threshold of 25 students compared to 50 students under Assam law and 100 students under Rajasthan law. It means Maharashtra is allowing smaller tuition classes under the ambit of the law. The other regulations that stand out under the Maharashtra draft law include no integration with schools.

Maharashtra has more stringent penalties compared to other states. The penalties in Haryana for a first violation are ₹25000; Assam penalises a flat fine of ₹1 lakh, while Maharashtra charges up to ₹50 lakh. The minimum age of enrollment under the State draft bill is 13, while Centre rules State 16 as the minimum age.

Penalties

The bill also enables the appointment of Inquiry Officers or Appellate Authorities having power to summon centres over violations, impose fines (₹1–5 lakh for minor violations, up to ₹10 lakh for repeat minor ones, ₹10–50 lakh for major violations), and suspension of center.

“The Inquiry Officer and the Appellate Authority, while conducting any inquiry, hearing any appeal, or deciding any matter under this Act, shall have the same powers as are vested in a Civil Court while trying a suit under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 [5 of 1908], in respect of the following matters,” stated the draft bill document.

After the review period is over, the Commission will review the feedback, and through the State legislative process, the bill will be passed.

World.title: Somalian pirates and their role in war | Explained
World.content:
The story so far: On August 21, 2026, a Shipping Ministry official said that pirates have hijacked two commercial vessels, with 22 Indian seafarers onboard, off Yemen and Somalia. While MT Sibu 1, an Eritrea-flagged oil products tanker with 20 crew members including 16 Indians, was hijacked in the Gulf of Aden, a Cameroon-flagged cargo ship, MV Luruf with six Indians among its 10-member crew and carrying Turkish weapons, was hijacked off Somalia’s Puntland coast on August 17.

Officials in New Delhi have maintained that the Indian crew members are safe.

According to FTL Somalia, a new outlet, Somali pirates have “demanded a ransom of approximately $2 million” to release Luruf and its crew. The two hijackings— against the backdrop of the West Asia war, the attack on shipping lines by Iran and the Houthis, and the U.S. and Iranian blockade of the Strait of Hormuz— have given rise to fears of a resurgence of piracy off Somalia.

Who are the pirates?

In 1991, the Somali government collapsed, and with it disappeared the navy and the coastal security apparatus. The resource-rich waters off the Somalian coast was left open for foreign vessels to plunder. ‘The Pirate Trails Study’ by the World Bank in 2013 noted that “the fishermen off the Somali coast could no longer be protected from foreign ships fishing in Somali waters. Illegal international fishing and maritime dumping went unchecked... which in turn undermined the Somali coastal communities’ economic prospects”.

A 2008 report by the UN International Expert Group on Piracy off the Somali Coast identified “poverty, lack of employment, environmental hardship, pitifully low incomes, reduction of pastoralist and maritime resources due to drought and illegal fishing and a volatile security and political situation” as reasons for the rise of Somalian piracy.

The 2013 World Bank study interviewed pirates who recounted their personal stories and said how the skiff and the rifle offered an easy, and perhaps only, way out of poverty. The study quoted a pirate as saying, “I was an unemployed, occasional fisherman and someone approached me... The man promised me money and khat. He explained how he got his wealth. The man was my cousin. He was a successful pirate...”

Another pirate recalled how he struggled during “times (that) got more and more difficult” when a litre of fuel cost more than $100 and his mother was sick. “But as my friends turned to piracy, they started to refuse lending me money. They were saying: We are working to get that money. Why don’t you do the same?”

How Somalian piracy worked?

At the peak of the Somalian piracy, ransom demands ran into millions. According to World Bank study, “$339 million dollars to $413 million dollars was claimed in ransoms between April 2005 and December 2012 for pirate acts off the Horn of Africa.”

The report, which offers a detailed view of 21st century piracy, analysed how ransom amounts were collected and distributed, and how the money was invested.

Acts of piracy are never isolated incidents and follow a network of finances and local logistics. The report said that “pirate financiers” are vital to the network. These “money kingpins” are investors and the biggest beneficiaries of piracy. “On average, they collect from 30% to 50% of total ransom, working individually or as a group,” it said.

Then comes the “low-level pirates” or the “foot soldiers” who get a “standard fee of $30,000 to $75,000 per ship, which only amounts to 1%- 2.5% of an average ransom payment.”

The local community helps the pirates with “goods and services... including food, repair services and khat.” Khat is an evergreen shrub that contains the alkaloid cathinone, which works as a stimulant and has been banned by the World Health Organization since 1980 but is legal to consume in Somalia.

‘The Pirate Trails’ study said the ill-gotten proceeds of piracy are mostly invested within Somalia. Some of these proceeds are recycled into financing criminal activities, including further piracy acts, human trafficking, including migrant smuggling, and investing in militias and military capacities on land in Somalia. Besides, money is invested in the khat trade, particularly in Kenya.

What the resurgence means?

Coordination between the Somalian government that was formed in 2012 and international naval forces brought about a decline in piracy. However, maritime observers have expressed concern that the ongoing conflict in the Persian Gulf, the attack on ships in the Red Sea by the Houthis, and the diversion of marine traffic via the Cape of Good Hope to avoid conflict may be contributing to the resurgence of piracy.

Maritime intelligence firm Lloyd’s List flagged the possible resurgence of Somalian piracy in April. In its analysis, it noted, “What started at the beginning of the year as a series of localised incidents has escalated to the point that there are now two confirmed pirate groups stalking the Somali coastline for targets.”

The U.S.-based Center for Maritime Strategy, in a report this July, noted that pirates have been involved in at least 17 incidents in Somali waters or in the Gulf of Aden between January and May. Somalian pirates struck successfully for the first time in six years in 2023 and “conducted high-profile hijackings of commercial vessels in 2024 and 2025”, the report noted, adding that pirates captured three ships between April and May. The think tank said that three “active pirate groups” may be behind “coordinated operations” from Somalia and are “increasingly targeting vessels sailing hundreds of miles into the Indian Ocean”. This, the report said, is in contrast to previous Somali pirate attacks that were “largely contained to neighboring waterways”.

Is the Iran war helping pirates?

With the Strait of Hormuz virtually shut and the West Asia crisis continuing, elevated oil prices are encouraging pirates to target tanker ships. The Center for Maritime Strategy says that pirates “believe” that they can demand more ransom if they capture oil tankers.

In the last decade, the Somalian pirates approached ships in one or two skiffs, launched from a mothership, and brandished rifles and grenade launchers. A dramatic chase would end with the pirates boarding the ship using a ladder.

But now, they are operating with a “significantly higher level of sophistication previously seen”, using GPS and satellites to track vessels “far from the Somali coastline and using more sophisticated motherships to operate farther offshore”, the U.S.-based think tank said. Its report sad that today’s Somali pirates are more heavily armed because of their “partnerships” with the Houthis and al-Shabaab, an al-Qaeda offshoot active in southern Somalia. The report sees the resurgence of Somalian piracy in the broader context of disrupting regional shipping.

“Al-Shabaab has offered protection and logistical support to pirates in exchange for a share of their plunder, in addition to connecting the pirates with the Houthis who agreed to arm and train them in hopes of further disrupting regional maritime commerce.”

World.title: Amid distrust, Tehran wants US to initiate de-escalation
World.content:
Pakistan’s Chief of Defence Forces Field Marshal Asim Munir exchanges views with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian during their meeting in Tehran.—Reuters

• CDF Munir holds meetings with Pezeshkian, Ghalibaf and Rezaei

• Iranian leaders stress commitment to Islamabad MoU; say Washington’s approach hindering regional stability, eroding trust in US

• Discussions focused on preventing further escalation, reopening of Hormuz, swift end to conflict, ISPR says

• Oman FM due in Tehran today for next round of talks on Hormuz

ISLAMABAD: The United States must take the first steps towards de-escalation by fulfilling its commitments under the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding (MoU), Iran conveyed to Pakistan on Monday, as the latter sought to revive the diplomatic process for ending the US-Iran conflict.

The message was conveyed during Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir’s meetings in Tehran; with Iranian President Dr Masoud Pezeshkian, chief negotiator and Parliament Speaker Bagher Ghalibaf, and Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council Gen Mohsen Rezaei, as he sounded out Tehran on the possibility of reviving the June understanding.

“We are committed to implementing the terms of the Memorandum of Understanding. It is the United States that must adhere to its commitments based on the agreement,” Ghalibaf told Field Marshal Munir, according to an Iranian account of their meeting.

This sentiment was echoed by Gen Rezaei in his meeting with Field Marshal Munir, who was quoted by IRNA as saying: “We distrust America and it must change its behaviour”.

Field Marshal Munir said Pakistan would continue its efforts to help restore stability in the region, Press TV reported.

According to Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi accompanied the army chief during the one-day visit, which also included meetings with Iranian Interior Minister Eskandar Momeni and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.

“Comprehensive discussions focused on measures to prevent further escalation, reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and expedited termination of the conflict. The two sides also exchanged views on regional peace and the ways to arrive at a negotiated settlement to the disputes,” ISPR said.

The Iranian leadership appreciated Pakistan’s constructive role and sincere efforts towards facilitating dialogue, de-escalation and a peaceful resolution of the conflict, the statement noted.

The field marshal’s visit comes as the two warring sides have returned to hostilities following the expiry of the 60-day armistice brokered under the Islamabad MoU.

Pakistan has, however, continued to regard the agreement as the available framework for a return to dialogue, while Iran has insisted that Washington must first address what Tehran considers breaches of the understanding.

The visit assumes added significance because Field Marshal Munir spoke by telephone with US President Donald Trump last week, before travelling to Tehran. The contents of that conversation have not been made public, but the contact provided Islamabad with a direct channel to carry the US position to Tehran, while seeking to assess whether Iran was prepared to re-engage.

The army chief’s trip began just before Washington announced a fresh economic pressure campaign against Iran, with sanctions and restrictions on Iranian oil exports likely to form a major part of the new measures.

Tehran has warned that further US pressure would deepen the confrontation rather than create conditions for negotiations.

Ghalibaf described Washington’s approach as “hinder[ing] regional stability and further erod[ing] trust in Washington”.

“Americans know that no one buys their bombast, the United States is not in an economic position to further restrict its relations with other countries,” he said in a post on X after meeting Field Marshal Munir.

The Strait of Hormuz remains central to the impasse. Iran has been insisting that US first fulfil its commitments relating to the waterway, before it considers a wider reopening and a return to the next phase of negotiations.

Field Marshal Munir’s meeting with Gen Rezaei was particularly significant because the Iranian general has recently taken over as secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, placing him at the centre of Tehran’s national security decision making at this critical stage in its confrontation with Washington.

During their conversation, Rezaei particularly emphasised Iran’s security interests in the Strait of Hormuz and the need for any settlement to address the military and economic pressures imposed on Tehran.

The issue of Strait of Hormuz is meanwhile being discussed in a separate diplomatic track in the shape of Iran-Oman talks on arrangements for navigation in the strait.

Omani Foreign Minister Badr Al Busaidi is due in Tehran on Tuesday, adding to the diplomatic activity surrounding the strait at a time when Pakistan is seeking to regain its role in the wider US-Iran process.

Published in Dawn, August 25th, 2026

World.title: Govt fails to maintain quorum as PPP stays away from National Assembly
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: The ruling PML-N on Monday suffered an embarrassing setback in the National Assembly as the lower house was adjourned within minutes for lack of quorum after its estranged ally, the PPP, stayed away from the proceedings over the alleged rigging in the recently-held Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) elections.

The government failed to muster the required number of 84 lawmakers in the 336-member house, forcing the chair to adjourn the session without taking up any agenda item when quorum was pointed out by an opposition member from the PTI.

“No PPP, no quorum, simple,” posted PPP’s Sharmila Farooqui on her official social media account on X soon after the adjournment of the sitting.

Later, Ms Farooqui told Dawn PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari had already declared the party would “no more cooperate with PML-N on quorum and legislation” in the parliament till their grievances over the alleged rigging and mismanagement in the AJK polls were addressed.

Sharmila says ‘no PPP, no quorum, simple’

Even those party MNAs who were present at the start of the Question Hour left the chamber immediately seeing only 20 to 25 PML-N members on the treasury benches, she said, adding that the PPP had been completing the quorum in the assembly previously.

Ms Farooqui made it clear that the strategy would not change until their concerns over the AJK polls issue were addressed. She, however, did not elaborate any specific demand when asked as to what steps the party wanted the PML-N to take in order to allay their concerns when the election process had already been completed.

When Speaker Ayaz Sadiq earlier announced the opening of the Question Hour, PTI’s Iqbal Afridi pointed out lack of quorum. His action came when the speaker refused him the floor to speak on a point of order.

The speaker ordered a headcount and suspended the proceedings till the completion of the quorum. Some 35 minutes later, Deputy Speaker Ghulam Mustafa Shah was seen in the chair when the house resumed its proceedings. He adjourned the sitting till Tuesday after finding the house still not in order due to lack of quorum.

While the PPP had supported the government in the passage of the two security-related bills last week, Mr Bhutto-Zardari, in the presence of PM Shehbaz Sharif, had objected to the manner with which the government had been doing legislation.

After developing differences with the PML-N over the issue of AJK elections, a PPP delegation headed by Mr Bhutto-Zardari called on opposition leaders and sought their cooperation on the legislation in the parliament and its committees.

Hina Javed’s murder

At the outset of the sitting, the NA speaker expressed his concerns over the brutal murder of Hina Javed in Rawalpindi and referred the matter to the relevant house committee.

Mr Sadiq disclosed that Hina Javed had been posted in the National Assembly by the National IT Board on attachment from December 2019 till June this year after which she returned to her parent department. He said though such matters generally fell under provincial jurisdiction, the case was of particular concern since she had served at the NA.

He said the manner in which Hina Javed was murdered, and the violence against women, were matters of serious concern for everyone.

He appreciated the Women Parliamentary Caucus for taking up the matter and said the NA would provide full support in monitoring the case and extending whatever assistance was required.

Minister for Law and Human Rights Azam Nazeer Tarar said the ministry was in constant contact with the Rawalpindi police regarding the murder investigations. Two suspects were on three-day physical remand, he said, expressing the confidence that the culprits would be brought to justice.
