The group includes private lenders Kapital Bank and PASHA Bank. Banks linked to the family control a significant share of Azerbaijan’s banking-sector assets — more than 40%, according to some estimates. SOCAR: Azerbaijan’s state oil company is also entering Uzbekistan’s retail fuel market and plans to establish a network of filling stations there. At the same time, the company plans to cooperate with BP and Uzbekneftegaz on the Ustyurt field. SOCAR has also faced questions over transparency in the past, including in connection with the Azerbaijani Laundromat scandal.

Azerbaijan’s state oil company is also entering Uzbekistan’s retail fuel market and plans to establish a network of filling stations there. At the same time, the company plans to cooperate with BP and Uzbekneftegaz on the Ustyurt field. SOCAR has also faced questions over transparency in the past, including in connection with the Azerbaijani Laundromat scandal. Other projects: Other businesses entering the Uzbek market include the Matanat-A gypsum plant, Landau STEAM schools, the Sur gold and silver processing plant, Gold Fresh Fruits orchards, the Baku City residential complex and other projects. Some are being implemented as public-private partnerships.

Statements by the two presidents

President Ilham Aliyev said in a statement to the press that relations between the two countries were built “on a very solid foundation, both spiritually and materially”. He said the range of projects under discussion in energy, transport, investment, tourism, mining, automotive manufacturing, agriculture, processing and banking gave the cooperation an “unprecedented character”.

Aliyev said that on every visit he was struck by the rapid development of Tashkent and Uzbekistan as a whole. He said increasing bilateral trade to $1bn was “no longer a dream of the distant future, but a target that can be achieved within a few years”. He also highlighted Mirziyoyev’s particular role in attracting investment to Karabakh and invited him to make a state visit to Azerbaijan at a time convenient to him.

Shavkat Mirziyoyev described Aliyev’s visit as a “historic event”, saying the “Treaty on Eternal Friendship” was evidence of this and that the provisions on strategic partnership and alliance were being backed up by concrete action. In his remarks, he highlighted a threefold increase in bilateral trade over the past five years, the goal of raising it to $1bn, the joint development of the Middle Corridor, and the idea of creating a separate Azerbaijani-Uzbek corridor across the Caspian Sea with a single operator.

Mirziyoyev also said the two countries spoke “with one voice” on the international stage. He described Azerbaijan’s full participation in the consultative meetings of Central Asian heads of state as a historic step and praised Aliyev’s policy of restoring Azerbaijan’s territorial integrity, as well as the meeting in Washington and the declaration signed there.

Hikmet Hajiyev, a representative of the Azerbaijani presidential administration, said before and during the visit that relations between the two countries had reached a new level: moving from strategic partnership to alliance and then to “eternal friendship”. He said this was the first such step in the history of Azerbaijani diplomacy. According to Hajiyev, the “eternal friendship” that had already existed de facto between the two peoples had now been formally enshrined at the political level as well.

World.title: “When the state serves an oligarch, villages and cities empty out.” Video podcast “Protests in Georgia”
World.content:
Video podcast “Protests in Georgia”

The traditional pro-European “Saturday march” in Tbilisi on August 22 was dedicated to Georgian citizens who have left the country in search of work and better opportunities.

Participants said the growing emigration is driven by the policies of the ruling Georgian Dream party, which they say have pushed the country away from the European integration path enshrined in the Constitution.

Many blame the party’s founder and honorary chairman, oligarch Bidzina Ivanishvili, personally.

“Villages and cities are emptying out when the state serves Ivanishvili” — this was the central message of the march, reflected in the slogans and statements by speakers.

Organisers announced that throughout September, the traditional “Saturday marches” will be held in support of Georgian emigrants.

For more than a year and half – since November 2024 – continuous protests have been taking place in Georgia, with demonstrators demanding that the country return to the path of European integration. The results of the parliamentary elections held in autumn 2024 are still not recognised by part of Georgian society. Every evening thousands, and often tens of thousands, gather in Tbilisi and several other cities. Over this time dozens of participants have been detained, many have faced criminal charges, and some have been sentenced to prison terms. For the first time in the history of independent Georgia, the country has up to 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the popular outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti. In 2025 she was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer. Protesters demand the release of all political prisoners and the repeal of all anti-democratic laws adopted over the past two years. To suppress the protests, the ruling Georgian Dream party has increasingly tightened repression against civil society and the media. However, protests in various forms continue.

News in Georgia

World.title: Armenia’s new parliament: balance of power, tools of government and opposition’s dead end
World.content:
Balance of power in Armenia’s new parliament

The parliamentary election results in Armenia have confirmed the continuity of the country’s political system while exposing deep structural contradictions. Political competition has shifted decisively towards intense polarisation. The National Assembly risks turning into little more than a platform for mutual accusations resembling a television talk show, rather than the country’s highest legislative body.

Political analyst Alexander Iskandaryan’s assessment

Continuity of the system, limits of influence and a fragmented opposition

“The new National Assembly has retained the key feature of its predecessor. The Constitution allows the ruling Civil Contract party to make almost any decision on its own, except on issues that require a constitutional majority. The two opposition factions — former president Robert Kocharyan’s Armenia Alliance and businessman Samvel Karapetyan’s Strong Armenia — have access to the media and the parliamentary platform, and can openly express their views and criticise the government. However, they have no real leverage over current policy.

The opposition forces have undergone a reshuffle. In the eighth National Assembly, Kocharyan’s faction held the largest number of seats. In the new parliament, however, it is the smaller of the two opposition factions. They are also unlikely to build a stable coalition or an “umbrella” structure. Because of their different origins and the lack of a practical basis for cooperation, even if they unite, they will not secure 50% of the seats needed to take the initiative. A long-term alliance is impossible. In 35 years of the Third Republic, the opposition has never managed to produce a successful example of unity. The minority is therefore left with little more than keeping the protest movement alive.”

Legitimacy, voters and the government’s narratives

“The ruling party has significant external legitimacy. This includes recognition of the election results by the US, EU, Turkey and Azerbaijan, as well as Russia’s refusal to withhold recognition from Nikol Pashinyan. The ruling force also relies on support from the bureaucracy. In fact, bureaucratic legitimacy has grown stronger. Civil servants clearly understand their ties to the political leadership and recognise the risks that a change of elites could bring.

At the same time, the government’s social legitimacy remains low. Kocharyan won 10% despite his high negative rating, while Karapetyan’s party, hastily assembled over six months with its leader under arrest, won a quarter of the vote despite high turnout. This is a serious signal of the level of public dissatisfaction.

Realising that its support will not grow, the government abandoned any real ideology. Political strategists pragmatically discarded the “high-minded Yerevan intelligentsia”, which would not have voted for the government anyway and would not have gone to the polls. Instead, they focused on their target audience: residents of small towns and villages with lower levels of education, young people and older generations.

To maintain control, the government uses several narratives:

“Peace versus war” — portraying opponents as the “party of war” and frightening voters with the prospect that an opposition victory would lead to a new war in September.

“Democrats versus oligarchs” — selectively labelling businesses. Wealthy entrepreneurs who support the government are simply called “businessmen”, while any affluent opponents are automatically branded “oligarchs”.

“Europe versus Russia” — systematically linking the entire opposition to Moscow. Karapetyan is portrayed this way because he came from Russia, Gagik Tsarukyan because of his ties to Belarus, and Kocharyan as Putin’s personal friend.

Accusing voters of supporting the opposition solely for money. This new level of polarisation has emerged in official statements by the authorities.”

The government’s geopolitical narrative and the opposition’s dead end

“The government’s anti-Russian discourse found fertile ground. These sentiments had been developing for years, and the events of 2020 and 2023 — the war in Karabakh, followed by the exodus of the entire Armenian population from Nagorno-Karabakh — only strengthened them.

At the same time, people across the post-Soviet space have traditionally associated the word “European” with quality and development: European healthcare, European education, European cars and so on. The government has effectively exploited this perception. Direct public support for Pashinyan from senior US officials, up to and including the US president, also played an important role.

The opposition has found itself in a strategic dead end. It cannot openly say “we are pro-Russian” or “we are not pro-Russian”. Unable to reject the geopolitical trend that enjoys broad public support, opposition parties have had to adapt and repeat that they are “also in favour of cooperation with Europe, but for a more carefully calibrated policy”.

Personal attacks instead of alternative programmes

“Instead of substantive work, the opposition is sliding into negative rhetoric and personal attacks: who is corrupt, who got their wife a job, who owns which flat and who once “didn’t even have a washing machine”. Armenian society knows perfectly well how the bureaucratic hierarchy works, so such “exposés” do not work. All these scandals only play into the government’s hands, allowing it to say: “Look who we have to work with in parliament.”

A constructive alternative would be to develop concrete programmes in different areas — healthcare, pensions, the economy, the army and so on. Even if the ruling majority rejects, say, 15 such professional programmes in a row, a systematic effort to offer solutions will eventually resonate with society. For now, trolling has replaced politics.”

Real state priorities: security, energy and meritocracy

“While parliament is busy trolling, the country’s key problems remain unresolved. One of them is security.

It is wrong to call the situation with Azerbaijan peace. You can see what real peace looks like on the border with Georgia, for example: people can cross freely using an ID card, while there are no transport corridors, European observers, military guards or concrete walls, even though 30% of the border remains undelimited. With Baku, however, there is only a state of “no war”. That is far from peace. At the same time, Azerbaijan is rapidly expanding its military capabilities in every sphere, including its air force.

Armenia needs to make foreign policy decisions and find ways to overcome the energy crisis.

Relations with all four neighbours — Russia, Turkey, Azerbaijan and Iran — are in crisis. Meanwhile, the Armenian-American TRIPP “Trump Route” project — a transit route through Armenia — remains little more than a political narrative. At the same time, launching new facilities, such as an AI data centre in Hrazdan, could create an acute electricity shortage that talk of American small modular nuclear reactors alone cannot solve.

In the Armenian city of Hrazdan, Firebird AI’s artificial intelligence factory has begun operations. The facility is the largest AI data centre in the region. The first phase of the project, worth more than $500 million, uses advanced NVIDIA accelerators and server equipment from leading global manufacturers. Some experts believe the factory’s launch could put additional pressure on the country’s energy system. (firebird.ai)

The state needs a competent administration to overcome these challenges.

The country needs to embrace meritocracy, appointing people based on competence rather than loyalty.

Finally, the country’s leadership needs to reconsider its attitude towards citizens.

Nikol Pashinyan is the prime minister of all Armenians, not just the voters of Civil Contract. The claim that people could only have voted against the government in exchange for money is false and toxic. The government now faces a vast array of real problems. Its first task is to recognise the scale of those challenges and start addressing them.

Balance of power in Armenia’s new parliament

World.title: Anea the raccoon’s favourite activity at Tbilisi Zoo – video
World.content:
Anea the raccoon at Tbilisi Zoo

Raccoons love water. You can often see them swimming, wetting their fur or carefully washing their paws. Anea, a resident of Tbilisi Zoo, is no exception.

On hot days, Anea particularly enjoys dipping her paws in water and having a cool shower. So her keepers set up an improvised shower in her enclosure, which, as you can see in the video below, delighted her.

There is a metal container in her enclosure for drinking water, but who says she cannot take a bath in it too? Despite its small size, Anea fits perfectly inside, happily splashes around in the water and uses it to escape the summer heat. After noticing the raccoon’s love of bathing, her keepers have already ordered a bigger “bath”.

Tbilisi Zoo‘s history spans nearly a century. It was founded on 10 February 1927 on the basis of the Caucasian Society for the Acclimatisation of Animals, which had been keeping wild animals since the early 20th century, though without official zoo status.



The zoo was originally built on 70 hectares in the Vere River gorge. Over the years, the expansion of the capital — and later the devastating flood of 13 June 2015 — significantly reduced the territory of the old zoo. Today, it covers five hectares and is home to around 1,500 animals, each with its own story. In this video series, we will introduce you to the residents of Tbilisi Zoo.



We will show how their day unfolds, how they interact with other animals and people, and how their behaviour changes depending on the weather and the season. Get ready to hear many fascinating stories.

Anea the raccoon at Tbilisi Zoo

World.title: Opinion: ‘Moscow’s main fear is that Armenia will choose European Union’
World.content:
Opinion on Russia’s demand for a referendum in Armenia

In recent days, Russia‘s demand for Armenia to hold a referendum on whether the country should remain in the Russian-led Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) or choose the European Union has increasingly been seen as a threat. Experts from the “Armenian Council” think tank made the assessment in an article.

Russia has long demanded such a referendum, including at the highest level. But there are now threats to initiate proceedings concerning Armenia’s membership of the EAEU. Decisions within the bloc require consensus, and Yerevan has the right to veto them.

“Russia’s main phobia is that the situation will deteriorate over time, leading the Armenian people to choose the European Union,” the authors argue.

They stress that this is not only Russia’s “main phobia”, but also its “main misconception”. The analysts believe that even the “economic pressure and blackmail” that Russia began applying to Armenia in May, during the pre-election period, have not changed Armenian public opinion. They cite the results of the parliamentary election on 7 June as evidence: Armenia’s ruling party won, rather than pro-Russian forces.

Ahead of Armenia’s parliamentary election, Russia imposed restrictions on imports of Armenian agricultural products. It also banned imports of flowers, Jermuk mineral water, certain alcoholic drinks and fish products. The authorities justified the measures by citing failures to meet required quality standards. However, Armenian experts and officials viewed the issue in the context of the election campaign. They therefore expected the pressure to end after the election. But that did not happen. Moreover, Russia introduced new restrictions after the election. At the same time, in early June, four EAEU member states called on Armenian authorities to hold a referendum as soon as possible on choosing between the Eurasian bloc and the EU. Yerevan responded that there were currently no grounds for such a vote because Armenia’s European integration process had not yet reached the stage at which citizens could make a choice. Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan has repeatedly said that Armenia should first obtain EU candidate status or, at the very least, put the issue on the agenda. However, Moscow continues to insist. Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin said the EAEU expects Armenia to hold a referendum by December. Otherwise, the bloc’s leaders would “take this fact into account when determining appropriate further joint steps”. He said a report on the possible consequences of suspending the EAEU Treaty in relation to Armenia would be discussed at the December meeting of the Supreme Eurasian Economic Council.

Armenia’s prime minister spoke about a referendum on EU membership

“No one in Armenia has ever talked about holding a referendum on EAEU membership or an alternative in the form of the EU.

On 9 January 2025, when the Armenian government discussed and approved a bill to launch the EU accession process, Prime Minister Pashinyan said:

“Armenia can begin the process of joining the EU only if a certain number of referendum participants vote ‘yes’ in accordance with the procedure established by the Constitution.”

Senior Armenian officials later repeated this point on various occasions.

The key point is that Armenia will hold a referendum on joining the European Union, not on whether to remain in or leave the EAEU.

This fundamental difference significantly changes the forecasts for the expected outcome. However, if Armenia votes to join the EU, it will inevitably leave the EAEU at some stage of the subsequent process.”

Russia is pushing for a referendum on a different question

“Armenia’s willingness to hold a referendum on EU membership is fundamentally different from what Moscow wants to impose.

Russia is clearly manipulating the situation by demanding a referendum on the EAEU now, when Armenia is at least a decade away from joining the EU.

We need to understand the real reason for this urgency.

The Kremlin understands that if EU membership becomes a genuine possibility, no rational society could vote against it.

Therefore, to keep Armenia in the EAEU and have a chance of stopping its move towards the EU, a referendum must take place as soon as possible, while the prospect of EU membership remains unclear and uncertain.”

Moscow is trying to “beat” Europe by exploiting Armenian businesses’ dependence

“The EAEU mechanisms currently work in favour of Armenian businesses, creating influence and dependence.

At the same time, Armenia is steadily diversifying its economy, reducing that influence and dependence.

The question of whether to remain in the EAEU directly affects many companies with specific interests in Russia. By contrast, EU membership remains a more abstract issue for them for now.

Moscow does not expect to “beat” Europe in economic competition over the next few years or even decades and offer Armenia more attractive conditions. It therefore believes it still has an opportunity to influence the situation now. That is why it is in such a hurry.”

Opinion on Russia’s demand for a referendum in Armenia

World.title: Uzbekistan’s investment boom: Can capital deliver sustainable growth?
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 25. Uzbekistan is accelerating its investment drive as the government seeks to expand industrial capacity, attract foreign capital and deepen the role of private investment in the economy. With 338.9 trillion soums ($28.6 billion) invested in fixed capital in the first half of 2026, a 17.5% year-on-year increase, and $32.9 billion in foreign investments and loans utilized in the period from January through July, the scale of capital formation is becoming a defining feature of the country's growth model.

The government is now moving beyond simply attracting investment. It is attempting to build the financial, industrial and human-capital infrastructure needed to turn inflows of capital into higher productivity, stronger exports and sustainable economic growth.

This shift is increasingly visible in the composition of investment. Manufacturing, construction and energy-related activities accounted for nearly half of fixed-capital investment in the first half of the year, while the government is simultaneously preparing new industrial and infrastructure projects worth billions of dollars and expanding companies' access to international capital markets.

However, the key question is whether Uzbekistan will be able to turn this investment boom into long-term productive capacity, rather than simply an increase in capital inflows.

Investment becomes a central pillar of growth

Uzbekistan's investment expansion is taking place against a backdrop of sustained economic growth.

Speaking at the Silk Road Finance & Technology Forum, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Economy and Finance Jamshid Kuchkarov said average annual GDP growth had remained around 6–7%, while the economy had tripled in nominal terms from approximately $60 billion to $180 billion.

The country's economic expansion has been accompanied by improving macroeconomic indicators. Kuchkarov said inflation, which had previously remained in double digits, is expected to reach around 6.5% this year, with the government targeting the 5% level next year. External public debt has remained around 27% of GDP, while budget deficits have stayed below 3% of GDP in recent years.

This combination of relatively rapid growth and improving macroeconomic stability is important for investors. A predictable macroeconomic environment reduces some of the risks associated with long-term projects, particularly in infrastructure and manufacturing, where investment returns often depend on conditions over many years.

At the same time, Uzbekistan is seeking to improve its sovereign credit standing, complete accession to the World Trade Organization, and further reduce the state's role in the economy.

These reforms suggest that the government sees foreign investment not as a temporary source of financing, but as part of a broader transition toward a more market-oriented economic model.

Manufacturing is at the heart of the investment drive

The distribution of fixed-capital investment in the first half of 2026 provides an important indication of where Uzbekistan's growth strategy is heading.

Manufacturing attracted 100.5 trillion soums ($8.5 billion), making it by far the largest recipient and accounting for almost 30% of total fixed-capital investment.

Agriculture, forestry and fisheries followed with 32.9 trillion soums ($2.7 billion), while construction attracted 32.5 trillion soums ($2.7 billion).

Electricity, gas, steam and air-conditioning supply received 29.9 trillion soums ($2.5 billion), residential construction accounted for 27.3 trillion soums ($2.3 billion), and mining and quarrying attracted 21.8 trillion soums ($1.9 billion).

Transportation and storage received another 16.3 trillion soums ($1.4 billion).

Taken together, manufacturing, construction and energy-related activities attracted approximately 162.9 trillion soums ($13.8 billion), or about 48% of all fixed-capital investment during the first half of the year.

The concentration is significant. It suggests that Uzbekistan is prioritizing sectors that can directly expand physical production capacity and address infrastructure constraints.

Manufacturing investment alone was more than three times the amount allocated to agriculture, forestry and fisheries, the second-largest recipient.

For Uzbekistan, this could support a gradual transition from an economy reliant on commodity production and domestic demand toward one with a larger industrial and export-oriented base.

But the size of investment will not by itself determine whether that transition succeeds. The critical issue will be whether new factories and infrastructure generate sufficient productivity gains, exports and local value creation.

$27 billion project pipeline signals continued expansion

The investment drive is also being reinforced by a large pipeline of new projects.

Uzbekistan plans to launch 105 industrial and infrastructure projects worth $27 billion this year, covering energy, transport, manufacturing, logistics and urban development.

Among the major projects are a nuclear power plant in Jizzakh, a fourth copper processing plant in Almalyk, new highways connecting Tashkent with Samarkand and Andijan, an environmentally friendly aviation-fuel complex in Khorezm, a large greenhouse complex in Surkhandarya and the New Tashkent airport in Yukori Chirchiq.

The scale and diversity of these projects illustrate an important feature of Uzbekistan's investment strategy: capital is being directed simultaneously toward production, energy security, transport connectivity and urban infrastructure.

This matters because infrastructure bottlenecks could otherwise constrain the country's rapid economic expansion.

Electricity and gas supply attracted almost $2.5 billion in fixed investment during the first half of 2026, while transportation and storage received around $1.4 billion. These investments can provide the underlying infrastructure required for industrial expansion.

The challenge is to ensure that infrastructure investment remains closely linked to productive economic activity rather than creating excess capacity or placing unnecessary pressure on public finances.

The next stage: bringing private companies to international capital markets

One of the most significant developments in Uzbekistan's investment strategy is the government's attempt to diversify the sources of corporate financing.

Uzbekistan aims to attract at least $1 billion in foreign capital annually through IPOs, creating an alternative to traditional bank lending.

The initiative follows the listing of a 30% stake in the National Investment Fund, which holds assets in 13 strategic companies, on the Tashkent and London stock exchanges.

The government plans to select 50 companies each year with annual revenues exceeding 1 trillion soums for an IPO acceleration program. It will cover half of the costs associated with preparing companies for listings and bringing their financial reporting into line with international standards.

This could become an important structural change for Uzbekistan's economy.

The country's investment boom has so far relied heavily on large projects, bank financing and foreign investment. Developing equity markets could broaden access to capital and allow successful domestic companies to finance expansion without relying exclusively on bank loans.

The policy is also consistent with the government's wider objective of reducing the state's presence in the economy.

If more Uzbek companies become capable of raising capital internationally, the result could be greater corporate transparency, stronger financial reporting and increased participation by institutional investors.

However, turning the initiative into a sustainable source of foreign capital will require Uzbek companies to strengthen transparency, corporate governance and financial reporting while demonstrating strong growth potential to international investors.

The banking system is also being redirected toward smaller businesses

While the government is developing equity markets for larger companies, it is simultaneously attempting to improve access to finance for small and medium-sized businesses.

The share of small businesses in banks' loan portfolios has increased from 45% to 63%, while 76.5 trillion soums ($6.4 billion) was allocated to SMEs during the first half of 2026.

A new digital portal allows entrepreneurs to submit a single credit application while banks compete to provide financing. New entrepreneurs can apply online for loans of up to 5 billion soums (about $423,026).

The government is also introducing three programs — Business Start, Business Lift and Business Rise — designed to support businesses at different stages of development.

Under Business Start, entrepreneurs will receive assistance with project development, loan documentation and financial reporting, including through artificial intelligence. The program will have 100 billion soums ($8.4 million) in funding and offer ready-made business plans and unsecured loans of up to 200 million soums (around $16,921).

This approach is important because a sustainable investment economy cannot rely exclusively on large foreign-funded projects.

The development of domestic SMEs is necessary to create local suppliers, services and employment around major investment projects. If small businesses can scale into larger companies, the benefits of foreign investment could spread further through the domestic economy.

Human capital may become the next investment bottleneck

One of the more important aspects of Uzbekistan's current investment policy is the growing emphasis on skills.

President Shavkat Mirziyoyev has highlighted the need to link investment in advanced technologies with workforce development, noting that Uzbekistan is implementing $50 billion worth of high-tech investment projects annually and that training must form part of such projects.

This is an important consideration because the productivity gains from foreign investment depend not only on the arrival of new equipment or technology, but also on the ability of local workers to operate and maintain it.

A vocational training model based on German and Chinese experience has already been introduced in Urgench, covering professions including green energy, construction, nursing, agronomy and electrical engineering.

The government aims to train 1 million young people in modern professions and help them secure higher-paying jobs.

For an economy experiencing rapid industrialization, this could be decisive.

Uzbekistan can attract factories, power plants and infrastructure projects relatively quickly. Building a workforce capable of supporting increasingly sophisticated industries takes considerably longer.

A shortage of skilled workers could therefore become a constraint on the country's ability to absorb foreign technology and move into higher-value manufacturing.

Logistics is another piece of the investment equation

Uzbekistan's investment strategy is also increasingly linked to its ambition to become a regional logistics hub.

The government has abolished import duties and recycling fees on trucks and plans to reduce VAT on the provision of railway wagons for international transportation to zero.

A logistics center with a capacity of 500,000 tons is expected to begin operations at Georgia's Poti port next year, while work on the Anaklia port project is also planned.

Major logistics hubs are planned in Alat, Termez, Yangiyul, Akhangaran and Khanabad.

For a landlocked country, improvements in logistics can have an economic impact extending far beyond the transport sector. Lower transportation costs and improved access to international markets can make Uzbek manufacturing more competitive and encourage foreign companies to use the country as a production base.

The development of transport links therefore complements investment in manufacturing.

A factory can increase production, but without efficient access to export markets its potential remains limited.

Azerbaijan-Uzbekistan investment cooperation adds another dimension

The growing scale of Uzbekistan's investment needs is also creating opportunities for bilateral investment partnerships.

During the third meeting of the Supreme Interstate Council of Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan, President Ilham Aliyev said the projects already envisioned and contracted between the two countries significantly exceed the capacity of the $500 million Uzbekistan-Azerbaijan Investment Fund.

According to Aliyev, around $160 million of the fund had already been allocated, while the overall portfolio of projects is considerably larger.

He specifically pointed to plans for approximately $5 billion in investment in Uzbekistan's tourism sector alone, in addition to hotel and residential projects in Tashkent that fall outside the investment fund's current scope.

The comments indicate that the existing investment mechanism may need to expand if bilateral projects continue to grow.

More importantly, the Uzbekistan-Azerbaijan example illustrates how foreign investment is increasingly moving beyond individual projects toward broader investment ecosystems involving funds, infrastructure, tourism, logistics and real estate.

For Uzbekistan, diversified bilateral investment partnerships can provide additional sources of capital while reducing dependence on any single investor or financing channel.

The diversification question

Despite the positive momentum, Uzbekistan's investment figures also reveal areas where diversification could go further.

Investment remains heavily concentrated in manufacturing, construction, energy, mining and infrastructure.

By comparison, sectors such as finance, healthcare, information and communications, professional services and other knowledge-intensive activities attracted substantially smaller amounts.

Financial and insurance activities received only 2.4 trillion soums (about $203 million), while information and communications attracted 5.8 trillion soums (around $490.7 million), and healthcare and social services received 4.6 trillion soums (approx. $389.1 million).

This does not necessarily indicate weakness. In a rapidly industrializing economy, infrastructure and manufacturing naturally require substantial capital.

However, as Uzbekistan's physical infrastructure expands, the next stage of growth could require greater investment in digital technologies, financial services, healthcare, education, professional services and other high-value sectors.

Greater diversification would also make the economy less dependent on capital-intensive industries.

The real test is what happens after the investment arrives

Uzbekistan has already demonstrated that it can attract substantial capital.

The more difficult question is whether the investment will generate sufficient economic returns.

The country's 17.5% increase in fixed-capital investment, $32.9 billion in utilized foreign investments and loans during January-July, and a $27 billion project pipeline demonstrate strong investor and government activity.

But the ultimate success of the strategy will depend on several factors.

First, new projects must generate higher productivity and exports, rather than simply increasing domestic capacity.

Second, foreign investment needs to create stronger links with Uzbek companies through local procurement, technology transfer, and workforce development.

Third, the expansion of capital markets must give successful domestic businesses access to financing beyond bank credit.

Fourth, investment in infrastructure must keep pace with industrial expansion.

And finally, the country must continue strengthening macroeconomic stability and regulatory predictability.

Uzbekistan's government appears increasingly aware of this shift. Its policies now connect investment with privatization, IPOs, SME financing, logistics, vocational education, and international market integration.

That suggests the country is moving from an investment-attraction model toward an investment-conversion model.

The objective is no longer simply to bring more dollars into Uzbekistan. It is to turn those dollars into factories, exports, technology, skilled workers, competitive domestic companies, and higher incomes.

The scale of investment now being mobilized allows Uzbekistan to accelerate its transformation into a more diversified and productive economy.

But the size of the opportunity also raises the stakes.

The success of Uzbekistan's investment boom will ultimately be measured not by how much capital enters the country, but by how effectively that capital changes what the economy produces, exports and earns.

World.title: Haskoning flags business climate as key for Turkmenistan ties (Exclusive)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 25. A favorable business environment will influence the pace of international companies' engagement with Turkmenistan.

Haskoning made the assessment in an exclusive response to questions from Trend about prospects for cooperation with Turkmenistan in water management, infrastructure and sustainable development.

"Companies typically consider factors such as transparency, ease of doing business, regulatory predictability and good governance when evaluating opportunities in developing markets," the company said.

According to Haskoning, these factors can affect the scale and pace of engagement by international firms with Turkmenistan.

"These aspects can present challenges in Turkmenistan and will naturally influence the level and pace of engagement by international firms, such as Haskoning," the company noted.

At the same time, Haskoning sees opportunities for cooperation with Turkmenistan and other countries across the South Caucasus, Caspian region and Central Asia.

"The South Caucasus, Caspian region and Central Asia offer significant opportunities for sustainable development. With our expertise in water management (climate adaptation), water technology, port infrastructure and renewable energy, Haskoning could contribute to projects that support long-term economic and environmental resilience in the region," the company said.

Haskoning also expressed conditional interest in participating in a planned bilateral business forum between Turkmenistan and the Netherlands.

"We would also welcome the opportunity to participate in a bilateral business forum between Turkmenistan and the Netherlands, should an invitation be extended, Haskoning would be happy to look into that," the company added.

For reference, Haskoning is an independent Dutch consulting engineering company with roots dating back to 1881. Royal Haskoning and DHV merged in 2012 to form Royal HaskoningDHV, which became the Netherlands' largest independent engineering and consultancy firm at the time. In 2025, the company adopted the shorter name Haskoning while retaining its Royal designation. Today, Haskoning employs around 6,800 people and operates internationally across aviation, climate resilience, data centres, energy, industry, maritime, mobility, tunnels and bridges, and water technology.

Haskoning has a history of work related to Turkmenistan and the wider Central Asian region. From 2007 to 2009, as part of the Caspian Environmental Programme, Haskoning led the "Caspian Water Quality Monitoring and Action Plan for Areas of Pollution Concern" project, funded under the TACIS programme. During this period, Haskoning also maintained its regional project office in Ashgabat.

World.title: QazaqGaz reports net profit decline in first half of 2026
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 25. QazaqGaz recorded a net profit of 41.79 billion tenge ($91.21 million) for the first six months of 2026, representing a 61.65% decline compared to 108.97 billion tenge ($237.8 million) reported in the same period of 2025.

This was announced in a financial statement published by the QazaqGaz.

According to the statement, in the second quarter of 2026 (April–June), the company's net profit reached 88.37 billion tenge ($192.86 million), down 8.1% from 96.17 billion tenge ($209.88 million) earned in Q2 2025.

''Despite the decrease in overall net profit, revenue from contracts with customers grew by 13.22% in the first half of 2026, reaching 720.79 billion tenge ($1.57 billion), up from 636.64 billion tenge ($1.39 billion) in the first six months of 2025,'' the financial statement indicates.

QazaqGaz reduced its consolidated gross loss for the six-month period to 48.90 billion tenge ($106.71 million), compared to a gross loss of 123.94 billion tenge ($270.47 million) recorded in 1H 2025.

The company's performance was further supported by its share of profit from joint ventures and associates, which contributed 145.36 billion tenge ($317.22 million) during the six-month period, compared to 161.03 billion tenge ($351.38 million) in the corresponding period of last year.

As of June 30, 2026, total assets of QazaqGaz stood at 5.22 trillion tenge ($11.39 billion), up from 4.67 trillion tenge ($10.19 billion) at the end of 2025. Currency conversions are based on the official exchange rate of $1 = 458.23 tenge as of August 21, 2026.

According to Trend analysis, QazaqGaz's financial results reflect a widening gap between revenue growth and bottom-line performance. The increase in operating revenue indicates stronger commercial activity and the effect of tariff adjustments, while profitability remains constrained by the company's role in ensuring domestic gas supply and meeting regulated-market obligations.

The significant narrowing of the gross loss points to improving cost efficiency and could indicate that recent pricing and operational measures are beginning to have an effect. However, the decline in earnings from joint ventures and associates suggests that external income sources provided somewhat less support than in the previous year.

The continued expansion of the company's asset base points to an ongoing investment cycle focused on gas transportation infrastructure, network modernization and field development. These investments could strengthen QazaqGaz's long-term capacity to meet growing domestic demand, although they also imply sustained capital requirements and pressure on financial resources.

World.title: Kyrgyzstan advances major Suusamyr-Talas-Taraz highway reconstruction
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 25. Reconstruction of the fourth phase of the Suusamyr-Talas-Taraz highway is currently underway in Kyrgyzstan’s Talas region, involving 220 units of specialized equipment and 473 specialists.

This was announced in a report published by Kyrgyzstan's Ministry of Transport and Communications.

According to the report, Deputy Minister of Transport and Communications Baktyluu Mombekov inspected the progress of works on the highway during a working visit to the Talas region and issued relevant instructions to responsible services.

''The fourth phase covers the 104.6–197.6-kilometer section of the Suusamyr-Talas-Taraz road. The project began in April 202,'' the report says.

The ministry notes that trees have been cleared along 61.3 kilometers of the route, while the old asphalt-concrete pavement has been removed along 39.21 kilometers.

Road widening works have been completed along 53.1 kilometers on both sides. The lower road foundation layer has been laid along 10.4 kilometers, while the upper foundation layer has been completed along 5.95 kilometers.

The lower layer of asphalt concrete has also been laid along 4.35 kilometers.

As part of the relocation of engineering infrastructure, 15.7 kilometers of communication lines and 15.8 kilometers of power transmission lines have been relocated. In addition, 2.7 kilometers of lighting lines have been dismantled.

Construction of artificial structures included in the project is also underway. Work is currently being carried out at seven facilities, including bridges and an underpass, with their completion ranging from 11% to 90%.

Of the 190 culverts planned under the project, 41 have been fully completed.

According to the approved schedule, the overall completion rate is expected to reach 25% by the end of 2026, while 20 kilometers of new asphalt-concrete pavement are planned to be laid by then.

The project is expected to improve travel conditions and road safety for residents and transit traffic once completed.

Construction is scheduled for completion by April 25, 2028. The reconstruction is being carried out by China-based Shaanxi Construction Engineering Group Co., Ltd.

The contractor will provide a five-year warranty after the facility is commissioned, according to the ministry.

According to Trend's analysis, the ongoing reconstruction of the Suusamyr-Talas-Taraz highway reflects Kyrgyzstan's broader efforts to upgrade its road infrastructure and strengthen transport links between the country's regions and neighboring markets.

The reconstruction of the 104.6–197.6-kilometer section is expected to improve road safety, travel conditions, and transport efficiency along an important route connecting Kyrgyzstan's northern regions with international transit corridors. The relocation of communication and power infrastructure, construction of bridges, an underpass and culverts, as well as the installation of new asphalt-concrete pavement, are key components of the modernization effort.

The project is also likely to support the movement of people and goods, improve access to local communities, and create more favorable conditions for transit traffic. Better road infrastructure can contribute to greater economic activity in the Talas region by facilitating trade, logistics and regional mobility.

Looking ahead, the completion of the project could further strengthen Kyrgyzstan's domestic transport network and its connectivity with neighboring countries. Continued investment in major road corridors is likely to remain important for improving logistics efficiency, supporting regional economic development and expanding the country's transit and tourism potential.

World.title: Turkish construction adjusts as infrastructure offsets building slowdown
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 25. Türkiye’s construction output declined 6.0% year-on-year in June 2026, reflecting weaker building activity alongside continued expansion in civil engineering projects.

According to data from the Turkish Statistical Institute (TÜİK), building construction decreased 7.5% year-on-year and 0.4% compared with May. Specialized construction activities, including drilling, demolition and installation works, declined 7.6% annually and 1.0% month-on-month. At the same time, civil engineering was the only subsector to record growth, increasing 4.5% year-on-year and 0.1% from the previous month. Overall construction production decreased 0.5% compared with May. "When the subsectors of the construction (based on 2021=100) were examined, construction of buildings index decreased by 7.5%, civil engineering index increased by 4.5% and specialised construction activities index decreased by 7.6% in June 2026, compared with same month of previous year," the statement of TÜİK says.

The data shows a divergence between different segments of Türkiye’s construction sector. The 12 percentage point gap between building construction (-7.5%) and civil engineering (+4.5%) indicates that infrastructure-related activity is providing support while the residential segment continues to adjust to tighter financial conditions.

Civil engineering, which includes road construction, bridges, utilities and public works, has benefited from ongoing infrastructure investments. Building construction and specialized activities, meanwhile, remain influenced by the impact of the monetary tightening cycle, which saw the Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye’s policy rate reach 50% in 2024, affecting financing conditions for housing projects.

The construction data is consistent with June 2026 housing market indicators. Calendar-adjusted new home sales declined 1.5% year-on-year, while existing home sales decreased 8.6%. At the same time, headline new home sales increased 23.1%, supported partly by calendar effects. The combination of softer construction output and mixed housing indicators suggests that Türkiye’s residential market is undergoing a transition period rather than a broad-based contraction.

Mortgage activity has shown signs of recovery. Mortgaged home sales increased 72.1% year-on-year in June 2026, although the comparison base remains low following limited mortgage activity in 2024. The impact of improving financing conditions on construction activity is expected to appear with a time lag, as building permits, land purchases and construction starts typically precede completed projects by one to two years.

Trend’s calculations show that the current monetary easing cycle — with the policy rate declining from 50% toward approximately 35% by mid-2026 — could begin supporting construction production indicators from late 2026 or early 2027 as financing conditions gradually improve.

The decline in specialized construction activity also reflects changes in the structure of earthquake-related reconstruction work. Following the February 2023 earthquake affecting 11 provinces, activities such as demolition, foundation works and structural reinforcement remained elevated through 2023–2025. The 7.6% annual decline in June suggests that the reconstruction process is moving from the most intensive emergency-related phase toward more standard building activity.

Additional context comes from TÜİK industrial production data on construction materials. In June 2026, construction materials output increased 9.4% year-on-year, while construction production declined 6.0%.

This divergence suggests that demand for construction inputs remains supported despite weaker residential construction activity. Trend’s calculations indicate that the difference between materials production growth (+9.4%) and construction output decline (-6.0%) represents a 15.4 percentage point gap, which can be explained by several factors, including stronger demand from infrastructure projects, export activity and preparation for future construction activity.

The increase in construction materials production is also consistent with the 14.8% rise in industrial export delivery values, indicating that part of the additional output may be linked to external demand.

In Trend’s assessment, Türkiye’s construction sector is currently experiencing a rebalancing phase: infrastructure projects and improving financing conditions provide support, while residential construction adjusts after a period of high interest rates. The divergence between segments is likely to narrow as lower financing costs gradually translate into new housing activity.
