World.title: National Trust volunteers treated 'like servants', inquiry hears
World.content:
The National Trust of South Australia (NTSA) treats volunteers like "servants" and needs tighter government oversight, a parliamentary inquiry has been told.

The remarks were made on Monday at a packed Moonta Town Hall, where members of parliament on the Environment, Resources and Development Committee heard from locals affected by the shutdown of the Moonta Mines Heritage Precinct.

NTSA closed the tourist attraction in February and locked out volunteers, after months of management disagreement with the Moonta governing committee.

After a bitter legal dispute, the local committee was re-instated last month, but the episode exposed rifts within the charity, which owns more than 80 historically significant properties around the state.

National Trust of South Australia Moonta branch chair Sharron Ward speaks at the parliamentary inquiry. (ABC News)

NTSA Moonta branch chair Sharron Ward told the inquiry the organisation showed a "lack of respect to its volunteers" and "[needed] to be brought into modern standards".

"They're like lord of the manor and we're like servants," Ms Ward said.

"There needs to be a mutually beneficial relationship, whereas most branches feel like they're done unto."

Under parliamentary privilege, Ms Ward said the NTSA used "embellishments and distortion" to justify her committee's sacking in February over alleged compliance breaches, which she said had come from a "disgruntled former staff member" of NTSA.

The charity's head office only offered the committee details about the breaches three weeks later, according to Ms Ward.

"These actions assumed that the breaches were accurate without any attempts to investigate their validity," she told the inquiry.

The parliamentary inquiry was held at the Moonta Town Hall on Monday. (ABC News: George Yankovich)

She said the Moonta branch wanted "autonomy" from the wider organisation, including greater control over their properties and finances, while keeping the National Trust name.

The National Trust Act has not had major updates since 1955 and does not outline how the organisation should operate.

"At the current time, we're at their beck and call," Ms Ward said.

In a statement, the NTSA said it "continues to cooperate" with the parliamentary inquiry and has agreed to work with the Moonta branch to reopen and operate the heritage sites after recent mediation.

"With respect to the ongoing parliamentary inquiry, we feel it is inappropriate to be drawn on evidence given about suggested changes to the NTSA's future structure or operation," the trust said.

"The branch and the NTSA have agreed to implement measures to improve and ensure the proper administration of branch affairs, for the benefit of all, into the future.

"The parties have also agreed on a range of steps they will each take to improve their future working relationship."

Visitors vanished

Copper Coast Residents and Ratepayers Association chair Neil Windsor said Moonta experienced a "major drop in visitors" during the closure, citing reports from business owners.

"It's just ripped our guts out," he said.

"When all this was closed, you could see this town was crying. You just had to walk around."

The inquiry heard the closure of the Moonta Mines sites impacted the community's tourism. (ABC News: Shannon Pearce)

Mr Windsor endorsed a "complete review" of the legislation "to take into account the true value and respect of volunteers".

The parliamentary inquiry also canvassed whether NTSA should require ministerial approval before selling assets, following reports that historic properties were being sold to cover administrative costs.

Copper Coast Council chief executive officer Dylan Strong told the inquiry the idea warranted exploration.

"It is in the public interest that that portfolio be protected and there should be a comprehensive investigation to ensure that protection," he said.

Ms Di Lernia previously told the ABC the organisation was "asset-rich" but struggling with cash flow after recording a more than $300,000 deficit last financial year.

To increase cash flow, she said the organisation would "from time to time sell off assets" and was "actively working" to sell some non-core assets.

The NTSA Moonta branch committee members, who care for heritage sites in the area, were reinstated last month. (ABC News: Shannon Pearce)

Goyder Regional Council chief David Stevenson, whose council also works with the NTSA, told the inquiry people should be allowed to lodge ombudsman complaints about the organisation.

"They are the custodians of a very large asset group and there is significant public interest in what they do," he said.

The inquiry is expected to hear from the NTSA executive at a separate hearing next month.

World.title: Brisbane bans secret filming with AI glasses at council pools
World.content:
Brisbane City Council has banned the use of AI smart glasses to secretly film people in its public pools.

Today the council announced a blanket ban on the non-consensual use of all camera-enabled devices, including wearable technology, phones, and action cameras.

Under the new conditions of entry, people will still be able to bring smart glasses into the pool, but will not be able to film without permission.

The ban will apply to video recordings as well as photographs.

Under Queensland law it is legal to film people in public areas, even without their knowledge or consent.

However, the council's new rules will allow its lifeguards to eject pool visitors who film others without their permission.

An evolving problem

Adrian Schrinner says smart glasses are becoming more accessible. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

Brisbane Lord Mayor Adrian Schrinner said swimmers were increasingly worried about smart glasses being used to surreptitiously film them.

He said these concerns were mounting due to the rise of Anko smart glasses, which were much cheaper than Meta Ray-Bans.

"We want everyone that uses our pools to know that they're not secretly being recorded by other users of the pool, that their children are not being recorded," Cr Schrinner said.

" It's everyone's right when they visit a council pool to feel safe and comfortable. "

The council says the ban will be rolled out "in the coming weeks" across all 21 of its public pools.

Tom Tulston, head of policy at Digital Rights Watch, welcomed the ban.

He said the state and federal governments should also be regulating the use of this smart technology.

"We all need to be able to go out in public without fear of being covertly recorded and having the images uploaded to the internet without our consent," Mr Tulston said.

"We look forward to seeing not just councils following Brisbane's lead, but also state and federal governments."

Luke Twyford says smart glasses pose a risk to child safety. (ABC News: Nickoles Coleman)

Queensland Family and Child Commission principal commissioner Luke Twyford said the ban would safeguard children.

"Child harm and abuse can be hard to recognise, and all organisations need to ensure the services and spaces they operate are safe for children and prevent exploitation," he said.

"I'm really glad to see Brisbane City Council considering its role in making Queensland a safe place and taking steps to reduce foreseeable risks."

World.title: Sightings of 'Sammy' the seal lying next to dead birds spark concerns
World.content:
For the past seven years, Scott Kempton has taken boats out of the waters of Portland, Victoria for maintenance — but for the past three weeks, he has used a long-handled shovel to clear the same slipway of dozens of dead birds.

"There was one day last week where there was 22," said the slipway operator.

Scott Kempton says Sammy is "not as aggro" as Tasmania's famous "Neil the Seal". (Supplied)

While he said the removal efforts were partly to prevent "stinking the joint out", Mr Kempton's mission is further fuelled by the presence of "Sammy", a celebrity seal.

Locals have seen the multi-tonne elephant seal resting near birds that have died close to one of his frequent hang-out spots.

"The first one was a [crested] tern … He was laying with it for probably five or six hours," said Mr Kempton, a resident of the coastal city in the state's south west.

" [The community] are worried that he'll get bird flu and he'll tip over. "

Locals have called for elephant seals, like Sammy, to be protected at all costs. (Supplied: Helen Oakley)

Attention on the ground

The local concerns come as Australia confirms the first bird flu mammal death in a long-nosed fur seal — a different species of seal to Sammy — in Beachport on SA's Limestone Coast.



Portland residents are calling for authorities to protect the local icon and other seals.

"They are vaccinating penguins as it's a money raiser," resident Helen Oakley said.

" Why not ensure this unique seal is protected at all costs? "

Locals have taken to bagging and removing dead birds from Portland's beaches. (ABC News: Jean Bell)

Ms Oakley, who is a wildlife advocate, said the authorities needed to ensure there were no bird carcasses lying around Sammy when the seal was resting on land.

She said she recently counted 15 dead terns in the vicinity of Sammy.

High-profile and high-risk

Across the subantarctic, the population of southern elephant seals like Sammy have been dealt a heavy blow by the deadly avian flu.

University of Tasmania Antarctic ecologist Jane Younger worked on the island of South Georgia, where tens of thousands of seal pups died from the virus.

"We're coming ashore and there's hundreds or even thousands of carcasses in some places," she said

Dr Younger said not a lot could be done to limit the spread of bird flu among elephant seals, though a vaccine trial on northern elephant seals in the United States was underway.

Sammy the Seal near a dead seagull. (Supplied: Scott Kempton)

But she said Sammy's isolation may actually help the seal avoid infection.

"He doesn't have other seals to transmit it to him, so that's a good thing," she said.

"But he could get it from infected birds, or possibly the environment if the environment is infected.

"Carcass removal from the area that he's living is something that could be looked at, but making sure that's all done in a safe way."

Keep a distance

Sammy the elephant seal is a regular visitor to the south-west Victorian town of Portland. (Supplied: Shirley Stanford)

Back in Portland, Ms Oakley called on people to keep away from elephant seals to ensure their safety and that of the mammal.

"If the seal does attack anyone it gets euthanased, so please follow guidelines to protect it all costs," she said.

Ms Oakley said there had been "idiot people" getting too close to Sammy the seal and harassing and yelling at the mammal.

"They need to back off and let the animal rest in peace and quiet, particularly with the prevalence of bird flu," she said.

She said people needed to stay 30 metres away from a seal, and keep dogs away.

Mr Kempton said while he was satisfied with the Victorian government's response, he believed many in the community were angry at what they felt had been inaction.

Sammy the elephant seal at the port in Portland. (Supplied: Helen Oakley)

"I don't really know what the government can do," he said.

"It's a bird flu, [birds] are going to die.

"You can't stop the birds from dying, but if people keep moving them away from [Sammy], it’s got to help."

Agriculture Victoria was contacted for comment, but did not respond in time for publication.

World.title: Sailor codenamed 'Aquaman' to face trial over alleged plan to smuggle dealer
World.content:
A seafaring couple accused of attempting to help a wanted drug trafficker flee Australia to avoid criminal justice have been committed to stand trial in Darwin.

German national Thomas Goertz and his partner Jade Siu Ying Ormiston were arrested on a yacht in the Arafura Sea with fugitive drug trafficker Hussein Chamas on January 26, 2025.

Mr Goertz and Ms Ormiston are alleged to have sailed their yacht, the SS Coconuts, to the remote Northern Territory town of Nhulunbuy where they met Chamas on a beach.

The Darwin Local Court heard today that Mr Goertz had been communicating with a shadowy international syndicate under the codename "Aquaman" with a plan to take Chamas, codenamed "VIP", into international waters to allegedly escape facing justice in Australia.

Chamas had absconded from a New South Wales rehab facility earlier that same month.

Thomas Goertz and Jade Siu Ying Ormiston onboard the boat where they were arrested by Australian Federal Police in 2025. (Supplied: Australian Federal Police)

Judge David Woodroffe said suspicion was aroused after an Australian Border Force (ABF) officer in Nhulunbuy saw Chamas fishing off East Woody Beach with no fishing line.

The judge said written submissions indicated there was a "clandestine meeting with fugitive Chamas" at the beach where Mr Goertz and Ms Ormiston took him aboard and "below deck for him to be taken to international waters in the direction of West Papua".

"The tendency of that conduct, the transportation of the fugitive Chamas to an international destination point out of Australia, would be contrary to requirement for the person not to leave both NSW and the country, as required in the criminal proceedings," the judge said.

" It would be self-evident that with the location of Chamas, in a foreign country, the course of justice would be perverted or obstructed. "

Earlier this month Chamas was sentenced to more than 10 years in jail for drug trafficking charges and for trying to flee Australia.

With time served he is eligible for release in 2030.

Loading...

'High-risk activity for high-end gain'

In delivering his decision for Mr Goertz and Ms Ormiston to stand trial, Judge Woodroffe said there was evidence from encrypted messages which showed Mr Goertz had a history of "extracting" wanted criminals from Australia aboard his yacht for lucrative financial reward.

"This was no mere series of coincidences," he said.

"Goertz, since 2023, has been involved in high-risk activity for high-end gain."

Thomas Goertz, 51, of Germany, has faced the Darwin Local Court. (Supplied)

Judge Woodroffe said the submissions contended there was evidence of "long-term planning and coordination over extended periods of time" by the pair, including by purchasing the SS Coconuts and leaving it in dry-docks in Darwin prior to the operation.

"As well as being trustworthy to the syndicate they had the ability to deliver successful extractions," he said.

"Such abilities and resourcing for international travel, secretive codes, encrypted discussions, avoidance detection payments through transfers, are all indicative of a higher-end criminal activity than people smuggling."

The pair have had their bail extended and will be next required to face the NT Supreme Court on the charge of attempting to pervert the course of justice on September 17.

A fourth man involved in the operation, Irish national Stephen Roche, has pleaded guilty to attempting to pervert the course of justice in driving Chamas nearly 5,000 kilometres to Nhulunbuy.

World.title: Robots replace soldiers in Ukraine's first-ever drone parade
World.content:
It was not soldiers marching down Kyiv's main street to mark 35 years of Ukrainian independence, but robots designed to take their place on the frontline.

On the city's stretch of Dnipro River travelled a fleet of nine unmanned surface vessels, also known as drone boats, while the skies overhead were filled with bomber drones and aerial-target interceptors.

The display of military might was all part of Ukraine's "first-ever" aerial, ground and naval drone parade, according to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

"Over the years of war, Ukraine has built an almost entirely new defense industry. Modern. Technological. An industry that meets the challenges of war," he said in a social media post.

Ukraine's autonomous aerial fleet, as shown in a screen grab from a promotional military video. (Supplied: Ukrainian President's Office)

One of the main technologies on display at the Independence Day celebrations on Monday, local time, was 30 unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) trundling in formation along Khreshchatyk, one of the city's main historical avenues.

The Ukrainian President's Office said the UGVs, some equipped with heavy machine guns, "conduct reconnaissance, lay and clear mines, deliver ammunition, provisions and equipment, and evacuate the wounded".

It said UGVs had carried out more than 66,000 missions this year alone, as the war between Russia and Ukraine drags through its fifth year.

The reality of Ukraine’s impersonal, sci-fi drone war Inside a secret bunker with the Ukrainians launching kamikaze drones at Russian troops.

Also this year, Ukraine's defence forces have contracted more than 22,000 UGVs to be produced domestically, according to the office.

The military's aerial and naval unmanned weaponry have similar capabilities to its ground vehicles, creating an "ecosystem" of modern warfare according to Oleksandra Molloy, an expert in Ukraine's drone technology.

"These are quite capable systems that are dominating the battlefield today," Dr Molloy, a senior lecturer in aviation at the University of New South Wales, said.

"It's a demonstration of an emerging, multi-domain uncrewed force … [showing] Ukraine's military transformation over the last four-and-a-half years.

"It also gives the message to its allied partners that Ukraine is an invaluable partner to them in terms of knowledge, experience and technology developed during the war."

Ukraine's drone boats can carry out reconnaissance and patrol missions, strike maritime targets and launch drones. (Supplied: Ukrainian President's Office)

Featuring nearly 100 pieces of Ukrainian weaponry, the military parade was the country's first since Russia launched its full-scale invasion into Ukraine in early 2022.

It comes after Ukraine became the first country in the world to create a separate branch of its military dedicated to drone warfare, when its Unmanned Systems Forces was established in 2024.

"The most important part of the parade that used to be there is missing; no traditional formations of soldiers, armour or conventional tanks," Dr Molloy said.

"We do often think about whether [drones are] a weapon of the future or the future of warfare. I would say it's a glimpse, seeing how rapidly the systems and ecosystem are developing.

"But this is how modern warfare is being fought right now … the uncrewed and autonomous systems are present and will continue being in the mix."

European leaders joined Mr Zelenskyy in Kyiv on Monday to mark the 35th anniversary of Ukraine's break from the Soviet Union.

Ukraine marks 35 years of independence As Ukraine marks 35 years since independence from the Soviet Union, Volodymyr Zelenskyy repeats that his country will not surrender to Russian aggression.

At a meeting of allies, the leaders of Britain and France pledged to provide Ukraine with stronger military support and keep pressure on Russia.

US-led talks aimed at ending the war fell apart earlier this year as Ukraine refused Russian demands to cede more territory.

While fighting continues along a 1,200-kilometre frontline, Ukraine has succeeded in bringing Russian advances to a virtual halt this year.

Ukraine has increased its long-range attacks on Russian refineries and logistics infrastructure, aimed at undermining Moscow's war effort.

World.title: Trump administration proposes $103,000 fee for skilled worker visas
World.content:
The Trump administration has revived a proposal to charge employers seeking skilled foreign workers through the H-1B visa program more than $US100,000, according to a new filing from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

The policy was introduced last year by President Donald Trump but had been blocked by a federal judge.

It is the latest step in the administration's sweeping immigration crackdown.

Here is what we know.

Catch me up, what's the H-1B visa again?

The H-1B program allows domestic employers to recruit foreign talent for high-skilled jobs that are difficult to find American workers to fill.

The program offers 65,000 general visas annually, plus 20,000 for workers holding advanced degrees, for terms of three to six years.

Deep-pocketed technology companies such as Amazon and Microsoft are the biggest users of the program, with nearly three-quarters of approvals going to workers from India.

China is a distant second at 11.7 per cent, according to government data.

Didn't Trump already propose this?

Mr Trump first proposed payments of $100,000 ($142,000) as a presidential proclamation in September last year in an effort to prioritise American workers.

Before this proposal, standard fees ranged between $2,000 and $5,000.

The president and other critics believe the H-1B program is exploited by companies replacing American workers with cheaper foreign labour.

The administration has since faced multiple lawsuits by labour unions, research universities and dozens of states, saying that the fee would curb US employers' ability to hire global talent, up-end the tech industry and decimate hospitals with an already fragile workforce.

In June, a federal judge blocked Trump's bid to impose the six-figure fee.

Judge blocks Trump's $142k skilled worker visa fee The Trump administration's planned fee for the H-1B visa was announced to prevent foreign workers from taking American jobs.

US District Court Judge Leo Sorokin concluded that it was an unlawful "tax" that required congressional approval.

The Trump administration has maintained that the fee is not a traditional tax and that courts have little power to question the president's authority to restrict ⁠entry into the country.

A Boston-based appeals court is reviewing that decision while a different court considers whether a judge properly rejected a challenge to the fee by a major business group.

Mr Trump's temporary $100,000 fee increase expires in September, one year after it was issued.

According to court filings, about 70 employers had paid the fee on a total of 85 visa applications as of late February.

What is this new proposal then?

On Monday (US time), the DHS revived the proposal, submitting it online in the Federal Register to be officially published on Tuesday (US time).

From then, the public will be given a 30-day period to submit comments on the proposal.

This proposal would charge employers $103,265 for the H-1B visa applications. The cost would not apply to foreign citizens already in the US on student visas.

It must be paid before the government decides whether to approve an application.

US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) spokesperson Zach Kahler said the payments would support "immigration programs that otherwise must be funded by taxpayers".

The fee could be finalised by the end of the year.

What will the money be used for?

Revenue from the fee would be used to run the legal immigration system, a statement from the USCIS said.

The DHS estimates the proposed fee would generate approximately $US8.8 billion annually, based on a projected annual volume of 85,000 H-1B cap-subject petitions.

Markwayne Mullin (right) is the DHS secretary. (Reuters: Evan Vucci)

How will this impact Australians?

The new proposal likely won't have a big impact on Australians entering the US for work.

That is because most workers apply to enter the US via the Aussie-only E-3 visa, a special pathway introduced in 2005 after Canberra and Washington negotiated a free trade agreement.

The E-3 visa allows US employers to sponsor up to 10,500 Australians a year for work in a "specialty occupation" that only requires a university degree and pay equal or above the "prevailing wage" for the specific role.

Thousands of Australians in the US are on the E-3 visa.

Largest mass visa revocation in history

The revival of the H-1B visa isn't the only news to drop this week.

The Trump administration says it is planning to revoke the non-immigrant visas of foreigners who claim to be short-term visitors but then file for asylum to stay in the US permanently.

The State Department statement did not specify the number of visas that would be revoked in the process.

However, the Associated Press (AP) is reporting up to 200,000 foreigners could be affected.

If implemented, the move would be the largest single mass revocation of visas in US history.

Donald Trump has cracked down on immigration extensively since he came into office last year. (Reuters: Alyssa Pointer)

The revocations of so-called B1 and B2 visas would not necessarily result in immediate deportation, the AP report said, adding that most of those with asylum cases currently pending would be re-categorised but would lose their status as business or tourism travellers.

In a social media post on X, Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau alleged that the US immigration system "has long been swamped by frivolous asylum claims".

"Asylum isn't supposed to be a loophole to circumvent immigration law," Landau wrote.

Why is the US targeting immigration?

Since Mr Trump took office for his second term his administration has aggressively cracked down on immigration in a bid to improve domestic security.

In January, the State Department paused immigrant visas from 75 countries, a ban that was struck down by a federal judge last week.

It also proposed that visa-exempt foreign tourists, including Australians, needed to disclose information about their social media accounts before being approved for travel.

The administration also moved to end birthright citizenship, although to no avail.

Rights groups say the proposed immigration changes have violated free speech and due process rights and ⁠created an unsafe environment, particularly for ethnic minorities who have raised concerns about racial profiling.

ABC/AP/Reuters

World.title: 'Everyone is on edge' as migration policy confusion reigns
World.content:
Multicultural advocate Carmel La Rocca feels an overwhelming sense of frustration when she reflects on the state of Australia's debate on migration policy.

"There's a lot of confusion and all the community want is just a balanced, constructive conversation," the president of the Multicultural Council of Griffith said.

" Everyone is on edge and there's no harmony. "

Political discourse on the topic reached fever pitch this week after One Nation MP David Farley talked up policy of a "rotating workforce" of a "minimum of 100,000" in addition to his party's headline migration policy platform of slashing net overseas migration (NOM) to 130,000.

It led to him conceding that when the figures were combined, his party's policy was "not too different" to Labor's target.

Loading...

Cue a rebuke from leader Pauline Hanson, a clean-up from colleague Barnaby Joyce and cavalcade of government and opposition spokespeople gleefully pointing out One Nation's mixed messaging, without providing the long-called-for detail on their own migration policies.

Ms La Rocca, who lives in Mr Farley's southern New South Wales seat of Farrer, said politicians needed to stop arguing and lead "for the good of the country".

"They should look at Australia as a whole and look at Australia moving forward in a good way, in a professional way, in a skilled way, and having a good population to move it forward," she said.

'Should be allowed to stay'

When speaking in a round of media interviews last week, Mr Farley said Farrer needed "dexterity and flexibility" when it came to migration policy.

His stance broadly has the backing of staunch One Nation supporter and Griffith winemaker Darren De Bortoli.

"Politics is getting in the way of common sense, and what David certainly said on the weekend was common sense, very reflective of the seat of Farrer," he said.

Darren De Bortoli says David Farley's contribution to the migration debate is "common sense". (ABC News: Emily Doak)

When asked about the focus on a "rotating workforce", Mr De Bortoli was not as certain.

He said seats like Farrer should be exempt from cuts to migration and wanted to see more long-term pathways for migrants based in the regions.

"We still struggle to get people in even with the current policies, and you still have trouble filling positions in the seat of Farrer," he said.

" If we've got a skill set shortage and we need to bring people in fix it, and if there's no problem with immigration with their criminal records or whatever, they should be allowed to stay. "

Ms La Rocca said the idea of a rotating workforce was nonsense and would create a mess.

"With skilled migration, you need people who will do the job on a long term so that the job is done properly," she said.

'Revamp' needed

When the Australian Bureau of Statistics calculates the net overseas migration (NOM) figure, it includes people who are in Australia for at least 12 months in a 16-month period, regardless of the type of visa they are on.

Mr Farley has said the "minimum" of 100,000 workers on "rotating" visas that he wanted to see in addition to the NOM figure included 40,000 on the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (PALM) scheme.

The June 2026 data from the PALM program shows that of the 32,645 participating in the scheme, more than half (16,595) were long-term workers, meaning they were in Australia for 12 months to four years and therefore counted in the net figure.

It was not clear if the 40,000 figure Mr Farley quoted was a projected figure or if he was rounding up the current total figure of those on short and long-term visas.

Ms La Rocca said the PALM program, which was recently the subject of a Four Corners program investigating modern slavery, was one area that should be "revamped".

"If they're skilled enough to stay here and continue to stay here, the government should look at that," she said.

The hidden human cost of cheap food Behind the fruit and vegetables on Australia's supermarket shelves are workers whose stories are rarely heard.

She also said employers should be forced to provide housing and wanted to see more investment in public infrastructure such as transport and health.

Mr De Bortoli said issues with Australia's immigration policy seemed to be in the cities, and around how those migrants were contributing.

"There are obviously problems with the nature of the immigration policy … are they positively contributing to the Australian economy and productivity and society wise?"

David Farley was unavailable for interview for this story.

World.title: Former NT Young Australian of the Year to run for Labor in remote by-election
World.content:
A trailblazing nurse and Yolŋu man from remote Elcho Island has been announced as Labor’s pick to run in the upcoming race for the Northern Territory seat of Mulka.

Yiwarr McGrath, a former NT Young Australian of the Year (AOTY), was preselected by Territory Labor last night to contest the East Arnhem Land seat, vacated by independent Yiŋiya Guyula.

Mr Guyula quit last week after 10 years in parliament, triggering a by-election to be held on September 12.

Yingiya Guyula held Mulka for 10 years. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

Mr McGrath was named the NT Young AOTY in 2021 when training to become the first Yolŋu registered nurse.

He grew up in Galiwin'ku on Elcho Island, a remote north-east Arnhem Land community, before moving to Canberra then Darwin for study.

In 2025, Mr McGrath won the NT Health Excellence in Early Career Award for his "exceptional contribution" to Yolŋu-focused patient care as a nurse working for Miwatj Health Aboriginal Organisation.

Loading...

"It's an honour to have been preselected, and I look forward to campaigning to continue the incredible legacy of Yiŋiya Guyula," he said in a statement.

"Mulka is my home, and I want to fight for it. Healthcare is my profession, and I want to it thrive in our area.

"Nhulunbuy and the remote communities and homelands deserve the same dignity of access to healthcare as any other Territorian.

"It's a short campaign, but I'm ready to get out there and fight to become part of the Labor opposition and hold the divisive CLP government to account."

Mulka takes in the town of Nhulunbuy and a number of other remote NT communities. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

In its statement, Labor also said during the preselection process, Mr McGrath disclosed that about 16 years ago he was charged with drink driving and lost his license for six months.

The disclosure follows a recent scandal involving the driving record of Labor shadow minister Manuel Brown.

Mulka win would bring Labor's seats to six

A win in the seat of Mulka would take Labor's minority in NT parliament from five to six, after it also picked up the seat of Nightcliff from the Greens in a by-election earlier this year.

NT politician Manuel Brown dumped as opposition whip Manuel Brown's dumping from the role comes after weeks of scrutiny over his driving record.

Prior to Mr Guyula's first victory in 2016, Labor had safely held the seat of Nhulunbuy (which was renamed in 2020) since 1980.

Opposition Leader Selena Uibo said Labor would "look to restrengthen those strongholds".

"We also want to show communities and the township of Nhulunbuy that we will back them, we will support them, and with a strong candidate with the Mulka seat, they will be represented in the best possible way in territory parliament," she said.

"We do not want to see divisive politics play out in an important seat like Mulka, which is going through a huge transition process when it comes to the Nhulunbuy township and the [looming] exit of the Rio Tinto mine."

Selena Uibo says a strong candidate is the best way to make sure the remote region is supported. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

As well as the town of Nhulunbuy and the Gove Peninsula, the electorate comprises large remote Yolŋu communities including Mr Guyula's home of Milingimbi and Galiwin'ku.

The Country Liberal Party (CLP) said it was open to fielding a candidate for the seat, which it has not won since the 1970s, but would further advise after nominations closed on Thursday.

World.title: Tracking devices, drones and a poisoned dog: CFMEU probe told of intimidation
World.content:
Updated NationalQueenslandCFMEU Tracking devices, drones and a poisoned dog: CFMEU probe told of intimidation Cameron Atfield Updated August 25, 2026 — 2:55pm ,first published 2:25pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A security professional hired to protect a CFMEU-targeted worksite found a tracking device attached to his car and believes his dog was poisoned by baited meat dropped from a drone in a campaign of intimidation by the union, a commission of inquiry heard on Tuesday. Concentric Concepts managing director Grant Killen was providing security services to construction firm BMD at the Centenary Bridge worksite when, he told the Commission of Inquiry into the CFMEU and Misconduct in the Construction Industry, he became the target of a sustained campaign of harassment. After attending the site on May 17, 2024, Killen said he sensed he was being followed during his drive back to his company headquarters near the Port of Brisbane. The tracking device found on Grant Killen’s vehicle. Commission of Inquiry Upon arrival, Killen said he immediately placed his car on a hoist, lifted it, and found a tracking device attached beneath the chassis.



“Once I found the device, I immediately put the vehicle on the ground as quick as I could. Then I left the facility,” he said. “Then I gave the admin staff at the office a call and directed them to pack up and close up for the day and go home.” Killen said he sped away from the site to put distance between the device and his staff. “I left the device on the vehicle mainly because I knew the device had a particular anti-removal device on there, an anti-tilt switch,” he said. “As soon as it gets removed, the people who put it on there, who have the software for that, would immediately be notified.”



Suspecting he was being followed by someone in a Toyota RAV4, Killen said he engaged in some “aggressive driving”, including deliberately running a red light to check if he was being followed. “I was followed through that red light,” he said. Concentric Concepts managing director Grant Killen giving evidence on Tuesday. Commission of Inquiry “Further down the road, we did an aggressive U-turn [to] see if it would keep up, and it did follow.” Killen eventually lost his tail, he said, and removed the device by the side of a road.



But he said the intimidation did not stop there, instead spreading to his family home. There were drive-bys in his cul-de-sac, and Killen said he managed a brief look at one of the drivers, who he identified as former police detective Mick Featherstone, whom the inquiry heard the CFMEU had engaged to collect intelligence on BMD personnel. Separately, Killen said he noticed several drones overhead. Then, the family dog got sick. “One of the questions the vet asked me, after a point where the vet had to operate on the dog and remove its stomach contents, was ‘Do you feed your dog cubed meat?’,” Killen said.



“We don’t, and I thought that was a strange question. But as I reflected shortly after and recalled, I formed the opinion that there was a possibility that the dog had been baited at some stage.” Related Article Building Bad Inquiry and CFMEU bosses seek answers and action over alleged bikie plot When counsel assisting the inquiry, Eddy Gisonda, KC, put it to Killen that he suspected one of the drones may have dropped baited meat on his property, he responded “yeah, correct”. Killen said the campaign was enough to make him walk away from the BMD contract. “With the tracking device on our vehicle, with everything that was occurring, I needed to step back and just concentrate on the safety of me and my family and our business,” he said.



Commissioner Stuart Wood asked Killen, a military veteran with service in Iraq, whether he had experienced anything of that level while deployed. “An assailant or an offender always has the upper hand about how they plan to do an overt act or assault someone or conduct an attack,” he said. “They choose the time, they choose the place, they choose the method. “All we can do is simply react the best that we can and try and mitigate it by having that planning in place. “So to put that in context, that’s what we tried our best to do in this particular situation.”



After lunch, BMD chief executive Scott Power recounted a similar experience at his father’s house. His father, Mick Power, still served as BMD chairman. BMD chief executive Scott Power giving evidence on Tuesday. Commission of Inquiry Similar to Killen’s situation, Power said, drones had been spotted above his father’s home before his dog fell ill. “They were concerned, obviously, for the well-being of their pet, but the timing of it seemed to coincide with the campaign in the local area surrounding their home, so they formed the view that it was connected [with the CFMEU,” he said. Gisonda: “And was it unusual for them to observe drones flying above their property?”



Power: “Yeah, it was particularly unusual. It’s not something they have ever previously discussed having observed.” Related Article Building Bad ‘Burn your house and kill your kids’: Construction giant accused of using bikies Earlier, Queensland Council of Unions general secretary Jacqueline King said relations between the state trades and labour council and the CFMEU had greatly improved since the latter went into administration. “We have developed, I think, a fairly good working relationship, completely unlike what it was, and on the basis that we work with the Queensland branch to try to assist them on their path to getting out of administration,” she said. But King said there was still some way to go before the CFMEU could be reaffiliated with the Queensland Council of Unions.



“It is going to take time because, while the people who are in the union now are not the same people who were doing the activities and the conduct that was occurring pre-the High Court decision, relationships still take time to mend, and trust takes time to rebuild,” she said. The hearing continues. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Western Power rocked by second sexual assault claim
World.content:
Breaking PoliticsWAWorkplace safety Western Power rocked by second sexual assault claim Hamish Hastie August 25, 2026 — 2:48pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Western Power’s workplace culture will be put under the microscope after Energy Minister Amber-Jade Sanderson revealed her office had fielded a “very credible” historic sexual assault complaint from a former employee. Energy minister Amber-Jade Sanderson. Photo Ross Swanborough The utility’s staff were recently asked about the culture at the organisation following the conviction of former employee Jeffrey Spinner, 59, for raping a colleague during a work trip in 2024. Several of Spinner’s colleagues who provided glowing character references to help have his prison sentence reduced have been stood down from their roles pending a review. Sanderson and Western Power chief executive Gair Landsborough revealed, since announcing the internal review, they had been inundated with complaints from staff and former employees about the culture that ranged from minor to very serious, including the new sexual assault claim.



Sanderson said the new complaint came through to her office and showed the Spinner case was not an outlier. “The recent reported case was not an outlier. It’s unusual, but the fact that we’ve now had another serious allegation presented to us from a former Western Power employee – a very credible complaint – we’re taking this very, very seriously,” she said. Jeffrey Spinner. Sanderson declined to provide further details about the complaint but said it had not been taken to police and her office had taken advice from the Sexual Assault Resource Centre to help support the woman who no longer works at Western Power. An independent review into Western Power’s workplace culture will be launched, to be headed up by workplace culture advisory Intersection and led by founder Natasha de Silva and former Australian Sex Discrimination Commissioner Kate Jenkins.



Jenkins led the inquiry into Parliament House in 2021 after Brittany Higgins first alleged she had been raped in the building. “They bring extensive experience to the process, and there are probably not any more qualified people in the country than these two women,” Sanderson said. Sanderson said the complaints streaming in revolved mostly around bullying and misconduct and, while most of them were historic, it did not matter. “As a state-owned utility, I expect the highest standard of Western Power. The standard has not been met,” she said. “This review is a line in the sand. It is an opportunity for current and former employees of Western Power to be heard and to have their voices heard.



“It will deliver real change, and it will deliver safety for all Western Power workers.” Related Article Courts End of the ‘good bloke’ defence? WA’s plan to ban character references draws mixed response Landsborough said to date none of the complaints received have required alerting WA Police or the Corruption and Crime Commission. “The general themes of what’s coming out are historical experiences within Western Power, particularly around bullying and potential misconduct, which is just not acceptable and needs to be improved,” he said. “Some of them are under investigation now to see if any action needs to be taken by Western Power.”



The review will take six months from September. Spinner’s conviction and the good character references triggered the Cook government to expand its planned ban of good character references in child abuse cases to now include all criminal convictions. Law firm Minter Ellison is conducting an investigation into the employees and the good character references, which were criticised by Sanderson. It is not unlawful to provide good character references. Sanderson and Landsborough would not reveal what, if anything, the employees did wrong but said they would await the outcome of the investigation, due by the end of the week. “The investigation isn’t a legal proceeding. It’s an investigation into workplace conduct and the conduct of those employees and I wouldn’t like to speculate the outcome of that investigation. It’s ongoing,” Landsborough said.

World.title: Thredbo’s woes: Is a ski resort without snow like a pub with no beer?
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesSkiing Opinion Thredbo’s woes: Is a ski resort without snow like a pub with no beer? Elizabeth Knight Business columnist August 25, 2026 — 2:44pm

August 25, 2026 — 2:44pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

For sale: large Australian ski resort with unreliable snow. All offers considered. It is more than 10 years since James Packer saw the writing on the wall – or at least the patches of grass popping up from the snow on the ski fields of Kosciuszko’s Perisher resort – and offloaded the resort to US-based ski resort giant Vail. Skiing was long considered a rich person’s sport and there was historically a vanity aspect to ownership of both Australia’s major alpine resorts, Thredbo and Perisher. But global warming has melted their appeal. Snow machines can provide some relief, but the ski seasons in Australia are getting patchier. Boen Ferguson After an underwhelming season at what is arguably Australia’s premier ski resort, Thredbo, the hotel group controlled by the billionaire Rydges family, EVT, is weighing the possibility of offloading it.



It is one of a laundry list of assets the company is considering for sale. Finding a buyer and getting a reasonable price will determine that outcome. On Tuesday, EVT wrote down the value of Thredbo from $292 million to $143 million to reflect the declining, or at least unreliable, performance of the resort. Surely, it must also give a nod to the rise of the Japanese ski resorts as worthy competitors – some of which have been likened to winter Bali for Australian tourists. Package deals for Japan skiing, even after airfares, are now priced comparably to a week’s skiing in Australia, which is notoriously expensive for accommodation and lift tickets. And Japan’s snowfall and snow cover is famously reliable.



Climate is of course the culprit and has been for 70 years, according to a report from the CSIRO, which speaks to the variability and long-term deterioration in the falls and depth of snow at three sites in the Snowy Mountains. CSIRO’s research shows that over the Alps in south-eastern Australia, the annual average temperature has risen by about 1.4 degrees Celsius, or about 0.2 degrees per decade, since 1950. Average annual precipitation has decreased by about 140 millimetres (20 millimetres per decade). The decrease in rainfall means less snowfall, and the warming means more snowmelt. The slopes at Nagano in Japan. Getty Images Thredbo and Perisher resorts are reportedly experiencing the third-lowest snow levels since records began in 1954, and a couple of smaller resorts have already called it quits on this year’s season – a few weeks shy of the usual close. As of Monday, August 24, Thredbo had just 19 of 53 slopes open. Perisher had 39 of its 100-plus runs open.



Last year’s season was strong, but resort owner EVT has flagged that Thredbo’s earnings this financial year (covering the 2026 winter season) will fall, largely because snowfall had been so patchy. Snowies Beer Food & Wine Festival in summer: Resort owners have been busy shifting the marketing of these winter wonderlands into year-round destinations. Bronte Crawley The write-down of the value of the resort reflects the ongoing variability in conditions and possibly the investment needed in artificial snow-making machines to ensure that the lower slopes are skiable. In some respects, Thredbo’s season was saved by its all-weather snow factory, which has an ability to produce snow at 20 degrees. Yet while snow cannons can stave off the decline or soften its trajectory, the reality is that booking a ski trip in Australia has its risks.



Resort owners have been busy shifting the marketing of these winter wonderlands into year-round stays that offer hiking, biking and natural beauty – a kind of natural theme park. Related Article Opinion

Big four accountants KPMG’s sackings are just the start of the fallout for the firm Elizabeth Knight Business columnist But is it enough to attract people to the extensive (and expensive) accommodation, restaurants, bars and equipment sellers/hire on offer in Thredbo village? Australia’s ski industry is at risk of major disruptions and shorter seasons if the current level of climate pollution continues, according to new modelling from Protect Our Winters Australia (POW) and The Australian National University. The report found the average ski season across all resorts in Australia will be 44 days shorter by 2050 under a mid-range greenhouse-gas emissions scenario, and 55 days shorter under a high-emissions scenario.



This is the medium-term scenario facing EVT, which has already stated its desire to focus on its core hotel business instead. Interest in Thredbo could be cooler than our winters these days. The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: Commuters face ‘isolated delays’ in afternoon peak after Sydney train chaos
World.content:
Repairs to a wiring fault on Sydney’s T1 North Shore Line that caused mass delays for city-bound commuters on Tuesday were completed by late morning, clearing the way for the rail operator to start restoring train services before the afternoon peak. The loss of tension in an overhead wire south of Chatswood station resulted in the cancellation of city-bound services from Gordon to North Sydney, leaving commuters waiting for replacement buses in queues which stretched for more than 100 metres at stops during the morning peak. Limited bus services had been replacing trains from Gordon to Chatswood, where commuters could travel towards the city on metro trains. The problem was due to a failure in a counterweight mechanism on the wires, causing them to sag. Commuters queue to go to platforms 1 and 2 at Chatswood train station after a wiring fault on Sydney’s T1 North Shore Line. KATE GERAGHTY



Sydney Trains crews completed repairs shortly after 11am, and the rail operator worked to restore passenger services for the afternoon peak. Repair crews had been on the scene since Monday night when the failure was discovered about 9pm. Crews work on repairing the counterweight which failed on the T1 line south of Chatswood. Transport for NSW Sydney Trains chief executive Matt Longland said the T1 line had been fully repaired and power restored, and the priority was to return to timetabled services ahead of the busy afternoon peak. “Our objective is to minimise delays for passengers travelling on the rail network this afternoon, particularly those passengers travelling on the T9 and the T1 lines,” he said shortly after 1pm on Tuesday. Longland said passengers should not expect significant delays to trains in the afternoon peak, although he conceded that there may be “isolated delays” to some services.



While the root cause of the failure is under investigation, Longland said a cable that held a counterweight mechanism appeared to have snapped on Monday night near Chatswood, causing the loss of tension in the overhead power lines. “It was a steel cable that was suspending a set of weights that provide tension in the overhead line,” he said. Commuters stand in long queues for replacement buses on the Pacific Highway at Roseville. James Brickwood “As a result of that cable snapping [on Monday night], it created a sag in the lines, which meant that it was no longer safe to operate trains through that section of line inbound of Chatswood.” The counterweight failure severely disrupted city-bound commuters on the T1 North Shore Line, but has also had a knock-on effect on the T9 Northern Line which runs between Hornsby and Strathfield. It also resulted in a reduction in train frequencies on the T1 Western Line.



Uber fares in Sydney’s north surged on Tuesday morning amid increased demand for the service. Two commuters who had been queuing for a bus at Roseville decided to split the cost of a $100 Uber ride to the Sydney CBD. Commuters endure long queues for replacement buses at Gordon on Tuesday morning. Nine News Roseville resident Anna Hill was stuck in a queue stretching for more than 100 metres from the train station to the Pacific Highway. “It’s crazy,” she said of the absence of buses running between Roseville and Chatswood station. Another Roseville commuter, Toby Little, said he had been waiting about 40 minutes for a bus, and had seen four packed replacement buses pass him by in that time. Commuters Eden Cleaver and James Brown were left waiting for an hour in a queue for a replacement bus on the Pacific Highway at Roseville.



Traffic was much heavier on local roads as commuters opted to drive. “You definitely don’t see traffic like this in Roseville,” said paralegal James Craig, who was late for work in North Sydney. Crowds of commuters queue to enter platforms for the Metro train line at Chatswood on Tuesday morning. Kate Geraghty Trains that usually started from or ended at Lindfield and Gordon were beginning and ending at North Sydney. The latest failure comes less than two weeks after overhead wiring fell onto a train near Redfern, causing power outages across critical sections of the rail network and major disruptions during the evening peak. Coalition transport spokesperson Natalie Ward said commuters who were late for work or school were rightly frustrated by the latest failure. “This is the second major disruption in as many weeks on Labor’s watch,” she said.



“Just two months ago, the Minns Labor government was boasting of a $2.1 billion investment in train maintenance. Commuters this morning will be rightly asking what they have to show for it.” Rail repair staff work on overhead wires near Chatswood station on Tuesday morning. Kate Geraghty Transport Minister John Graham said the government was investing a record $2.1 billion in maintaining the train network to minimise the number and severity of rail incidents like the one that had occurred. “This was a serious incident. I want to thank passengers for their patience and the Sydney Trains team for working through the night to recover as quickly as possible,” he said. Longland said the failure at Redfern on August 14 involved a piece of equipment short-circuiting and effectively melting an overhead wire, whereas Monday’s incident was due to a mechanism which was meant to keep the power lines tense.



“What we saw [on Monday] night was not an incident with the overhead wiring that carries power,” he said. Related Article Updated

Public transport ‘Significant disruptions’, trains stranded in Sydney peak hour chaos “Any time that overhead wiring is impacted, it does create a significant impact because trains can’t operate on the network when the power is out.” Longland reiterated that there had been significant investment in improving the rail network’s reliability since a major review last year. “What we want to eliminate are these incidents that cause these significant delays,” he said. World.title: Crispy hash meets buttery lemon fish – your new weeknight go-to
World.content:
Step 1 Preheat the oven to 200C fan-forced (220C conventional). Place a large skillet in the oven to preheat for 10 minutes.

Step 2 Carefully remove the hot skillet from the oven. Add most of the oil, reserving 1 tablespoon for cooking the fish, then add the potatoes, garlic and Brussels sprouts. Season with salt and pepper and toss to coat. Return to the oven and roast for 20 minutes. Add the smoked paprika and celery salt, toss again and return to the oven for a further 10 minutes or until the vegetables are golden and crisp.

Step 3 Meanwhile, dust the fish in flour. Heat the remaining oil in a large frying pan over high heat. Add the fish, skin side down, and cook for 3 minutes, flip and cook for a further 2 minutes. Add the butter and sage leaves and cook, spooning the melted butter over the fish for 1 minute or until the sage is crisp and fragrant.

Step 4 Add the lemon juice to the pan and season with salt and pepper.

World.title: Grossly negligent: Woodside called out for abandoning scope 3 emissions plans
World.content:
NationalWAGas Grossly negligent: Woodside called out for abandoning scope 3 emissions plans Michael Philipps August 25, 2026 — 2:18pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Oil and gas giant Woodside has announced it plans to abandon its current scope 3 greenhouse gas emission targets, with the company claiming its climate objectives will be now guided by the pace of global energy transition. Woodside Energy chief executive Liz Westcott. Roy VanDerVegt The announcement comes as the company delivered a 27 per cent increase in net profit to $US1.67 billion despite lower production, citing a jump in prices caused by the global oil crisis due to the ongoing war in the Middle East. According to the company’s latest presentation to stockholders, it plans to shelf investment of US$5 billion in new energy products and lower-carbon services by 2030 and take a financial investment decision on new energy products and lower-carbon services. Woodside chief executive Liz Westcott said strong sustainability performance remains fundamental to the long-term success of the business and the company made good progress in key areas during the half.



“Having achieved our 2025 net equity scope 1 and 2 greenhouse gas emissions reduction target we remain on track to meet our 2030 target of a 30 per cent reduction against our baseline,” she said. “We have taken the disciplined decision to retire our Scope 3 investment and emissions abatement targets. “These targets were established in a different market context and based on a different expected pace of the energy transition.” The Conservation Council of Western Australia labelled the move to abandon its scope 3 investments as “grossly negligent”. CCWA executive director Matt Roberts said Woodside’s decision to dump targets for reducing emissions released when customers burn the gas it sells was a dereliction of its clean energy obligations.



“These emissions account for about 90 per cent of the company’s total climate impact and to walk away from its responsibility for the global climate carnage inherently caused by its product highlights its profits at all cost approach,” he said. Related Article Updated

World markets ASX gains as Woodside result boosts energy stocks; miners and banks also rise “Woodside’s gas is displacing renewables in Asia, as well as here in Western Australia. Woodside uses lobbyists and donations to secure government subsidies that keep the gas industry alive. “It’s time they were held accountable and not allowed to cut and run at a time when the impacts of climate change have never been more prevalent in Australia and around the world.” Meanwhile, the company said its Scarborough project off Karratha in the state’s Pilbara region is on track for first production before the end of the year.



“We continue to make excellent progress on the Scarborough energy project, which was 98 per cent complete at the end of the half,” Westcott said. “It remains on track for first LNG cargo in the fourth quarter of 2026. “Subsequent to the period, the floating production unit achieved ready-for-startup status and first gas, marking another significant milestone as we move closer to production.” “We are taking the time to ensure we are bringing these facilities online safely and reliably as we move toward first LNG cargo and a significant new source of cash generative production to our portfolio.”

World.title: Liam Martin’s contract call as Panthers prepare to hit pause and chase title
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Liam Martin’s contract call as Panthers prepare to hit pause and chase title Dan Walsh August 25, 2026 — 2:02pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Liam Martin and the Panthers have paused talks around a potential contract extension as the club prepares to do the same across their star-studded roster while they chase another premiership. Penrith officials met with Martin’s manager Allan Gainey on Tuesday, with both parties agreeing to hold fire on further negotiations until after the Panthers season, ideally with a fifth premiership in six years. Panthers back-rower Liam Martin. Getty Images Martin, 29, is seeking a three-year deal that would tie him to Penrith until the end of 2030. Sources speaking on the condition of anonymity given the confidential nature of the matter have indicated the Panthers are open to that length of deal for Martin, while a two-year deal was also discussed.



However, the dollar amount of any potential offer is still in flux given superstar halfback Nathan Cleary is yet to begin any meaningful extension talks of his own. Fellow co-captain Isaah Yeo is closing in on a deal beyond 2027 which, as revealed by this masthead, is a good chance of being locked in before the finals kick off in a fortnight. Nathan Cleary is no closer to sorting out his future. Getty Images The Panthers won’t employ a hard-and-fast shutdown on contract negotiations once the post-season starts, but will prioritise their premiership tilt over the next six weeks. “Talks were productive,” Gainey said of Tuesday’s meeting with Panthers general manager Shane Elford and chief executive Matt Cameron.



“Both parties are mindful of the timing and potential distractions around upcoming finals. “We are confident we can get to a mutually beneficial position once Panthers have finished their commitments for 2026.” The Panthers have had several retention wins recently despite losing star winger Brian To’o (PNG Chiefs) and Liam Henry, Scott Sorensen and Jack Cole (Perth Bears) to the NRL’s incoming clubs. Back-rower Isaiah Papali’i has recommitted on a yet-to-be-announced two-year extension, while centre Paul Alamoti has also re-signed until the end of 2029. Rising NSW Origin star Casey McLean was also extended until the end of 2030 last week.



Cleary said last week he is not ready to address his future, and is yet to confirm privately or publicly whether he wants to re-sign before the November 1 free agency date or test his value on the open market. Related Article Updated

NRL 2026 How a personal pitch from the PNG prime minister helped seal Manu’s NRL return Sources close to the champion No.7 have indicated the lack of clarity does not necessarily point to an exit from Penrith, despite the Chiefs making Cleary their halfback priority if he comes off-contract. Martin’s market value, along with fellow off-contract Panthers star Moses Leota, has been a source of intrigue given PNG’s entry to the market, predictions of a 15 per cent rise in the salary cap and a spate of public brinksmanship between managers and clubs of late. Along with Canterbury’s Jacob Preston (24) and Canberra’s Hudson Young (29), Martin is the most accomplished back-rower coming off-contract in 2027. Despite being tabled a $3.3 million, three-year offer – the largest in Canberra’s history – Young will be granted permission to negotiate with PNG next month as he and the Raiders look to bring his future to a head.

World.title: Tracking devices, drones and a poisoned dog: CFMEU probe told of intimidation
World.content:
Updated NationalQueenslandCFMEU Tracking devices, drones and a poisoned dog: CFMEU probe told of intimidation Cameron Atfield Updated August 25, 2026 — 2:55pm ,first published 2:25pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A security professional hired to protect a CFMEU-targeted worksite found a tracking device attached to his car and believes his dog was poisoned by baited meat dropped from a drone in a campaign of intimidation by the union, a commission of inquiry heard on Tuesday. Concentric Concepts managing director Grant Killen was providing security services to construction firm BMD at the Centenary Bridge worksite when, he told the Commission of Inquiry into the CFMEU and Misconduct in the Construction Industry, he became the target of a sustained campaign of harassment. After attending the site on May 17, 2024, Killen said he sensed he was being followed during his drive back to his company headquarters near the Port of Brisbane. The tracking device found on Grant Killen’s vehicle. Commission of Inquiry Upon arrival, Killen said he immediately placed his car on a hoist, lifted it, and found a tracking device attached beneath the chassis.



“Once I found the device, I immediately put the vehicle on the ground as quick as I could. Then I left the facility,” he said. “Then I gave the admin staff at the office a call and directed them to pack up and close up for the day and go home.” Killen said he sped away from the site to put distance between the device and his staff. “I left the device on the vehicle mainly because I knew the device had a particular anti-removal device on there, an anti-tilt switch,” he said. “As soon as it gets removed, the people who put it on there, who have the software for that, would immediately be notified.”



Suspecting he was being followed by someone in a Toyota RAV4, Killen said he engaged in some “aggressive driving”, including deliberately running a red light to check if he was being followed. “I was followed through that red light,” he said. Concentric Concepts managing director Grant Killen giving evidence on Tuesday. Commission of Inquiry “Further down the road, we did an aggressive U-turn [to] see if it would keep up, and it did follow.” Killen eventually lost his tail, he said, and removed the device by the side of a road.



But he said the intimidation did not stop there, instead spreading to his family home. There were drive-bys in his cul-de-sac, and Killen said he managed a brief look at one of the drivers, who he identified as former police detective Mick Featherstone, whom the inquiry heard the CFMEU had engaged to collect intelligence on BMD personnel. Separately, Killen said he noticed several drones overhead. Then, the family dog got sick. “One of the questions the vet asked me, after a point where the vet had to operate on the dog and remove its stomach contents, was ‘Do you feed your dog cubed meat?’,” Killen said.



“We don’t, and I thought that was a strange question. But as I reflected shortly after and recalled, I formed the opinion that there was a possibility that the dog had been baited at some stage.” Related Article Building Bad Inquiry and CFMEU bosses seek answers and action over alleged bikie plot When counsel assisting the inquiry, Eddy Gisonda, KC, put it to Killen that he suspected one of the drones may have dropped baited meat on his property, he responded “yeah, correct”. Killen said the campaign was enough to make him walk away from the BMD contract. “With the tracking device on our vehicle, with everything that was occurring, I needed to step back and just concentrate on the safety of me and my family and our business,” he said.



Commissioner Stuart Wood asked Killen, a military veteran with service in Iraq, whether he had experienced anything of that level while deployed. “An assailant or an offender always has the upper hand about how they plan to do an overt act or assault someone or conduct an attack,” he said. “They choose the time, they choose the place, they choose the method. “All we can do is simply react the best that we can and try and mitigate it by having that planning in place. “So to put that in context, that’s what we tried our best to do in this particular situation.”



After lunch, BMD chief executive Scott Power recounted a similar experience at his father’s house. His father, Mick Power, still served as BMD chairman. BMD chief executive Scott Power giving evidence on Tuesday. Commission of Inquiry Similar to Killen’s situation, Power said, drones had been spotted above his father’s home before his dog fell ill. “They were concerned, obviously, for the well-being of their pet, but the timing of it seemed to coincide with the campaign in the local area surrounding their home, so they formed the view that it was connected [with the CFMEU,” he said. Gisonda: “And was it unusual for them to observe drones flying above their property?”



Power: “Yeah, it was particularly unusual. It’s not something they have ever previously discussed having observed.” Related Article Building Bad ‘Burn your house and kill your kids’: Construction giant accused of using bikies Earlier, Queensland Council of Unions general secretary Jacqueline King said relations between the state trades and labour council and the CFMEU had greatly improved since the latter went into administration. “We have developed, I think, a fairly good working relationship, completely unlike what it was, and on the basis that we work with the Queensland branch to try to assist them on their path to getting out of administration,” she said. But King said there was still some way to go before the CFMEU could be reaffiliated with the Queensland Council of Unions.



“It is going to take time because, while the people who are in the union now are not the same people who were doing the activities and the conduct that was occurring pre-the High Court decision, relationships still take time to mend, and trust takes time to rebuild,” she said. The hearing continues. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

Last year’s season was strong, but resort owner EVT has flagged that Thredbo’s earnings this financial year (covering the 2026 winter season) will fall, largely because snowfall had been so patchy. Snowies Beer Food & Wine Festival in summer: Resort owners have been busy shifting the marketing of these winter wonderlands into year-round destinations. Bronte Crawley The write-down of the value of the resort reflects the ongoing variability in conditions and possibly the investment needed in artificial snow-making machines to ensure that the lower slopes are skiable. In some respects, Thredbo’s season was saved by its all-weather snow factory, which has an ability to produce snow at 20 degrees. Yet while snow cannons can stave off the decline or soften its trajectory, the reality is that booking a ski trip in Australia has its risks.



Resort owners have been busy shifting the marketing of these winter wonderlands into year-round stays that offer hiking, biking and natural beauty – a kind of natural theme park. Related Article Opinion

Big four accountants KPMG’s sackings are just the start of the fallout for the firm Elizabeth Knight Business columnist But is it enough to attract people to the extensive (and expensive) accommodation, restaurants, bars and equipment sellers/hire on offer in Thredbo village? Australia’s ski industry is at risk of major disruptions and shorter seasons if the current level of climate pollution continues, according to new modelling from Protect Our Winters Australia (POW) and The Australian National University. The report found the average ski season across all resorts in Australia will be 44 days shorter by 2050 under a mid-range greenhouse-gas emissions scenario, and 55 days shorter under a high-emissions scenario.



This is the medium-term scenario facing EVT, which has already stated its desire to focus on its core hotel business instead. Interest in Thredbo could be cooler than our winters these days. The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: Commuters face ‘isolated delays’ in afternoon peak after Sydney train chaos
World.content:
Repairs to a wiring fault on Sydney’s T1 North Shore Line that caused mass delays for city-bound commuters on Tuesday were completed by late morning, clearing the way for the rail operator to start restoring train services before the afternoon peak. The loss of tension in an overhead wire south of Chatswood station resulted in the cancellation of city-bound services from Gordon to North Sydney, leaving commuters waiting for replacement buses in queues which stretched for more than 100 metres at stops during the morning peak. Limited bus services had been replacing trains from Gordon to Chatswood, where commuters could travel towards the city on metro trains. The problem was due to a failure in a counterweight mechanism on the wires, causing them to sag. Commuters queue to go to platforms 1 and 2 at Chatswood train station after a wiring fault on Sydney’s T1 North Shore Line. KATE GERAGHTY



Sydney Trains crews completed repairs shortly after 11am, and the rail operator worked to restore passenger services for the afternoon peak. Repair crews had been on the scene since Monday night when the failure was discovered about 9pm. Crews work on repairing the counterweight which failed on the T1 line south of Chatswood. Transport for NSW Sydney Trains chief executive Matt Longland said the T1 line had been fully repaired and power restored, and the priority was to return to timetabled services ahead of the busy afternoon peak. “Our objective is to minimise delays for passengers travelling on the rail network this afternoon, particularly those passengers travelling on the T9 and the T1 lines,” he said shortly after 1pm on Tuesday. Longland said passengers should not expect significant delays to trains in the afternoon peak, although he conceded that there may be “isolated delays” to some services.



While the root cause of the failure is under investigation, Longland said a cable that held a counterweight mechanism appeared to have snapped on Monday night near Chatswood, causing the loss of tension in the overhead power lines. “It was a steel cable that was suspending a set of weights that provide tension in the overhead line,” he said. Commuters stand in long queues for replacement buses on the Pacific Highway at Roseville. James Brickwood “As a result of that cable snapping [on Monday night], it created a sag in the lines, which meant that it was no longer safe to operate trains through that section of line inbound of Chatswood.” The counterweight failure severely disrupted city-bound commuters on the T1 North Shore Line, but has also had a knock-on effect on the T9 Northern Line which runs between Hornsby and Strathfield. It also resulted in a reduction in train frequencies on the T1 Western Line.



Uber fares in Sydney’s north surged on Tuesday morning amid increased demand for the service. Two commuters who had been queuing for a bus at Roseville decided to split the cost of a $100 Uber ride to the Sydney CBD. Commuters endure long queues for replacement buses at Gordon on Tuesday morning. Nine News Roseville resident Anna Hill was stuck in a queue stretching for more than 100 metres from the train station to the Pacific Highway. “It’s crazy,” she said of the absence of buses running between Roseville and Chatswood station. Another Roseville commuter, Toby Little, said he had been waiting about 40 minutes for a bus, and had seen four packed replacement buses pass him by in that time. Commuters Eden Cleaver and James Brown were left waiting for an hour in a queue for a replacement bus on the Pacific Highway at Roseville.



Traffic was much heavier on local roads as commuters opted to drive. “You definitely don’t see traffic like this in Roseville,” said paralegal James Craig, who was late for work in North Sydney. Crowds of commuters queue to enter platforms for the Metro train line at Chatswood on Tuesday morning. Kate Geraghty Trains that usually started from or ended at Lindfield and Gordon were beginning and ending at North Sydney. The latest failure comes less than two weeks after overhead wiring fell onto a train near Redfern, causing power outages across critical sections of the rail network and major disruptions during the evening peak. Coalition transport spokesperson Natalie Ward said commuters who were late for work or school were rightly frustrated by the latest failure. “This is the second major disruption in as many weeks on Labor’s watch,” she said.



“Just two months ago, the Minns Labor government was boasting of a $2.1 billion investment in train maintenance. Commuters this morning will be rightly asking what they have to show for it.” Rail repair staff work on overhead wires near Chatswood station on Tuesday morning. Kate Geraghty Transport Minister John Graham said the government was investing a record $2.1 billion in maintaining the train network to minimise the number and severity of rail incidents like the one that had occurred. “This was a serious incident. I want to thank passengers for their patience and the Sydney Trains team for working through the night to recover as quickly as possible,” he said. Longland said the failure at Redfern on August 14 involved a piece of equipment short-circuiting and effectively melting an overhead wire, whereas Monday’s incident was due to a mechanism which was meant to keep the power lines tense.



“What we saw [on Monday] night was not an incident with the overhead wiring that carries power,” he said. Related Article Updated

Public transport ‘Significant disruptions’, trains stranded in Sydney peak hour chaos “Any time that overhead wiring is impacted, it does create a significant impact because trains can’t operate on the network when the power is out.” Longland reiterated that there had been significant investment in improving the rail network’s reliability since a major review last year. “What we want to eliminate are these incidents that cause these significant delays,” he said.
