World.title: Crispy hash meets buttery lemon fish – your new weeknight go-to
World.content:
Step 1 Preheat the oven to 200C fan-forced (220C conventional). Place a large skillet in the oven to preheat for 10 minutes.

Step 2 Carefully remove the hot skillet from the oven. Add most of the oil, reserving 1 tablespoon for cooking the fish, then add the potatoes, garlic and Brussels sprouts. Season with salt and pepper and toss to coat. Return to the oven and roast for 20 minutes. Add the smoked paprika and celery salt, toss again and return to the oven for a further 10 minutes or until the vegetables are golden and crisp.

Step 3 Meanwhile, dust the fish in flour. Heat the remaining oil in a large frying pan over high heat. Add the fish, skin side down, and cook for 3 minutes, flip and cook for a further 2 minutes. Add the butter and sage leaves and cook, spooning the melted butter over the fish for 1 minute or until the sage is crisp and fragrant.

Step 4 Add the lemon juice to the pan and season with salt and pepper.

World.title: Grossly negligent: Woodside called out for abandoning scope 3 emissions plans
World.content:
NationalWAGas Grossly negligent: Woodside called out for abandoning scope 3 emissions plans Michael Philipps August 25, 2026 — 2:18pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Oil and gas giant Woodside has announced it plans to abandon its current scope 3 greenhouse gas emission targets, with the company claiming its climate objectives will be now guided by the pace of global energy transition. Woodside Energy chief executive Liz Westcott. Roy VanDerVegt The announcement comes as the company delivered a 27 per cent increase in net profit to $US1.67 billion despite lower production, citing a jump in prices caused by the global oil crisis due to the ongoing war in the Middle East. According to the company’s latest presentation to stockholders, it plans to shelf investment of US$5 billion in new energy products and lower-carbon services by 2030 and take a financial investment decision on new energy products and lower-carbon services. Woodside chief executive Liz Westcott said strong sustainability performance remains fundamental to the long-term success of the business and the company made good progress in key areas during the half.



“Having achieved our 2025 net equity scope 1 and 2 greenhouse gas emissions reduction target we remain on track to meet our 2030 target of a 30 per cent reduction against our baseline,” she said. “We have taken the disciplined decision to retire our Scope 3 investment and emissions abatement targets. “These targets were established in a different market context and based on a different expected pace of the energy transition.” The Conservation Council of Western Australia labelled the move to abandon its scope 3 investments as “grossly negligent”. CCWA executive director Matt Roberts said Woodside’s decision to dump targets for reducing emissions released when customers burn the gas it sells was a dereliction of its clean energy obligations.



“These emissions account for about 90 per cent of the company’s total climate impact and to walk away from its responsibility for the global climate carnage inherently caused by its product highlights its profits at all cost approach,” he said. Related Article Updated

World markets ASX gains as Woodside result boosts energy stocks; miners and banks also rise “Woodside’s gas is displacing renewables in Asia, as well as here in Western Australia. Woodside uses lobbyists and donations to secure government subsidies that keep the gas industry alive. “It’s time they were held accountable and not allowed to cut and run at a time when the impacts of climate change have never been more prevalent in Australia and around the world.” Meanwhile, the company said its Scarborough project off Karratha in the state’s Pilbara region is on track for first production before the end of the year.



“We continue to make excellent progress on the Scarborough energy project, which was 98 per cent complete at the end of the half,” Westcott said. “It remains on track for first LNG cargo in the fourth quarter of 2026. “Subsequent to the period, the floating production unit achieved ready-for-startup status and first gas, marking another significant milestone as we move closer to production.” “We are taking the time to ensure we are bringing these facilities online safely and reliably as we move toward first LNG cargo and a significant new source of cash generative production to our portfolio.”

World.title: Liam Martin’s contract call as Panthers prepare to hit pause and chase title
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Liam Martin’s contract call as Panthers prepare to hit pause and chase title Dan Walsh August 25, 2026 — 2:02pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Liam Martin and the Panthers have paused talks around a potential contract extension as the club prepares to do the same across their star-studded roster while they chase another premiership. Penrith officials met with Martin’s manager Allan Gainey on Tuesday, with both parties agreeing to hold fire on further negotiations until after the Panthers season, ideally with a fifth premiership in six years. Panthers back-rower Liam Martin. Getty Images Martin, 29, is seeking a three-year deal that would tie him to Penrith until the end of 2030. Sources speaking on the condition of anonymity given the confidential nature of the matter have indicated the Panthers are open to that length of deal for Martin, while a two-year deal was also discussed.



However, the dollar amount of any potential offer is still in flux given superstar halfback Nathan Cleary is yet to begin any meaningful extension talks of his own. Fellow co-captain Isaah Yeo is closing in on a deal beyond 2027 which, as revealed by this masthead, is a good chance of being locked in before the finals kick off in a fortnight. Nathan Cleary is no closer to sorting out his future. Getty Images The Panthers won’t employ a hard-and-fast shutdown on contract negotiations once the post-season starts, but will prioritise their premiership tilt over the next six weeks. “Talks were productive,” Gainey said of Tuesday’s meeting with Panthers general manager Shane Elford and chief executive Matt Cameron.



“Both parties are mindful of the timing and potential distractions around upcoming finals. “We are confident we can get to a mutually beneficial position once Panthers have finished their commitments for 2026.” The Panthers have had several retention wins recently despite losing star winger Brian To’o (PNG Chiefs) and Liam Henry, Scott Sorensen and Jack Cole (Perth Bears) to the NRL’s incoming clubs. Back-rower Isaiah Papali’i has recommitted on a yet-to-be-announced two-year extension, while centre Paul Alamoti has also re-signed until the end of 2029. Rising NSW Origin star Casey McLean was also extended until the end of 2030 last week.



Cleary said last week he is not ready to address his future, and is yet to confirm privately or publicly whether he wants to re-sign before the November 1 free agency date or test his value on the open market. Related Article Updated

NRL 2026 How a personal pitch from the PNG prime minister helped seal Manu’s NRL return Sources close to the champion No.7 have indicated the lack of clarity does not necessarily point to an exit from Penrith, despite the Chiefs making Cleary their halfback priority if he comes off-contract. Martin’s market value, along with fellow off-contract Panthers star Moses Leota, has been a source of intrigue given PNG’s entry to the market, predictions of a 15 per cent rise in the salary cap and a spate of public brinksmanship between managers and clubs of late. Along with Canterbury’s Jacob Preston (24) and Canberra’s Hudson Young (29), Martin is the most accomplished back-rower coming off-contract in 2027. Despite being tabled a $3.3 million, three-year offer – the largest in Canberra’s history – Young will be granted permission to negotiate with PNG next month as he and the Raiders look to bring his future to a head.

World.title: Coalition namecalling as Labour backs social media ban
World.content:
Labour will support National's under-16s social media ban to select committee, having earlier in the day indicated "no rush" to take a position.

It encouraged the government to hold the first reading before the election but Leader of the House Louise Upston said there would not be enough time.

Coalition partners ACT and NZ First - who have long opposed the ban - have criticised the handling of the legislation, pointing to the prime minister's "lack of understanding" and National "panicking" in recent weeks.

Education Minister Erica Stanford - who had been leading the work - welcomed Labour's support, but said she would have liked to introduce it earlier.

She pointed to the time taken in discussion with Labour, despite her announcement of the bill's introduction to Parliament on Monday coming with no guarantee of Labour's support.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins said the party had discussed the matter at caucus on Tuesday morning.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins. (File photo) RNZ / Nathan McKinnon

"We will support that bill, and I've written to Erica Stanford conveying that support and encouraging the government to give the bill its first reading before the election, so that the select committee process can get under way," he said.

"The bill undoubtedly can use improvement. I'm not going to let a quest for perfection, though, delay progress ... we think through the select committee process there will be significant improvements ... the sooner we get that under way, the sooner that can happen."

Stanford had clearly not yet read the letter, finding out about Labour's backing from reporters on Tuesday afternoon.

"Oh, do they?" she said. "Well, they're in step with the rest of New Zealand, then, aren't they? Because they've just seen today what 80 percent of people on a Stuff poll [support it]. And we knew that, I'm out talking to parents every day."

Stanford said the timing of the bill's first reading would be up to Prime Minister Christopher Luxon and Leader of the House Louise Upston.

Upston confirmed that would not happen before the election, given there was already a lot of legislation to get through in just three sitting weeks until Parliament rises.

Peters, Seymour criticise process

David Seymour and Winston Peters. (File photo) RNZ

Heading to the debating chamber on Tuesday, NZ First leader Winston Peters took issue with the way the bill had been promoted.

"It's not a government bill. That's my point. The second thing is, if they've answered all 75 or 79 of Labour's questions I'd be astonished - but then, the Labour Party has pretty low standards so I don't see that's going to be too much difficult."

The bill went through Cabinet and was introduced under the authority of a minister - which makes it a government bill, even if calling it a government "announcement" without the support of ACT or NZ First may be a stretch.

"The National Party leader doesn't seem to understand. Don't blame the system. Don't blame the past. In all the other negotiations we've had and arrangements we've had, this has not happened," Peters said.

"It's a lack of understanding of how the system works, but then again we did say that he hasn't been around here long."

Asked how he would try to avoid such misunderstandings in future, Peters said: "Oh, we take people by the hand and take them through it very slowly".

ACT's leader David Seymour was similarly dismissive, saying the party would not necessarily campaign against the ban but would just point out that "this is not going to help and may harm".

"Clearly the National Party has been a bit panicked in recent weeks so, you know, we've got to give them a bit of relief from time to time.

"But certainly, you wouldn't want it to become normal that ... a third of the government, two of the three parties, disagree with something, and then they go it alone with Labour.

"I mean, there's not much point having a government on the right if your best friends are in Labour."

Stanford comments on tight timeframes

Stanford said it had been "always the intention" to introduce the legislation in time to progress it before the election "but we've just sort of run out of runway, unfortunately".

She was asked what the hold-up was.

"Well, I've been working with Labour for the last five months on this, answering multiple questions, having multiple briefings, showing them the bill multiple times, and here we are."

Stanford agreed it was a technical piece of legislation, saying that was "exactly why I made it available so many times, and my officials, and answering lots of questions".

"They have taken some time to get that understanding of the bill. Spend time with my officials, but we have done absolutely everything that has been asked of us. In fact, I've offered on multiple occasions, "Do you need more? Do you need more? So, I really wanted to get this across the line, and we worked really constructively together."

Labour's Media and Technology spokesperson Reuben Davidson earlier on Tuesday said Stanford's office had provided over 100 pages of documents on the bill, and it was the first time they had all the information.

Facing questions about whether she was suggesting Labour had caused the delays, Stanford did not answer directly.

"Well, I've been bending over backwards to make sure I got them everything they asked for," she said.

She was asked again.

"Look, I'm just saying they had lots of questions and they wanted to see the bill on multiple occasions, and then they asked for a copy of the bill which was a difficult thing to do, it had to get sign-off from the Attorney-General."

And again.

"Well, of course, we would have introduced it much earlier if we were able to."

Asked why had she introduced the bill on Monday when it was at that time unclear if it would have support to pass through Parliament, she said it was because she wanted to make sure the public could see "what we've been doing for the last year".

"That we take this issue really seriously, that they can unpack the bill, see that we've got a regulator - not only the age restriction, but also all of the things that we're requiring of social media companies to do - and that they can see we're putting ourselves in line with other countries."

Green Party co-leader Marama Davidson said a ban for young people was not the way to prevent harm, because the harm was felt by people of all age groups.

Social media platforms needed to be held to account rather than stopping certain people from using the platforms, she said.

Davidson was also concerned about the way the government went about introducing the law, with two of three coalition parties opposing it.

World.title: Name suppression sought for man facing historical sexual offending charges
World.content:
A man at the centre of a police investigation into alleged historical sexual offending had "considerable involvement with a great deal of young people," the Crown says.

Police investigating the case are set to make inquiries into the man's relationships with a "significant number of people," a court heard.

The 63-year-old's case was called in the Christchurch District Court on Tuesday before Judge Michael Crosbie. The man's appearance in court was excused.

The man faces five charges of unlawful sexual connection with a boy aged 12-16 and three charges of indecent assault on a boy aged between 12-16. The charges relate to three complainants and date between 1996 to 2005.

The man's lawyer Ethan Huda said on Tuesday that the man was seeking name suppression on the ground that publication of his name would give risk to a fair trial.

Do you know more? Email sam.sherwood@rnz.co.nz

Huda said there were two unique features of the case. This included that police would be approaching some people with what he referred to as a "scripted questionnaire" to "elicit" information from them.

He said police would identify the defendant to the people spoken to as part of their approach.

"Police believe without identifying [the man] they cannot carry out the questionnaire in the way they would like to."

Huda submitted the man's name should not be published until police had finished administering the questionnaire.

He also wanted to know what the questionnaire would say.

In response, Crown prosecutor Courtney Martyn spoke of the approach that police were using as part of their investigation and what groups of people police would approach.

Martyn said the defendant had "considerable involvement with a great deal of young people…"

"The police aren't going around recruiting complainants or recruiting potential complaints," Martyn said.

She said at no stage would the police be trying to elicit complaints.

"What they're going to be saying is police are conducting an investigation into [the defendant] and as part of that investigation we are speaking to people who may have had contact with him and we understand you're one of those people."

Police would not be discussing any further details or specific allegations.

Judge Crosbie reserved his decision.

Detective Inspector Scott Anderson earlier said police would "continue to investigate whether there are other victims, however as the matter is before the courts and there are suppression orders no further comment will be made".

RNZ understands the defendant has lived in Auckland and Christchurch.

Oranga Tamariki deputy chief executive Thomas Ronan earlier told RNZ the agency had been made aware by police that they were investigating allegations of historical offending by a 63-year-old man.

World.title: Public raise almost $30k in support of injured Palmerston North police officer
World.content:
The organiser of a Givealittle page in support of a Palmerston North police officer critically injured over the weekend says the community's response has been "remarkable".

The officer was deploying road spikes ahead of a fleeing vehicle on Kairanga Bunnythorpe Road about 2am on Saturday, when he was struck and thrown several metres.

He was airlifted to Wellington Hospital in a critical condition, while a second officer was treated for minor injuries.

Police filed charges against two teenage boys in relation to the incident.

The scene where the officer was injured. RNZ/Jimmy Ellingham

Givealittle page organiser Dame Therese Walsh said she understood the officer was only "a couple of years out of police college" and had a young family.

She'd reached out to the officer's family and - while they were reluctant to be in the public eye - they agreed to allow her to set up the page.

"It's not a step they wanted to take lightly. But of course, with a young family and with a lot of unintended expenses that come out of a situation like this. I think they were keen for some support.

"The New Zealand Police are very good to their injured officers as well, but you know that the expenses do pile up when you're in a situation like this and the future is a little unknown," Walsh said.

Walsh said the page was well on track to reach $30,000 worth of donations by the end of its second day online on Tuesday.

Dame Therese Walsh. (File photo) RNZ / Cole Eastham-Farrelly

At the time of writing donations were already in excess of $29,000.

"I just feel a sense of community coming through with this. I think in a really volatile world to have moments where people come together with that strong sense of community to help somebody who's going to work every day to help all of us is quite special.

"As I've seen this Givealittle page grow, I have felt that deep sense of humanity and you know that's a wonderful thing," Walsh said.

Walsh said - as a patron for a police recruitment wing in 2023 - she was immediately concerned when she heard news of the officer's injuries.

"I did a number of training sessions with them and got to know them well. So whenever I hear something about the police, I always take notice to see if it's one of the recruits from that time. It wasn't, but I still have a great deal of empathy for what people in the police go through on the front line.

"And sitting through some of those training sessions, they deal with some really tough stuff. So it just really got me thinking and I wanted to do something to help."

Walsh said the family had asked her to pass on their gratitude for the thought, prayers and donations from the public.

"At this difficult time and that they were just wanting to focus on being at his bedside," she said.

Walsh said she understood the officer remained in a coma in Wellington Hospital.

On Sunday Central District Commander Superintendent Dion Bennett said the officer was in a stable condition and remained on a ventilator in hospital.

World.title: First-term Nelson city councillor Lisa Austin cleared to stay in role
World.content:
A Nelson city councillor who faced removal from her role or potential prosecution over the financial interests of her family trucking business, has been cleared by the Audit Office.

First-term councillor Lisa Austin was elected to Nelson City Council last October. She co-owns Austin Transport Tippers Ltd with her husband, a business that supplies trucks to two council contractors for haulage work but does not have any direct contracts with the local authority.

The law prevents people from being elected or appointed as a member of a council if they have contracts or subcontracts from the council totalling more than $100,000 per year, unless the auditor-general grants an exemption. The amount was previously $25,000, before it was increased on 6 June.

Last week, Nelson City Council made a new application to the auditor-general, seeking approval of Austin's business contracts between 16 October 2025 and 5 June 2026. It said subcontracts made after then did not need approval because of the higher financial threshold.

The council first raised the issue after Austin was elected in October last year, making an application for retrospective approval of her existing contracts.

In May, Austin was informed she might face prosecution or have to vacate her seat after the request for approval was declined by the auditor-general.

The Audit Office said it could not approve contracts made before a member was elected. It later said it would not prosecute Austin as it was not in the public interest.

A spokesperson for the auditor-general said the council had received new information that differed from the original application last November and had since granted Austin approval.

It found Austin's pre-election contracts qualified for a statutory "candidate exception", which meant she was eligible to stand for election or hold office.

The Audit Office said there was no opportunity for Austin to influence the council's original contracts or contractors' decisions to use Austin Transport Tippers.

Documents show there were no formal subcontracting agreements in place, instead the work was carried out under multiple subcontracts which were formed when a contractor called Austin Transport Tippers to request a truck for haulage, and the company agreed to provide one with the work to be charged at its usual rates.

The Audit Office also said the council had a sufficient reason for not seeking approval earlier because it first needed to resolve whether Austin had been validly elected and had prior approval been sought, it would have been granted.

The spokesperson said the Auditor-General's interpretation of the Local Authorities (Members' Interests) Act meant the Nelson City Council was responsible for any applications made under the act, for complying with the law, and for its own decision-making processes.

In May, Austin said she had become aware another councillor was questioning her right to remain in her role and had raised it with the mayor.

The matter was then discussed during a confidential section of an audit risk and finance committee extraordinary meeting in June, and again a week later in an hours long closed-door meeting where councillors discussed potential legal risks relating to Austin's election and her legal ability to sit on the council

Austin said she worked with lawyer Dr Mai Chen to ensure the council and the Audit Office had the correct information, which confirmed she was legally allowed to stand for election and be elected as a councillor.

"I am relieved the issues concerning eligibility to serve as a councillor at Nelson City Council have now all been resolved, which allows me to focus on giving back to the city I love."

She said she was grateful the parties had been able to work together to resolve the issue and she looked forward to working with her council colleagues in the city's best interests.

In early July, figures provided to RNZ showed the council had spent nearly $25,000 on external legal advice about the situation.

Nelson City Council's Civic House.

Nelson City Council chief executive Nigel Philpott said the council had been working with Austin and her team to navigate the issue and was pleased the new information had satisfied the Audit Office's concerns and enabled them to grant the relevant approvals.

"Council has always said we wish to avoid a by-election. The determination by the Audit Office allows council to move forward with confidence."

World.title: Property agent denies inspecting faulty pool gate at inquest into drowned toddler
World.content:
A coroner has heard a pool where a toddler drowned in 2023 had failed multiple inspections.

River Albert-Wihone had only recently turned one when he was found in the backyard pool at his family home in Auckland.

He was taken to Starship Children's Hospital, where he died in his mother's arms 12 days later.

A coroner's inquest examining whether concerns about the pool's gate and fence were adequately dealt with, and who was responsible for maintaining the area, has on Tuesday heard from property managers.

For River's parents, Matthew and Lauren, the inquest was a chance to set a standard for other similar cases.

Matthew wanted to see regulation changes, including for how often council's must inspect pools.

"That's something that I would like to see changed," he said, "three years is a very big gap."

Albert-Wihone was also about to take courses to become a pool inspector, in the hope of helping other families.

"That's something I feel we can do to just sort of help," he said.

"We want to work with families that don't really know and things like that [...] being a parent that's had to go through it, we understand how really hard it is in that situation."

A shrine set up at the coroners inquest of toddler River Albert-Wihone who drowned in a pool in 2023. RNZ / Finn Blackwell

River's mother, Lauren, was also hoping some good could come from their family tragedy.

"Maybe our case can help future cases, and maybe it sets a sort of standard," she said.

"I know that from here, we're not finished yet, we're not done, there's still other things that we want to look into."

The inquest has heard details about how a pool gate at the rental property would fail to latch, sometimes closing on the first try, other times not.

Concerns were raised about the state of the barrier, but River's family say they fell on deaf ears.

Alexander Silver, who runs a fencing company and who had looked at the state of the pool fence, said on Monday that the tragic accident could have been avoided, had the gate been installed using better quality hinges and latches.

"The way the work was done, how long it took to do the work, for the council to sign it off, if it had been done correctly it would have been signed off," he said.

Coroner Alison Mills has now heard from Michael Springett, a property manager for the home, who was asked by the lawyer assisting the coroner, Danielle Kelly, about pool inspections failed by Auckland Council prior to River's death.

"It had failed an inspection in 2016, and then continued to be non-compliant until at least it was declared empty in 2020, that's a period of four years, would it be common in your experience to have a pool non-compliant for that length of time?"

Springett said no.

"The property was vacant, it was 'defunct' for lack of a better word," Springett said.

Management changed in early 2023, when it taken over by Vinesh Haribhai acting on behalf of the landlord, who appeared over audio visual link.

He denied looking at the pool gate during an inspection, when asked by Lucy Wright, the lawyer for River's grandmother Christine Robinson, about evidence heard from Robinson's daughter earlier in the inquest.

"Ms Robinson then goes on to say that she saw her mother demonstrate the gate to you, and the fact it wasn't closing or self-latching, is that possible?"

"Nope I didn't see that," Haribhai replied.

"And further, that you said it needed fixing, is that possible?" Wright asked.

"No", he said.

World.title: A 'living room for the city': Nelson pub at risk of closure under council civic centre plans
World.content:
A popular Nelson pub in a 100-year-old former church could face closure under one of the city council's multi-million dollar options for a new library, community hub and civic centre.

The council is proposing three options: developing the current Civic House and the adjourning Savings Bank and State Advances sites at a cost of $73.3 million; or building a new hub, library and civic space in Collingwood Street for $74.1m, or in Church Street for $88.2m.

Under the Collingwood Street option, The Free House would be replaced with a new building.

The pub, which was established in 2009, has become a regular meeting place for many groups including knitters, singers, backgammon players and mountainbikers, among many others.

The Free House opened in 2009 in an old Reformed Church. RNZ / Samantha Gee

Owner Eelco Boswijk said he was aware of plans to develop the land adjacent to The Free House, but news the land the pub was on was also included in one of the council's options came as a bit of a surprise.

"It was only when we saw the pictures that the council put out that it was like, 'oh, okay, we're well included' but it is what it is and people have to decide which one they want, if they want anything at all."

Boswijk said the idea for The Free House came after he and former co-owner Mic Dover couldn't find anwhere in Nelson to get a decent beer.

"All the pubs were tied basically and we were lamenting the fact that there were craft breweries popping up all over New Zealand and we couldn't get the beer in Nelson."

The Free House owner Eelco Boswijk. RNZ / Samantha Gee

The pair ran beer fetes once a quarter at Founders Park, all the while hoping someone would see there was a market for craft beer and open a pub or change their taps, he said.

When the former Reformed Church on Collingwood Street came on the market, Boswijk and Dover decided to have a go at it themselves.

In the last 17 years, it had become a community hub, a neutral space that welcomed everyone, he said.

If the Collingwood Street option was chosen, he hoped there was scope for The Free House to be integrated into the design in some way.

"There are two other options on the table and they may well get chosen so there's no point in getting terribly worked up just yet."

The Nelson City Council's options for the combined Community Hub, Library and Civic Space. Supplied / Nelson City Council

'A nugget of gold', a 'living room for the city'

Jenny Smith started the Free House Knitters about five years ago, in a bid to make a hobby that was often solitary more social.

"We didn't want to meet anywhere where there's a room charge or a minimum drinks requirement or anything like that and The Free House was just always very accommodating,.

"It's just a great living room for the city, there's so many special interest groups that meet here and you always see your friends here too, even if you're not planning anything."

Fellow knitter Gera Verheul said people often asked if they could join the group and anyone was welcome.

The pub reserved a table by the fireplace for the knitters, and put a bright light so they could see what they were doing.

"It's so much more than a pub, like on Tuesdays when we're here, you'll see in the corner there's a bunch of backgammon players, they're always here, live musicians will come and play music, the mountain bikers love it here, artists, all sorts of people come here."

The Free House Knitters meet fortnightly at the pub. RNZ / Samantha Gee

Verheul said she was all for a new library, but not in place of The Free House.

"This is an institution, there's an inner city garden here, we can sit outside, there's greenery, this building is an old church from the 1900s.

"We've got to hang on to these things, we don't want everything big and new and modern."

Carolyn Phillips and usually one if not two of her brothers have been meeting at The Free House every week since it opened. The three grew up in Jamaica, but now live in Nelson.

Their group, known as The Jamaicans, had grown to include many others and every Thursday, they gather play dominoes.

"[It's] a great Jamaican tradition, very noisy, as you will hear, lots of banging and crashing and yelling and several glasses of beer and or wine, but such fun."

Chris, Carolyn and Christian Phillips, who are in a group known as The Jamaicans, play dominoes every week at The Free House. RNZ / Samantha Gee

Phillips said she couldn't believe it when she heard one of the council's options for a new civic building could mean the end of The Free House.

"What do you mean you want to take this down to build a community centre? This is a community centre, I meet so many people here, so many people I know and so many people I don't know, which I think is one of the healthiest aspects of it.

"Why aren't you taking some derelict place that nobody goes to or some bit of empty land or some horrible concrete box that is an eyesore? There must be other places.

"To me, it would be like removing a nugget of gold from this city and I think this city is under stress anyway as it is."

David Montgomerie started the Nelson Shanty Club about six months ago and it found a home at The Free House.

"Every month we get together and over the course of a couple of hours and probably a few drinks, sing some sea shanties together.

"We do kind of impose shanties on [pubgoers] a bit for the evening, but a lot of them really enjoy that, get involved in singing and singalong, so it's brilliant."

Nelson Shanty Club meets once a week at The Free House, with anyone welcome to join in and sing. RNZ / Samantha Gee

Whakatū Ultimate Frisbee Club member Jim Risner said for at least seven years, a group of players had been heading to The Free House after their Thursday night games.

"One, it's got a great selection of beer which always changes, two, the staff are great and three, I do like the decor, but that's why I stay, that's not why I come."

Risner said the pub was part of Nelson's history and world famous outside New Zealand.

"A couple years ago, it was in a guidebook. Tourists would be reading that from overseas that come here to the pub, you can't replace that, you can't tear it down."

Three locations, one decsision

Deputy mayor and city revitalisation taskforce chair Pete Rainey said the council been grappling with how to address the ageing library and council building for some time.

Plans to build a $46m library on the banks of the Maitai River were shelved in 2022 after the severe flood event caused millions of dollars worth of damage to the community, with the cost also considered unaffordable in the current economic environment.

That same year, the council building Civic House was served two earthquake-prone notices, despite strengthening works undertaken in 2021.

"This term of council we've taken it head on and given real thought to what we can do about both of those issues and that's when we came to the decision to go ahead with a plan to combine the facilities into one building because we think it's the most cost-effective, prudent and forward-thinking plan for the city."

Deputy mayor and city revitalisation taskforce chair Pete Rainey. VNP / Phil Smith

He said he really liked The Free House and that it encompassed many of the things he hoped that a new civic community space would too.

"A lot of the activity that happens in the Free House, the community aspects, are exactly the kind of things that I would like to see happening in a new community space that we would build for the city. Not necessarily the bar, but all of the community-facing type of activities that happen in there, are they the kind of things that we need real consideration to."

Rainey said there were multi-use facilities around New Zealand that were great examples of combining libraries with civic administration; the Te Kahu o Waipuna - Marlborough Library & Art Gallery in Blenheim, Te Ara Ātea in Rolleston and Te Whare Whakatere in Ashburton.

He encouraged people to make a submission on their preferred option.

"We need to know what people think, there's no doubt that it's tricky economic times, we certainly recognise that, but we don't think sitting still and parking the issue is the right move.

"We've got to start thinking ahead for the city for the next 50 to 100 years. This is not just about the current ratepayers and the current population of Nelson, it's about their children and their grandchildren."

World.title: Why are we paying $50 for instant coffee?
World.content:
Instant coffee creeping past $50 for a jar is a symptom of wider pressure on coffee prices, economists say.

New World is this week advertising Moccona classic medium roast in a 400g jar for $53.99.

A listing for $50+ instant coffee at New World supermarkets. Supplied

Woolworths has it on special for $42.99.

Woolworths said there were a number of factors that influenced the price of coffee including a tightening global supply, market volatility and a weaker New Zealand dollar.

Westpac senior economist Satish Ranchhod said global coffee prices were high, in part due to poor weather in some of the major producing regions, such as Vietnam and Brazil.

"Those production cost pressures will have been compounded by the recent increases in global fuel costs."

At BNZ, chief economist Mike Jones said he was caught out by the price when he went to buy more instant coffee on Sunday.

"A classic global supply shock appears to be at the root of the big price increase, in part caused by adverse weather. The global price for coffee is volatile but roughly doubled over the past four years. We haven't seen the full extent of that in NZ but the low NZ dollar over the first part of the year probably would not have helped given it raises the cost of imports."

Stats NZ data showed the average price of 100g of instant coffee has risen from $6.25 in July 2019 to $8.02 in July this year. It dropped as low as $5.40 in late 2020.

Commenters on Reddit expressed surprise at the price Moccona had reached.

"I've changed job now, but in my old job I was making around $850 a week working full time. When I see this coffee at nearly $50 that's like 1/17th of my weekly pay just to get a coffee. If I went shopping and bought coffee, milk, some chicken breasts, shower gel, cereal, and bread, that would likely be between $80-$100, like 1/8th of my entire income just to eat for a couple of days," one posted.

World.title: Labour promises to reinstate Smokefree Generation policy
World.content:
The Labour Party has announced plans to reinstate its Smokefree Generation policy if elected into government.

The party's health spokesperson Ayesha Verrall announced the policy at a panel discussion on health and harm prevention in Parliament this afternoon.

Labour had already signalled an intent to bring back the policy in speech from Labour leader Chris Hipkins in 2024.

It would reverse the government's heated tobacco policy - which introduced a 50 percent reduction in the excise duty for heated tobacco products, Verrall said.

She also said the party would introduce a common licensing regime for tobacco and vape products.

The Smokefree Generation policy, when it was announced under the previous Labour government, would have meant that people born on, or after 1 January 2009 would never be able to purchase tobacco products again.

It also heavily restricted the number of stores selling tobacco products, and dramatically reduced nicotine levels.

The Health Coalition Aotearoa panel, held at the Legislative Council Chamber in Parliament. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

It was repealed in 2024 by the current government.

Verrall said Labour would reinstate the policy, but the birthdate after which people could purchase products would now change if the law passed. She did not say what that date was.

She said future generations needed to be protected "against the harms of tobacco", and gains in reducing smoking addiction had been wound back under the current government.

She said the policy would no longer seek to reduce the amount of nicotine in tobacco products to very low-levels.

That could drive people into a black market, Verrall said.

"It is a very stringent control on tobacco products.

"I'm very aware that expert views on this matters have changed, as we have watched very stringent tobacco controls in Australia, coincide with growth in an illicit market," she said.

Hūhana Lyndon RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Greens Party health spokesperson Hūhana Lyndon and Te Pāti Māori co-leader Debbie Ngarewa-Packer, who were both at the panel event, said they supported re-instating the policy.

Lyndon said, "We're absolutely supportive of having that more stringent licensing approach. We know that vaping is also an issue, and it's an entry point for young people."

Debbie Ngarewa-Packer RNZ / Baz Macdonald

But associate health minister Casey Costello said she would not support a change to the heated tobacco excise policy.

"We are trying to get people to stop smoking and reduced-harm pathways are the best way to do it."

She said stringent policies in Australia had failed to deliver, resulting in a "massive" black market problem.

Costello said she was supportive of a common licensing policy for tobacco products.

It was also something which ACT's Todd Stephenson, who was also at the panel event, said the party was open to considering.

"I'd be open to considering it, but again it's not an ACT policy."

He said ACT was against prohibition-type policies, referring to black market concerns.

Finance minister and National deputy leader Nicola Willis said the government stood by its smokefree policies.

World.title: NRL changes rules to allow Jai Arrow to 'play' 100 games for Souths
World.content:
Jai Arrow will make cameo appearances in the final two rounds of the regular season in order to reach 100 games for South Sydney.

In one of the feel-good stories of the NRL season, the forward who retired with motor neurone disease in May has been approved to start on the field in rounds 26 and 27.

Arrow will then be substituted out in the opening seconds before any active involvement in play.

It came after the Rabbitohs made an appeal to the NRL to grant the former Queensland representative an on-field swansong while still able to walk and run.

The initiative gives Arrow two final chances to farewell an NRL career that featured a grand-final appearance in 2021 and 12 State of Origin caps.

The NRL has granted Souths special dispensation to name Arrow as an extra player on today's team list and an extra substitution in their rotation.

Arrow vows to help others fight MND Former NRL player Jai Arrow says he is determined to raise money and awareness for Motor Neurone Disease until a cure is found.

The matches, against Gold Coast and the Sydney Roosters, will bring Arrow's tally to 180 career games and 100 for the Rabbitohs.

Arrow will lead the team out on both occasions and sit on the interchange bench in Souths kit after being substituted out.

The Titans and Roosters have both approved the plan, as have the Rugby League Players Association.

"We are very grateful to Peter [V'landys] and the NRL, and Clint [Newton] at the RLPA, for supporting our proposal," Souths chief executive Blake Solly said.

"We believe this will provide great inspiration for everyone watching the game from the stadium or at home, showing that MND will not hold Jai, or anyone else, back from achieving what they want to achieve in life."

The NRL world has rallied around Arrow since his shock diagnosis and immediate retirement in May.

The league threw Arrow "the world's biggest birthday party" on the day Souths beat Newcastle in July, rolling out a birthday cake in the shape of the 31-year-old's jersey and presenting him with a commemorative jersey.

Fundraising efforts have already passed $1 million in support of Arrow, who is the father of a young daughter.

Players from all clubs have shown their support by marking tries with arrow celebrations throughout the month of July.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP

World.title: McVeigh to canvass Hird return as icon urges Bombers fans to unite
World.content:
New Essendon coach Mark McVeigh says he will speak to James Hird about returning to the club in a different capacity after a second failed bid to be coach.

McVeigh was unveiled on Tuesday in a press conference that was also attended by a number of Essendon's current players.

Both he and club president Andrew Welsh indicated their desire to have Hird involved.

"I'd love to see James as a part of the club going forward. He's such a fantastic football person," Welsh said.

"I feel there's significant value James can bring, not just tokenistic, but real value to our club and our playing group.

"Certainly, part of my messaging was that Mark and I would want to catch up with him when the time is appropriate."

While Welsh said a pair of calls to Hird had gone unanswered on Monday night, McVeigh said he had shared a conversation with his former captain.

"I love James Hird, he's one of my best mates. It was difficult to go through the process against a good friend," he said.

McVeigh (right) called Hird (left) one of his "best mates" after beating him to the Essendon job. (Getty Images: Ryan Pierse)

"I don't fear those people [Hird's supporters], I actually embrace how they feel, and I understand it, to be fair.

"He's been a constant in my life since I was 17 years of age. We spoke this morning, and the way he spoke of how proud he was of this moment for me, it hasn't broken us, we're still together, but I understand and embrace the feelings of the people that love James Hird, because I do too."

McVeigh, Welsh and club CEO Tim Roberts called for unity at the club amid rumours of a potential board challenge from unimpressed Hird fans.

"I don't ask for your patience, I ask for your re-alignment to our club," McVeigh said.

"I sit here year after year, and we get people coming out of the shadows that want to challenge the board," added Welsh.

"I can tell you since I've been here that this club has never been more united.

"These people want to keep living in the shadows and keep on trying to destabilise our club, we don't jump at shadows.

"We're a strong club and we'll continue to make sure that we make the right decisions on behalf of our members and our teams and our staff to get this club moving forward again."

Tim Watson (pictured) has called for unity at Essendon after Mark McVeigh's signing. (Getty Images: Michael Willson)

The plea for unity came as Essendon legend Tim Watson has the club's passionate supporters to "put [their] weapons down".

"There's got to be a unification of the club now," he told SEN on Tuesday morning.

"People have to put down their weapons and get behind this appointment of a former player — somebody who has been passionate about the football club.

"This is part of the healing process that needs to take place. Ultimately, it's a much bigger thing than the emotion that might be associated with it now. There is an enormous amount of work to do.

Live Moment Look back at Mark McVeigh's first press conference as Essendon's new senior coach. McVeigh says Bombers 'won't live in the past' Pretty good way to end the press conference from the new Essendon coach. He receives another round of applause from those in attendance before walking off the podium. Welsh with another clue on Hird returning I reckon it's going to be a full-court press on the Dons trying to get Hird to say yes to some kind of role within the club. "We have great people that we want to get back involved with the club in meaningful ways," Welsh says. "I look at this as a point that we can re-align that passion." McVeigh with an insight into his game plan McVeigh explains what areas he's going to try and fix on-field. "In the phases of the game, we can't focus on one. If you look at the numbers, we're the bottom of the table in a lot of areas. "I do want them to be brave, I do want them to play with flare, but we do need to fix up our defence. "They [the players] need to come back prepared physically and ready to learn. "The system we'll put in place, you need to understand, otherwise you'll get found out. "When we get all three phases going in the right direction, Essendon will fly." Show more

"Congratulations to him. He's been an Essendon man all his life. He's loved this football club, that was clear in the days that he played.

"He's had a great development profile if you look at where he's been and what he's been doing. He's been part of elite coaching departments [at GWS and Sydney]."

McVeigh has signed a three-year contract with Essendon and was the unanimous choice of the Essendon board.

World.title: Piastri searching for answers as teammate re-enters F1 title picture
World.content:
Oscar Piastri's "disappointing" end to the Dutch Grand Prix has left the Australian and his McLaren team searching for answers, while his teammate has roared back into the Formula 1 title picture.

Last weekend in Zandvoort was shaping to be a good weekend for Piastri.

The Australian was matching the pace at the front through qualifying, and after a terrific second start in the grand prix following Max Verstappen's heavy crash, Piastri was on course for a first podium finish since Miami in May.

Piastri struggles after slow pit stop, Norris wins as Verstappen crashes Reigning world champion Lando Norris has doubled his grand prix win tally in 2026, producing a pair of brilliant overtakes to win the Dutch Grand Prix.

Piastri had performed a breathtaking overtake on Mercedes driver George Russell to move into third and was not far off the pace set by leaders Kimi Antonelli and teammate Lando Norris, despite being on a harder compound tyre.

But a slow first pit stop knocked Piastri back behind Russell and out of third place, and it only got worse from there.

Piastri, who won the Dutch Grand Prix in 2025, fell right off the pace and finished a distant sixth as Norris surged to victory.

Piastri was running third until a slow pit stop knocked him out of the podium position at Zandvoort. (Reuters: Benoit Tessier)

The sudden pace drop-off has left Piastri with plenty of questions that he and the team will want answers to.

"The first stint felt reasonable, but from the second stint onwards, the pace was simply not there, and it became a real struggle," he said.

"We will review the entire weekend and analyse to understand why we experienced such a significant performance drop-off.

"A slow pit stop didn't help, but the fundamental issue was the lack of pace, which is something we'll work on ahead of Monza.

"That's the priority now, to dig into the data with the team to find the root cause and ensure we can move forward in a more positive direction for the upcoming races."

Piastri's situation is a far cry from where he was at the conclusion of last year's Dutch Grand Prix, when he claimed his seventh grand prix win of the season and was the championship leader.

But while Piastri is seeking answers to get back to the front of the grid, Norris is threatening to stay there.

'The fight's still on': Norris re-enters the F1 title picture

McLaren entered the 2026 season having won the previous two constructors' championships, and with Lando Norris as reigning drivers' champion.

Reigning Formula 1 drivers' champion Lando Norris has won the past two grands prix. (Reuters: Benoit Tessier)

But with a new era of regulations, McLaren's 2026 season started poorly.

Piastri crashed on his way to the grid in Melbourne and he and Norris did not start in Shanghai due to car issues.

Norris then had back-to-back retirements in Montreal and Monaco, meaning he failed to finish three of the opening six grands prix.

But the reigning world champion has returned to winning ways, triumphing in Hungary before the mid-year break and then again last weekend in the Netherlands.

With back-to-back wins and growing confidence in his season, Norris has re-emerged as a drivers' championship contender.

F1 drivers' championship standings after Dutch Grand Prix 242 — Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes

183 — George Russell, Mercedes

183 — Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari

159 — Lando Norris, McLaren

155 — Charles Leclerc, Ferrari

With 10 or 11 rounds remaining this season, depending on conflict in the Middle East, Norris is sitting fourth in the standings, 83 points behind leader Kimi Antonelli.

It is a huge gap, but recent history shows it is not an impossible feat.

At the conclusion of last year's Dutch Grand Prix, Max Verstappen was 104 points behind then-leader Piastri with nine rounds remaining.

Verstappen surged towards the end of the season while Piastri slumped. Verstappen fell two points shy of Norris in the standings, but finished a stunning 11 points ahead of Piastri.

Having seen what is possible, Norris has made this year's title fight a four-way race with Antonelli, George Russell and Lewis Hamilton.

Norris's message to his team over the radio after taking the chequered flag on Sunday certainly sounded like the Briton believed his championship hopes are far from over.

"Let's keep pushing. Thank you for the hard work. Let's keep bringing upgrades, let's keep bringing performance, please," he said.

"The fight's still on."

Out of the car, Norris was quick to point out that there is a long season still ahead of the drivers and that he was not getting ahead of himself with an 83-point deficit.

"One race at a time. A lot of people say it now, but it is the truth of it. There's no point in thinking that far ahead," he said after winning on Sunday.

"There are plenty of things we can do better, and we need to do better if we want to fight for a championship.

"We have to keep working hard. There's still plenty of races, plenty of opportunity for everyone."

Norris's deficit to Antonelli was 101 points prior to the weekend in Hungary, but the McLaren champion has reduced that by 18 with two tremendous weekends.

However, the 83-point gap is significant and Antonelli has extended his overall championship lead.

Entering the Dutch Grand Prix weekend, the young Italian's lead over Hamilton was 50 points, and 59 over Russell.

After the weekend, his lead is 59 points over both Hamilton and Russell.

F1 heads to Monza for the Italian Grand Prix in two weeks, one of the fastest tracks on the calendar and vastly different to the tight and twisting circuits in Hungary and the Netherlands where Norris has won this year.

World.title: 'A dangerous individual': Ex-snooker champ convicted of child sex abuse
World.content:
Former world snooker champion Graeme Dott has been convicted of sexually abusing two primary school children in Scotland in the 1990s and early 2000s.

Dott, 49, was found guilty of abusing a girl from 1993-96 and a boy from 2006-10 after a five-day trial at the High Court in Glasgow. The judge ordered Dott to be held in custody ahead of his sentencing on September 29.

The woman, now in her 40s, testified that Dott sexually abused her on multiple occasions, "caressing" her bottom over her clothing, exposing himself and touching her with parts of his body, including his penis.

The man, now in his late 20s, said he was abused on multiple occasions, with Dott touching him inappropriately, kissing him and performing sexual acts.

Dott with his wife Elaine after winning the snooker world championship in 2006. (Getty Images: Rui Vieira)

"Dott is a dangerous individual, and I hope this conviction provides some measure of comfort to those impacted by his crimes," Detective Inspector Gary Smillie from Police Scotland said.

Snooker's governing body suspended Dott in April 2025 after he was charged in the case. The Scot was ranked number 56 in the world at the time and dropped from the rankings after the season.

On Monday, the World Professional Billiards and Snooker Association revoked Dott's membership following an emergency board meeting. The WPBSA also said it wrote to the World Snooker Tour to request his immediate removal from the WST Hall of Fame.

Dott won the World Snooker Championship in 2006 and was a runner-up twice.

AP/Reuters

World.title: Zak Butters trade rumours dominate Port Adelaide's turbulent season
World.content:
It's been a tumultuous year for Port Adelaide.

Its newly-appointed coach Josh Carr had to navigate a new system with an injury riddled list; using 39 of its 44-listed players and finishing the season with 15 unavailable.

He also had to build chemistry and belief despite a contract decision overshadowing his campaign.

Its vice-captain and dual All-Australian Zak Butters has dominated headlines all season as one of the biggest free-agents available this off-season; and has now confirmed the worst-kept secret in football that he has requested a trade to Victoria.

"I've made a decision to head home. It's obviously been one that I've wrestled with for a while now. It's been a tough decision and one that I haven't taken lightly," Butters said on Monday.

"Although I've loved my time in Adelaide … I'm probably at a stage in my life where I'd like to get back around some family and friends and enjoy some more time with them."

Butters denied reports in June that he had begun telling those close to him he was eager to move east after a trip back home during the round 12 bye; another chapter in a compendium of updates on the dual Showdown medallist's future.

So why was the club so protective of Butters when he had a foot out the door?

There are two key foundations of any negotiation in any industry. Value and relationships.

Growing speculation

As the weeks progressed and the speculation grew, the four-horse race between Richmond, Geelong, Collingwood and the Western Bulldogs intensified as the coverage evolved into a public bidding war; increasing Butters' contract terms and giving the Power fuel for higher trade demands.

Every story has a source … and every source has an agenda.

Zak Butters to leave Port Adelaide Star Port Adelaide midfielder Zak Butters has informed the Power he wants to return to Victoria.

Player agents are looking to maximise demand and clubs want their outgoing stars to leave at a high price.

Relationships between the two parties are also incredibly important in future dealings. Clubs are constantly trying to find the balance between fair compensation and long-term favours.

For Port Adelaide this was the case two years ago when Dan Houston was desperate to move to Collingwood but the Magpies didn't have the capital for a reasonable return.

The Power settled for Picks 13, 29 and 36 plus forwards Jack Lukosius and Joe Richards in exchange for its dual All-Australian defender and a future first round pick.

It was a move that was widely panned at the time but hasn't done much damage given rising key forward Jack Whitlock was taken at 29 and Joe Richards is developing into a handy midfield option.

But Dan Houston and Zak Butters are different cases.

The Power is hoping to maximise its draft haul in moving its triple best-and-fairest winner given it has rarely had early selections in recent years leading to a gulf in young talent depth.

It also has a litany of upcoming academy and father-son draftees it will need to match bids on, such as expected number one pick Dougie Cochrane and Zemes Pilot.

Matthew Richardson spoke about the Butters trade rumous in May. (ABC News: Marco Catalano)

Back in May, Port chief executive Matthew Richardson flagged on ABC Sport that the club would match any bid on Butters to force a trade given the star is a restricted free agent.

"There will be offers that we can match and we will match. It does give the club a fair bit of control in what happens," he said.

The issue is Butters current suitors have a diverse availability of picks at their disposal and the Power's best option Richmond doesn't quite align with the values Butters claimed he was eyeing when I asked him back in March what would dictate his decision.

"I think you're stupid if you don't want to win premierships," he said.

"I want to win. Family is important as well … but you can't look too far ahead."

THE CONTENDERS (As of current ladder position, all four clubs have all future picks available) Geelong: 17, 35, 53, 71

Western Bulldogs: 10, 28, 46

Collingwood: 16, 34, 63, 66, 70

Richmond: 2, 20, 38, 56

While Port navigates its way through the 20 out-of-contract players it has held fire on due to the Butters decision, there will be time for Josh Carr to reflect on his inaugural season at the helm.

Season highlights

Despite double ups with four sides who missed finals; the Power managed seven wins in 2026 and had a clear narrative throughout; it could match it with the best but could rarely beat them.

Its campaign ended with an equal league record five losses by five-points or less and eight by as much as 14-points.

A Showdown win over Adelaide in June was the highlight, plus its April upset over Geelong; but its only road wins were against fellow bottom four sides West Coast and Richmond.

It finished 16th for ball movement from D50 to F50 but defensively was a powerhouse until the final month where 10-goal losses to the Lions, Swans and Demons blew out the team's average points against to 89, dropping it down from a Top 4 side into 10th.

The other positive was its clearance work. Despite missing Connor Rozee for the majority of the campaign, and Zak Butters for the final month, the side finished second for clearance differential, blooding future stars in Jase Burgoyne, Joe Richards and Miles Bergman on ball.

Port Adelaide won seven games in the 2026 season. (ABC Riverland: Catherine Heuzenroeder)

From a list perspective it was the only side not to have a player named in the AFL's 22-under-22 squad and some of the long-term signings from the Hinkley era like Todd Marshall and Brandon Zerk-Thatcher barely featured.

Former Port midfielder and four times Showdown medallist Josh Francou believes 2026 was a free hit for Josh Carr.

"It has been a difficult campaign … the way they're defending the ground is a real plus for them but they struggle to move the ball," he said.

"Next year things start to ramp up on Josh Carr and he's got to get it right."

Despite all the adversities, it feels like Josh Carr has laid the foundation for success but a critical off-season awaits as he looks to reshape the list and keep his stars healthy for the 2027 campaign.

World.title: Cyclists run for cover as hailstorm forces La Vuelta stage cancellation
World.content:
A torrential hailstorm in the French Pyrenees forced the abandonment of the third stage of the Vuelta a España on Monday.

With 15 kilometres remaining of the 174-km route from Gruissan to Font-Romeu, the skies darkened as the peloton neared the top of the Col de Mont-Louis and huge hailstones began bouncing off the tarmac and pelting the riders.

Mats Wenzel (Kern Pharma) and Lorenzo Fortunato (XDS Astana) were 25 seconds ahead of the peloton when the elements intervened, as race leader and favourite Tadej Pogacar was seen indicating to the peloton to pull off the course.

Bedraggled riders were then seen getting off their bikes and shuffling into a hotel for shelter.

Shortly afterwards, race organisers, ASO, announced the stage would not resume, leaving fans frustrated at the finish where thick layers of hail blanketed the road.

Slovenia's Pogacar (UAE Emirates-XRG) retained his overall lead of nine seconds from Belgium's Wout van Aert (Dutch Visma-Lease a Bike) with Britain's Matt Brennan 10 seconds back.

Earlier it had been warm and sunny on the flat approaches to the mountainous finish with no sign of the chaos to come as a five-man breakaway group stayed out ahead.

Pogacar, bidding to complete his Grand Tour collection by winning the Vuelta for the first time, was always near the front of the pack with his team setting the pace.

Sadly, his expected challenge for the stage victory fell foul of the weather in an anticlimactic finish.

He will get his chance to underline his superiority again on Tuesday, though with stage four featuring three first-category climbs as the race starts and finishes in Andorra la Vella.

Reuters

World.title: From almost drowning as a child to the pinnacle of surf lifesaving
World.content:
Under an expansive blue sky and bathed in the type of sunshine that typifies Queensland's mocking parody of winter, the ocean at Surfers Paradise is made to look incredibly inviting, even on a Thursday morning in August.

But the crashing of waves into the hard-packed sand offers a reminder that beyond the beauty of the scene, the power of the ocean remains a potent force.

Australian Iron Series athlete Tiarnee Massie knows about this more than most.

The 24-year-old is a third-generation surf lifesaver at Maroochydore Surf Life Saving Club on Queensland's Sunshine Coast.

Not only that, but she is the reigning and defending Iron Series champion and will wear the yellow number 1 seed bib when the series gets underway in October with the Coolangatta Gold.

Tiarnee Massie will look to once again win the overall title when the series finishes at Surfers Paradise early next year. (Getty Images: Iron Series/Chris Hyde)

Her story could have been very different, though.

"I think I was nine months old," Massie tells ABC Sport on the Gold Coast.

"I was at home and my older sister was playing in the pool with her friends.

"Someone left the pool gate open and I found myself in the pool and drowning at the bottom of the pool."

The scenario is one that is all too painfully familiar for far too many Australian families.

The 2025 National Drowning Report, published by Royal Life Saving Australia and Surf Life Saving Australia, identified 15 fatalities of children aged four or younger, eight of which occurred in a swimming pool.

In total, the report noted that there were 357 drowning deaths over the past 12 months, a 27 per cent increase on the 10-year average.

Tiarnee Massie is aware she could have become a statistic for Australia's downing deaths. (Getty Images: Matt Roberts)

"My mum was actually on the phone and she had this gut instinct that something was wrong, so she hung up and she came out and she found me in the water," Massie says, knowing how fortunate she is to not be a contributing statistic to the nation's drowning tally.

"She started doing resuscitation and she saved my life that day."

That near-death experience didn't seem to do Massie any long-term harm.

Even in the short term it seems the young Massie was relatively unperturbed by the experience — she tells ABC Sport she was back in the water the very next day.

"It didn't affect me at all," Massie says.

"But it certainly affected my mum," she adds with an infectious and earnestly cheeky grin.

"Still now, when she's watching me in the ocean, she just can't watch. She's actually fainted a few times.

"She's got demons there, but she knows that I'm capable and she knows that I love it.

"I have the best family who support me. They are always coming to all of my competitions, we stay together and to be able to share these incredible experiences and moments with them, it's a dream come true."

Tiarnee Massie says her mum sometimes struggles watching her race. (Getty Images: Matt Roberts)

That day sparked something in Massie's mother too, who has gone on to become a CPR trainer at the Maroochydore Surf Club, joining a club that her uncle, Ashley Massie, competed for in surf lifesaving competitions.

"She never was involved [in surf lifesaving] to the extent of being a trainer until the moment that I drowned in the pool," Massie says.

"You don't know if you are someone that deals well in those situations until you're literally in the situation.

"You know, you can do all the training, but unless you actually are in that situation, you don't know whether you can do it. And my mum did it."

And incredibly, that ability to remain calm under the intolerable pressure of a life or death situation, clearly passed on to her daughter.

"I was 15, I was on a family holiday in Thailand and we were out surfing with my friends and I actually noticed that this man was struggling in the water," Massie says.

"My mum signalled me from the beach saying he's in trouble and my friend and I went over and helped him and we saved his life that day."

Competing is serious for Tiarnee Massie, but so too is the bigger picture of saving lives. (Getty Images: Matt Roberts)

The magnitude of that moment may have passed the then-teenage Massie by somewhat: "I was so young that I actually didn't understand the importance of what I did, I was just doing what I was trained to do," Massie says.

"I was doing what I knew how to do, I was in the ocean, I understand the ocean and I didn't understand that he couldn't."

The enormity soon struck home when the man she saved wrote her a letter.

"Later on he wrote a letter to myself and my friend, Grace, saying how grateful he was for us saving his life and that we have changed his life forever and all of this incredible stuff," she says.

"It was from that moment on that I realised how important the work that we were doing is.

"You know, I may be training to be the best ironwoman in the ocean, but most importantly, I'm training to be the best person to save a life on the beach.

"I think that is so rare in sport and that is such a special gift that we have as surf lifesavers. We are literally training to save someone's life."

Tiarnee Massie (right) will lock horns with number two seed Lily O'Sullivan (left) in the Iron Series. (Supplied)

Massie will start the defence of her title at the Coolangatta Gold, an event she came into as favourite last year, only to suffer the heartache of a broken paddle on the ski leg.

Despite that disappointment, Massey was still able to claim the series title.

Now she looks forward to honouring that yellow jersey over the course of the Iron Series, with events taking place in Coolangatta, Thirroul, Newcastle and the season final at Surfers Paradise on February 7.

"I feel so honoured to be wearing the yellow jersey this season," Massie says.

"I have looked up to every woman and man before me who has worn this jersey and to be actually in those yellow togs with the number one on them is such an honour.

"I'm just so grateful, I did all the hard yards as a young girl and stuck it out through the highs and lows of sport and all the triumphs and failures and I finally got to achieve my dream of becoming the Iron Series champion."

World.title: England drop fast bowler Carse after nightclub incident
World.content:
England fast bowler Brydon Carse has been dropped from the squad for the second Test against Pakistan following an investigation into an incident at a club in Derby, the England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) says.

"Following a referral from the ECB, the Cricket Regulator has confirmed that they will investigate events on Saturday night in Derby," the ECB said in a statement.

Bazball's complex legacy Brendon McCullum deliberately set out to make England's men's Test team a less complicated team to play cricket for. After four years of Bazball's highs and lows, it leaves a very complicated legacy.

"Brydon Carse will no longer be available for selection for the second men's Test while this investigation is ongoing and the full facts are obtained."

Carse, who did not play in the opening Test victory at Headingley, will be replaced by Sonny Baker.

Videos circulated on social media appearing to show the 31-year-old Durham bowler in handcuffs being spoken to by police officers outside a venue.

According to reports, Carse was not arrested, and no charges were brought.

BBC reported that Derbyshire Police confirmed a man in his 30s was arrested, but then de-arrested shortly afterwards.

"A man in his 30s was arrested on suspicion of being drunk and disorderly in Derby city centre on Saturday night, 22 August," a police statement said, according to the BBC.

"However, the man was de-arrested shortly afterwards, having agreed to leave the area."

It has been a busy summer for England's Cricket Regulator, the body set up to investigate alleged breaches of the ECB's code of conduct.

In June it concluded an investigation into former Test captain Ben Stokes and fast bowler Gus Atkinson after a nightclub incident following the first Test against New Zealand.

Both were left out of the second Test before the regulator ruled that there was insufficient evidence to establish that any regulatory breach occurred.

The latest investigation came less than a week after England's returning Test captain, Joe Root, spoke of the players being "really good role models and human beings" following a series of incidents and accusations of a drinking culture.

Controversy has followed England in recent times, with off-field issues during last winter's tours, including Harry Brook being fined £30,000 ($57,200) following an altercation in Wellington, as well as reports of drinking during a mid-Ashes series trip to Noosa.

Stokes eventually announced his retirement from international cricket while Brendon McCullum was sacked as Test coach, with Root confirming that the team had done away with the curfews under new coach Stephen Fleming.

Reuters

Tech.title: Lenovo confirms Legion Go issues after gamers report bricked devices
Tech.content:
Lenovo is aware that some Legion Go devices may experience a blank screen during installation of BIOS version V42. BIOS V42 was not distributed through Windows Update or Legion Space, and Lenovo has removed the update from its support website while we continue our validation work. Users who have successfully completed the V42 update should not need to take further action at this time.

If a device encounters a blank screen during V42 installation, users may try pressing and holding the power button for approximately 10 seconds, waiting approximately one minute, and then powering the device on again. If the device does not resume normal operation, customers should contact Lenovo Support for further assistance.

Lenovo continues to evaluate and validate future BIOS updates for Legion Go.

Tech.title: The cat-and-mouse game over 3D-printed guns has begun
Tech.content:
The creator of the world’s first 3D-printed gun claims he’s developed a way to thwart government-mandated software meant to block 3D printers from making firearms. It’s an opening volley in what’s shaping up to be an evolving battle between regulators trying to stem the tide of ghost guns and individuals trying to create workarounds.

Cody Wilson, who claims to have made the detection-defying tool, is calling it “Hochulization” as a direct jab at New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, who pushed through the nation’s first law mandating gun file detection software on new printers earlier this year. “New York is trying to reach into the internet and police how open-source 3D printing is done,” Wilson, who’s based out of Austin, Texas, told The Verge. “I think of it as a self-defense measure.”

The tool is designed to break a relatively simple approach to a 3D-printed gun ban. Wilson’s company, Defense Distributed, runs DEFCAD, the world’s largest 3D gun file repository, which he says hosts over 200,000 files of gun designs and components, such as suppressors. Each of those files can be identified by a hash, a unique string of numbers that’s created by running the file through an algorithm. In theory, a gun file detection system that uses a hashing-based identification method would look for those exact hashes to determine whether a file is a potential gun, flag it, and prevent it from printing.

Hochulization mucks up that process by automatically changing those hashes. It adds a series of bytes to each file that changes the hash without altering the function of the end product. A 3D-printed suppressor or gun, in other words, would still work as intended. “Hochulizaiton is a de minimis policy to change the hash of every file that gets created and downloaded to where there is never going to be a complete library of hashes,” Wilson says.

Wilson says he wants to apply the Hochulization treatment to all files hosted on DEFCAD by default as a means of “self-defense” against growing calls for gun detection software, which he describes as invasive digital surveillance. Wilson says he will make the tool available to DEFCAD users, though he says he also intends to make it open source, which would let an individual user with a gun file apply the tool to scramble the hash and potentially sidestep detection.

Image: Cody Wilson

“I think all the files in the repository, the 3D files anyway, should be Hochulized,” he adds. “And so that is what we’ll do.” He claims he has begun this process.

Wilson’s approach is an early indicator of the resistance to 3D-print-blocking tech. In this case, the momentum is coming from a Second Amendment advocate, but that might not always be the case. Groups of makers, digital rights experts, and members of the entertainment industry who aren’t focused on guns have all spoken out against the tech, expressing fears that requiring file scanning on printers introduces a new level of digital surveillance into the process that could limit what everyone can create.

3D-printed firearms are growing in number but remain an evolving public threat. In 2021, the New York Police Department confiscated just one 3D-printed gun. That jumped to 109 in 2024. Prominent gun policy group Everytown found similar upticks across 20 other cities. Still, when compared with the percentage of conventional firearms confiscated around the country, 3D-printed models remain comparatively small. The total number of firearms in the US has been estimated to outnumber people.

Policymakers and gun control advocates argue cases like this demonstrate a glaring gap in the legal system. People with prior felony convictions and others who aren’t legally allowed to own guns can do so anyway with the help of a 3D printer. And while many states regulate the making and selling of so-called “ghost guns,” actually enforcing those laws is notoriously difficult. This new approach, which requires 3D printers to install mandatory file-blocking software, attempts to close that gap by stopping a print before it ever starts. Industry experts are still debating whether that’s technically feasible at scale. Gov.
